entries.name: checksum
doc: Computes the RFC 1950 Adler-32 checksum of `bytes`.

entries.name: checksumText
doc: Computes the Adler-32 checksum directly over a UTF-8 text string.

entries.name: combine
doc: Combines two adjacent Adler-32 checksums into the checksum of their concatenation.

entries.name: roll
doc: Performs an O(1) rolling update over a sliding window of size `length`.

entries.name: update
doc: Updates an existing Adler-32 checksum with additional bytes.

entries.name: App
doc: The program: what it is called, what it was told, what it serves, what has
to be running before it serves it, and what is wrapped around every handler.
The steps are part of the application rather than left to each program,
because the protections they carry are the ones a service should have
before anybody has thought about them. A program that needs them different
says so, and that is a line in its source rather than the absence of one.

entries.name: AppError
doc: Why a program could not run.

entries.name: configOf
doc: What the application was told.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says.

entries.name: explainReport
doc: What went wrong, as text.

entries.name: LifecycleReport
doc: Successful callbacks and every typed failure, in occurrence order.

entries.name: measuring
doc: The application measuring its own traffic into a cell the program holds,
and answering with what it has measured where the program says.
The cell is the program's because the measurements are: nothing here is
global, so two evaluations do not share counts and a test does not inherit
another's. The route is written rather than mounted automatically, for the
same reason a health report is.

entries.name: nameOf
doc: What the application is called.

entries.name: once
doc: A stage that has something to start and nothing to undo.

entries.name: over
doc: An application over settings the caller already has, for a program whose
configuration comes from somewhere this module does not know about.

entries.name: Report
doc: What a start or a stop did.
The stages that came up are named, not just counted, because the caller of
a failed start needs to know how far it got, and because a stop reports the
same shape so the two can be compared.

entries.name: reporting
doc: The application answering what it is asked about itself.
Mounted where the program says rather than at a path this module chose: an
endpoint that appears without being written is one nobody decided to
expose, and the same mechanism that publishes a health report publishes an
environment dump beside it.

entries.name: requestMeasurements
doc: Measurements a service takes of itself, declared and ready to be added to.
Declared here rather than left to each program because a service that
reports nothing about its own traffic is the ordinary failure, and the two
measurements every service wants are the same two.

entries.name: routerOf
doc: What the application serves.

entries.name: run
doc: Start everything, serve until the work is finished, then stop everything.
Stopping happens whether the serving succeeded or not, because the reason a
program stopped serving is never a reason to leave its pool open.

entries.name: serve
doc: A name and a router, and a service is running.
Configuration is found, the routes are served, and stopping is graceful.
This is the whole of what a first program needs, and it is built from the
public functions below it, so a program that outgrows it adds a stage
rather than starting again.

entries.name: serving
doc: An application with different routes.

entries.name: sharing
doc: The application, permitting the named origins to read its answers.

entries.name: stage
entries.signature: Str -> fn() -> Result[(), Str] -> fn() -> Result[(), Str] -> Std.App.Stage.Stage
doc: A stage from its two halves.

entries.name: Stage
doc: One thing that starts and later stops.
A stage holds both halves because they belong together: the thing that
knows how to open a pool is the thing that knows how to close it, and
separating them into two lists is how the halves come to disagree about
what exists.

entries.name: stageNames
doc: The names of the stages, in start order, for a program reporting itself.

entries.name: stagesOf
doc: What has to be running before it serves, in the order it starts.

entries.name: start
doc: Start every stage in order.
A stage that fails stops every stage already started, in reverse, before
answering. A caller told that a start failed will not then be told to clean
up after it, so the cleanup happens here or it does not happen.

entries.name: startDetailed
doc: Start in declaration order and retain failures from unwinding the started prefix.

entries.name: steppedBy
doc: The application with steps a program chose instead of the usual ones.
Named so that a service without the ordinary protections is a line
somebody wrote rather than a line nobody wrote — which is the same reason
a route states what it requires.

entries.name: stepsOf
doc: The steps wrapped around this application's handlers.

entries.name: stop
doc: Stop every stage in reverse and summarize all failures.

entries.name: stopDetailed
doc: Stop every stage in reverse, retaining each failure separately.

entries.name: succeeded
doc: Whether a report says everything worked.

entries.name: using
doc: An application with one more thing to start.
Order is the order written. Nothing infers it from what a stage needs,
because an inferred order cannot be read off the page and needs a second
mechanism to correct it in the cases that matter.

entries.name: web
doc: The same application, built and not run.
Worth having separately because an application is a value: a test builds
one, reads its routes and its settings, and never binds a port.

entries.name: wrapping
doc: The application with one more step around every handler, outside the ones
already there.

entries.name: anonymous
doc: Nobody in particular.

entries.name: attributeOf
doc: What is known about a principal under a name.

entries.name: decide
doc: What a requirement decides about a principal.
A pure function, so a program's authorisation can be checked by comparing
values and every branch reached without a request.

entries.name: Decision
doc: What a requirement decided.
Not knowing who is asking and not being allowed are different answers: one
the caller can fix and one they cannot, and answering the second as the
first sends them round a login loop that cannot succeed.

entries.name: describe
doc: What a requirement is, as text.

entries.name: get
doc: A route that requires something, for each method.
The requirement and the handler are given together, so there is no state in
which a route exists without one.

entries.name: Guarded
doc: A route that stated what it requires.
There is no other kind. A route with no requirement and a route needing
none are indistinguishable in source, and the first is invisible until it
is exploited — so the requirement is in the same call as the handler and
there is no way to leave it out.

entries.name: holds
doc: Whether a principal holds a role.

entries.name: knowing
doc: The same principal with one more thing known about them.

entries.name: on
entries.signature: Std.Http.Method -> Str -> Std.App.Access.Requirement -> fn(Std.Http.Server.Route.Request) -> Std.Http.Response -> Std.App.Access.Guarded
doc: A route requiring something, for a method this module does not name.

entries.name: openRoutes
doc: The routes anyone may reach.
Worth asking directly, because this is the list a review actually wants and
the one that is otherwise assembled by hand and incompletely.

entries.name: patch
doc: A route answering PATCH, allowed only when the requirement is met.

entries.name: permits
doc: Whether a decision permits.

entries.name: post
doc: A route answering POST, allowed only when the requirement is met.

entries.name: principal
doc: Somebody, identified.

entries.name: Principal
doc: Who is asking.
Assembled by whatever established the identity, not here. This module
decides given who someone is; proving who they are has its own failure
modes, and folding the two together is how a decision ends up trusting an
identity nobody proved.

entries.name: put
doc: A route answering PUT, allowed only when the requirement is met.

entries.name: query
doc: A route answering QUERY, allowed only when the requirement is met.

entries.name: reasonOf
doc: Why a decision refused, for a log rather than for a caller.

entries.name: refusal
doc: What a denied caller receives.

entries.name: remove
doc: A route answering DELETE, allowed only when the requirement is met.

entries.name: Requirement
doc: What a route requires.
A value, so a program's whole authorisation model can be listed and
compared without a request — including the check that matters most, which
is asking what every route requires and reading the answer.

entries.name: requirements
doc: What every route requires, in the order the routes were given.
The point of the whole module: a program can ask what it protects and read
the answer, rather than reading every handler to find out.

entries.name: routing
doc: A router over routes that all stated what they require.
The principal is read from each request by the function given here, so
establishing who is asking stays one decision made in one place rather than
something every handler repeats differently.

entries.name: statusOf
doc: The status a decision answers with.
The two refusals are different statuses because they are different
answers: the first says identify yourself, the second says you have and it
is not enough.

entries.name: AuditEvent
doc: An immutable, tamper-evident security audit record.

entries.name: auditLog
doc: Initialize a fresh in-memory audit ledger.

entries.name: AuditLog
doc: A thread-safe, append-only security audit ledger maintaining an unbroken SHA-256 hash chain.

entries.name: count
doc: Total count of recorded audit events.

entries.name: events
doc: Retrieve a snapshot copy of all recorded events.

entries.name: GENESIS_HASH
doc: The standard 64-hex-character genesis digest anchoring the audit chain.

entries.name: headHash
doc: Current head hash of the ledger.

entries.name: Outcome
doc: The outcome of an audited security action.

entries.name: record
entries.signature: &Std.App.Audit.AuditLog -> Str -> Str -> Str -> Std.App.Audit.Outcome -> Str -> &Map[Str, Str] -> Std.App.Audit.AuditEvent
doc: Record an audit event into the append-only ledger with cryptographic hash chaining.

entries.name: redactSensitive
doc: Redact sensitive credential keys to prevent secret leaks into audit trails.

entries.name: renderJson
doc: Serialize an individual audit event to canonical single-line JSON.

entries.name: renderNdjson
doc: Serialize all events in the ledger to newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON).

entries.name: verifyIntegrity
doc: Verify the entire cryptographic hash chain from genesis to head.
Returns false if any audit record was altered, deleted, or reordered.

entries.name: bind
doc: What a request carried, checked against what was wanted.
Reading and checking are one step, and every field that was wrong is in the
report rather than only the first: a caller correcting a request wants the
whole list.

entries.name: binding
doc: The bound values, or the refusal, in one step for the common handler.

entries.name: bound
doc: Whether everything wanted was there and was what it had to be.

entries.name: Bound
doc: What a request carried, once it has been read and checked.

entries.name: carriesDocument
doc: Whether a request carries a document.

entries.name: carriesForm
doc: Whether a request carries a form.

entries.name: count
doc: One bound field as a count, which may not.

entries.name: fromDocument
doc: A field read from a document body.

entries.name: fromForm
doc: A field read from a form body.

entries.name: fromPath
doc: A field read from the path.

entries.name: fromQuery
doc: A field read from the query.

entries.name: malformed
doc: The refusal a request of the wrong shape entirely receives.
Separate from the one above because they are different problems: this one
says the request was not the shape this resource reads, and no correction
to the fields would help.

entries.name: mediaType
doc: The media type a request states, without whatever follows it.

entries.name: optional
doc: One bound field, absent when it carried nothing.

entries.name: refusal
doc: The refusal a failed binding becomes.
The status says which kind of problem it was, and the body names the fields
and what each had to be. It names no values: the sender knows what they
sent, and a response is a place something they sent would be rendered.

entries.name: reportOf
doc: What was wrong, if anything.

entries.name: Source
doc: Where a field is read from.
Stated rather than searched for. A binding that looks in the path, then the
query, then the body and takes the first hit lets a caller move a value
between places to reach a different code path, and makes a handler's
behaviour depend on an order nobody wrote down.

entries.name: text
doc: One bound field as text.

entries.name: truth
doc: One bound field as a truth.

entries.name: Wanted
doc: One field: what it is called, where it comes from, and what it must be.

entries.name: whole
doc: One bound field as a whole number, which may be below nothing.

entries.name: absentLifetimeOf
doc: How long an absence is remembered.

entries.name: Cache
doc: A cache: bounded, with a lifetime for answers and a shorter one for
absences.

entries.name: capacity
doc: How many it may keep.

entries.name: emptied
doc: The cache holding nothing, keeping what it was told about lifetimes.

entries.name: Entry
doc: One thing kept, and when it stops being fresh.

entries.name: forgetting
doc: The cache with one thing forgotten, for when a program knows an answer
changed.

entries.name: Found
doc: What a lookup found.
Three answers rather than two, and that is the whole design. An interface
answering a value or nothing forces a caller to treat an expired entry as
an absent one — so when a much-read key expires, every request that wanted
it finds nothing and every one of them recomputes it at the same moment,
against whatever the cache was protecting. Told the entry is stale, a
caller hands back the old answer and refreshes once.

entries.name: hitRate
doc: How often it answered, as a percentage, counting a stale answer as an
answer — because it was one, and the request it saved is the point.

entries.name: hitsOf
doc: How many lookups were answered without asking anything else.

entries.name: holding
doc: A cache holding at most this many things, each for this long.
The bound is on entries rather than bytes: the size of a value is not
something this can know, and a bound it cannot enforce is a claim rather
than a bound.

entries.name: keeping
entries.signature: &Std.App.Cache.Cache[K, V] -> K -> V -> Int -> Std.App.Cache.Cache[K, V]
doc: The cache with an answer kept.

entries.name: keepingAbsence
doc: The cache remembering that there was no answer.
For less time than a real answer, because being wrong about an absence
costs less, and because a key that does not exist yet is the thing most
likely to start existing.

entries.name: lifetimeOf
doc: How long an answer stays fresh.

entries.name: lookup
doc: What a lookup found, and the cache that follows it.
The cache comes back because looking something up moves it to the front of
what is kept, and because what was asked for is counted.

entries.name: missesOf
doc: How many found nothing at all.

entries.name: peek
doc: What a lookup found, without counting it or moving anything.
For a program reporting on its own cache, which should not change what it
reports on.

entries.name: rememberingAbsence
doc: The same, saying how long an absence is remembered.

entries.name: render
doc: What a cache has been doing.

entries.name: size
doc: How many things are kept.

entries.name: staleHitsOf
doc: How many were answered with something old.

entries.name: usable
doc: Whether a lookup found something usable, fresh or not.

entries.name: valueOf
doc: What was found, when something was.

entries.name: worthRefreshing
doc: Whether what was found should be replaced.

entries.name: activeProfile
doc: The profile this invocation asked for, from the argument first and the
machine second, or none.
Read before the document rather than from it, because it decides which of
the document's sections applies and cannot be inside the thing it selects.

entries.name: Config
doc: Everything the program was told, and which profile selected it.
A default is held in the same table as everything else rather than applied
after a lookup failed. A default applied afterwards is invisible: nothing
can list it, report it, or say where it came from, so a program cannot show
its own configuration.

entries.name: ConfigError
doc: Why a setting could not be used.
A failure names the key, the layer, and the text, because a program that
stops over one setting has told the operator almost nothing if it only says
that a setting was wrong.

entries.name: declaring
doc: A configuration from declared defaults alone.
The starting point for a program that reads nothing from outside itself,
and the first layer of every program that does.

entries.name: discover
doc: The configuration a program gets when it does not say otherwise: its own
declared defaults, the named file, the machine, and this invocation, in
that order, with the profile selected by an argument or the environment.
This is the whole of what most programs want from configuration, and it is
one call so that they can have it in one call. Everything it does is a
public function below it, so a program needing a different arrangement
writes that arrangement rather than working around this one.

entries.name: empty
doc: An empty configuration, holding nothing and naming no profile.

entries.name: entries
doc: Everything the program was told, in key order, for a program that reports
its own configuration.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says, for a program reporting why it will not start.

entries.name: fractional
doc: A setting as an exact fractional number.

entries.name: Layering
doc: A configuration with one more layer written over it, each answering the
configuration rather than taking it apart.
Methods, so the layers read down the page in the order they are applied —
which is the order that decides which one wins. As functions taking the
configuration first, the layers had to be written wrapped in one another
and the last one applied appeared first on the page, which is exactly
backwards from how they are read.

entries.name: layerOrder
doc: The layers, in the order they apply, so a program can report the rule
rather than restate it.

entries.name: list
doc: A setting as a list, written separated by commas.

entries.name: profileOf
doc: Which profile is active.

entries.name: require
doc: A setting that must be there, for one the program cannot invent.
A database password has no sensible default, and a program that started
with an invented one would fail later and further away.

entries.name: Setting
doc: A setting, and the layer that supplied it.

entries.name: Source
doc: Where a setting came from.
Kept beside the value rather than discarded, because a program refused over
a setting should be able to say which of four places supplied it. Without
this, the answer to "why is the port 9000" is a search.

entries.name: sourceName
doc: The name of the layer, for a report.

entries.name: sourceOf
doc: Which layer supplied a setting.

entries.name: text
doc: A setting as text.

entries.name: textOr
doc: A setting as text, or a fallback when it is absent.
A fallback is for a caller that has one at the point of reading; a value
every caller shares belongs in the declared layer, where it can be seen.

entries.name: truth
doc: A setting as a truth.
The spellings accepted are the ones a configuration file is actually
written with. A value outside them is refused rather than read as false,
because a setting spelled `yes` that silently means no is worse than one
that stops the program.

entries.name: truthOr
doc: A setting as a truth, or a fallback.

entries.name: whole
doc: A setting as a whole number.

entries.name: wholeOr
doc: A setting as a whole number, or a fallback.

entries.name: bundledDrivers
doc: Built-in connectors remain ordinary values that applications can extend.

entries.name: create
doc: Select a bundled connector from the connection-string scheme.

entries.name: Database
doc: A backend-neutral resource shared by lifecycle callbacks and handlers.

entries.name: execute
doc: Run a statement that carries no values.

entries.name: fromConfig
doc: Prepare a database from the connection string a setting names.

entries.name: fromConfigWith
doc: Prepare a database from a setting, using the given driver.

entries.name: query
doc: SQL and placeholders follow the selected driver; values are always separate.

entries.name: queryAll
entries.signature: &Std.App.Database.Database -> Str -> &Array[Std.Db.Driver.Value] -> fn(Std.Db.Driver.Rows, Int) -> Result[T, Std.Db.Row.RowError] -> Result[Array[T], Std.App.Database.QueryError]
doc: Every row a query answered, each read by the mapper.

entries.name: QueryError
doc: Preserve the distinction between database execution and application row decoding.

entries.name: queryOne
entries.signature: &Std.App.Database.Database -> Str -> &Array[Std.Db.Driver.Value] -> fn(Std.Db.Driver.Rows, Int) -> Result[T, Std.Db.Row.RowError] -> Result[T, Std.App.Database.QueryError]
doc: The single row a query answered, or an error when it answered none or several.

entries.name: queryOptional
entries.signature: &Std.App.Database.Database -> Str -> &Array[Std.Db.Driver.Value] -> fn(Std.Db.Driver.Rows, Int) -> Result[T, Std.Db.Row.RowError] -> Result[Option[T], Std.App.Database.QueryError]
doc: The one row a query answered, or nothing.

entries.name: stage
doc: Add before stages that need the database; stage order determines dependency order.

entries.name: start
doc: Open the connections. Called by the stage rather than by a caller.

entries.name: stop
doc: Clear admission before closing; repeated stops are harmless.

entries.name: transaction
doc: The selected driver owns the connection for the complete action.

entries.name: withDriver
doc: Prepare any developer-supplied connector; sockets open during stage startup.

entries.name: withDrivers
doc: Select a connector from an explicit set, without a process-global registry.

entries.name: context
doc: Constructs an evaluation context.

entries.name: Context
doc: Context carrying subject and tenant identifiers for evaluation.

entries.name: flag
doc: Constructs a feature flag.

entries.name: Flag
doc: A named feature flag with its targeting strategy.

entries.name: isEnabled
doc: Evaluates whether a flag is enabled for the provided context.

entries.name: Strategy
doc: Activation strategies for feature flags.

entries.name: alive
doc: Whether this process should still be running.
Every check sees the same reading, so two checks cannot disagree about what
the process looked like at the moment they were asked.

entries.name: counting
doc: A reading with one more count.

entries.name: countOf
doc: A count the reading holds, or zero.
Declared comptime because a liveness judgement is, and a compile-time body
may only call compile-time functions — which is what makes that guarantee
transitive rather than a promise each function makes about itself.

entries.name: detailed
doc: A finding with something said about it, for a check that knows more than
its verdict.

entries.name: Finding
doc: One check's answer.

entries.name: flagging
doc: A reading with one more flag.

entries.name: flagOf
doc: A flag the reading holds, or false.

entries.name: fromTruth
doc: A verdict from a truth, for the many checks that are one.

entries.name: healthy
doc: Whether a report says everything is fine.

entries.name: liveness
doc: A liveness check.

entries.name: Liveness
doc: Whether this process should still be running.
The judgement takes a reading and answers. It is given nothing that reaches
outside the process, because a database being unreachable is not a reason
to kill a healthy program — a liveness check that consults one turns a
dependency's outage into every instance restarting at once.
Declare the judgement `comptime` and the language refuses a body that
reaches a clock, a socket, or a file, which turns the rule from a note in
review into a compile error.

entries.name: nothingToCheck
doc: A report with no checks in it, which is well: a program that declared
nothing has nothing wrong with it.

entries.name: readiness
doc: A readiness check.

entries.name: Readiness
doc: Whether this process should receive traffic.
This one may consult whatever it needs. Removing an instance from rotation
is cheap and reversible, which is what makes the different rule correct
rather than merely different.

entries.name: reading
doc: A reading with nothing in it.

entries.name: Reading
doc: What the program can see about itself.
A liveness judgement is given one of these rather than a connection, so it
has nothing to reach with. What a program puts in it is its own — a count
of workers, a queue depth, a flag set when something went irrecoverably
wrong — and every one of those is a value the process already holds.

entries.name: ready
doc: Whether this process should receive traffic.

entries.name: render
doc: A report as text, one check to a line, worst first so an operator reading a
truncated report sees the part that matters.

entries.name: Report
doc: What a set of checks reached.

entries.name: reporting
doc: A report from findings a caller assembled, for a program that gathered them
somewhere this module does not know about.

entries.name: statusOf
doc: The status a report answers with.

entries.name: Verdict
doc: How something is.
Ordered from best to worst, so the worst of a set is the one that survives
a comparison and an aggregate needs no ordering to configure.

entries.name: verdictName
doc: What a verdict is called.

entries.name: worstOf
doc: The worst of a set.
An aggregate is as healthy as its unhealthiest part. Every other rule is a
way of arranging for a failure not to count, and the failure still
happened.

entries.name: CacheEntry
doc: One cached rendered response.

entries.name: CacheLookup
doc: The result of an ISR cache lookup.

entries.name: CacheState
doc: Internal state tracked within the synchronized cell.

entries.name: create
doc: Creates a new thread-safe ISR cache with bounded capacity.

entries.name: get
doc: Looks up an entry by key, returning Fresh, Stale, or Miss.

entries.name: IsrCache
doc: A thread-safe, zero-copy Incremental Static Regeneration cache.

entries.name: purgeKey
doc: Evicts an entry by key.

entries.name: purgeTag
doc: Evicts all entries bearing the specified tag immediately from cache.

entries.name: put
doc: Stores or replaces an entry with lifetime and stale-while-revalidate duration.

entries.name: revalidateTag
doc: Marks all entries with the matching tag as stale (expired).
Subsequent lookups return `Stale`, allowing immediate serving while triggering revalidation.

entries.name: stats
doc: Returns (currentEntries, freshHits, staleHits, misses).

entries.name: Checking
doc: A check with one expectation set, each answering the check rather than
taking it apart.

entries.name: Claiming
doc: Claims with one field set, each answering the claims rather than taking
them apart.
Methods, so a token's claims are written down the page in the order they
are decided. As functions taking the claims first, a token setting five of
them had five calls wrapped in one another and the claims a reader looks
for first ended up furthest in.

entries.name: claims
doc: Constructs an empty set of JWT claims.

entries.name: decode
doc: Decodes and cryptographically verifies an RFC 7519 compact JWT against secret and validation rules.

entries.name: decodeUnverified
doc: Decodes claims without cryptographic signature verification.

entries.name: decodeWithKey
doc: Verify a token signed with a provider's private key, and read its claims.
This is the direction a service that trusts an identity provider needs, and
the only one it needs: the provider signs, the service checks. Nothing here
can produce a token, which is the point of using a key pair rather than a
shared secret — a service that could sign could impersonate the provider.
The algorithm is taken from the key rather than from the token. A token
naming its own algorithm and being checked with it is the oldest hole in
this format: an attacker changes `RS256` to `HS256`, signs with the public
key as though it were a shared secret, and the token verifies. Here a
header that does not name the key's own algorithm is refused before
anything is computed.

entries.name: encode
doc: Serializes and signs claims into an RFC 7519 HS256 compact JSON Web Token.

entries.name: getClaim
doc: Retrieves a claim by name from registered or custom claims.

entries.name: hasExpired
doc: Checks whether claims indicate the token has expired relative to a timestamp and leeway.

entries.name: isValidAt
doc: Checks whether claims are active and valid (neither premature nor expired).

entries.name: JwtClaims
doc: Standard claims contained within an RFC 7519 JSON Web Token.

entries.name: JwtError
doc: Structured failure conditions encountered while decoding or validating a JWT.

entries.name: JwtValidation
doc: Validation parameters applied during JWT signature and claims checking.

entries.name: keyAlgorithm
doc: The algorithm name that appears in a token's header for this key.

entries.name: keyFor
doc: Pick the key a token names, out of the set a provider published.

entries.name: keyId
doc: The identifier a provider gave this key.

entries.name: PublicKey
doc: A public key an identity provider publishes, and the algorithm it signs with.
A provider publishes its keys as numbers rather than as a file: a JWKS
carries an RSA key as a modulus and an exponent, and a curve key as the two
coordinates of a point, each base64url. So that is what this takes.
A key is named by `kid` because a provider holds several and rotates them;
a token says in its header which one signed it, and checking the wrong one
fails in a way that looks exactly like a forgery.

entries.name: tokenKeyId
doc: Which of a provider's keys a token says signed it.
Read before verifying, so a caller holding several keys picks the one to
check against. A token that names no key answers nothing, and a caller must
then decide for itself rather than being given a guess.

entries.name: validation
doc: Constructs default validation rules with zero leeway and no mandatory issuer or audience.

entries.name: about
doc: What a program says for a key about a number of things.

entries.name: catalogue
doc: A catalogue written in one language.

entries.name: Catalogue
doc: What a program can say, in each language it says it.
`reference` is the language the messages were written in, which is what a
missing translation is reported against.

entries.name: complete
doc: Whether a language says everything the reference does.

entries.name: fallbacks
doc: The locales to try, in order: the one asked for, the language without its
place, and then the one the messages were written in.

entries.name: fill
doc: A message's parts filled in.
A part is written between percent signs — `Welcome, %name%` — rather than
between braces. Braces are how this language writes a value into a string,
so a catalogue using them would need every message escaped, and a catalogue
is edited by people who are translating rather than programming. The
delimiter that costs them nothing is the one to use.

entries.name: filled
doc: The same, with the parts it leaves open filled in.
What comes out is text and stays text. A message that could carry markup is
whoever edits the catalogue writing into every page that shows it.

entries.name: keys
doc: The keys the reference language names.

entries.name: language
doc: A locale with no place.

entries.name: languages
doc: The languages a catalogue says anything in.

entries.name: locale
doc: A locale from its parts.

entries.name: Locale
doc: A language, and the place where that matters.
The place is kept apart from the language rather than folded into one name,
because falling back from one region's Spanish to Spanish is a different
step from falling back to the language a program was written in.

entries.name: missing
doc: The keys one language is missing against the one the messages were written
in.
The whole reason falling back is tolerable: a gap can be found by a build
rather than by a reader.

entries.name: negotiate
doc: The locale a request asked for, chosen from the ones a program has.
The request states several in order of preference with weights. Choosing
the first that happens to match ignores what the reader said; the best
available by weight is what they asked for.

entries.name: parse
doc: A locale read from how one is written, as `en`, `en-GB`, or `en_GB`.

entries.name: placed
doc: Whether a locale names a place.

entries.name: Quantity
doc: How many of something a message is about.
The categories a language actually has, rather than the two English has. A
translator given only a singular and a plural cannot write correct Polish,
and asking for those two has decided the translator is wrong.

entries.name: quantityFor
doc: Which form a language uses for a number.
The rule each language actually has, rather than a comparison with one.

entries.name: render
doc: How a locale is written.

entries.name: Saying
doc: What a catalogue can say, written one message at a time.
A catalogue is every message a program has, which is as many calls as there
are things it says. As methods they read as the list of messages they are;
as functions each call wrapped the one before it, so a catalogue of ten
messages was ten levels deep and the first message written was the last one
a reader reached.

entries.name: says
doc: Whether a language says anything at all for a key.

entries.name: text
doc: What a program says for a key, in the language it can.
Falls back through the language without its place to the one the messages
were written in. A key nothing says is answered as the key itself, which is
visible in a page rather than a blank — and `missing` is how it is found
before a reader finds it.

entries.name: withoutPlace
doc: The same language without its place, which is the first thing to fall back
to.

entries.name: countAt
doc: How many observations fell at or below one boundary.

entries.name: declarationOf
doc: What a metric was declared as.

entries.name: Declared
doc: What a metric is, apart from its values.

entries.name: Declared
doc: What a metric is, apart from its values.

entries.name: Declaring
doc: What a program measures, declared one metric at a time.
A program declares every metric it has in one place, which is several calls
over the same registry. As methods they read down the page as a list of what
is measured; as functions each call wrapped the one before it, so the
registry a reader looks for first ended up furthest in and the metric
declared first read as the last thing on the page.

entries.name: empty
doc: Nothing measured yet.

entries.name: Kind
doc: What a measurement is.
A counter only rises, so a fall in one means the process restarted, and
everything reading it is entitled to assume that. A gauge moves either way.
A distribution answers how many observations fell at or below each stated
boundary.

entries.name: Metrics
doc: Everything a program reports about itself.
Declarations are held in a map for lookup and an array for the order they
were declared in, because both questions are asked: rendering walks them in
order, and every measurement looks one up. A single array answers the first
and makes the second a scan of every metric the program has, on every
count — which is the one operation a busy program does most.
Series are keyed by their labels rather than held in a list, for the same
reason and more sharply: a metric broken down by route and method has as
many series as the product of those, and finding one by comparing label
lists reads every series to find one.

entries.name: names
doc: The names of everything declared, in the order it was declared.

entries.name: Recording
doc: What a program measured, recorded one value at a time.
A request records several things about itself, and as methods they read in
the order they are measured rather than inside out. Every one of these
answers a whole registry, so the value recorded last is the outermost call
when they are written as functions — which is the reverse of the order the
program measured them in.
A metric nothing declared is not measured and is not an error: a module
reporting something the program did not declare should not be able to stop
it, and the absence is visible in what is rendered.

entries.name: refusedCount
doc: How many measurements were refused for exceeding a metric's bound.
Counted rather than discarded silently, because a program whose labels are
wrong should be able to see that they are without waiting for the collector
to fail.

entries.name: render
doc: The measurements in the text form a collector reads.

entries.name: Series
doc: One labelled series of one metric.

entries.name: seriesCount
doc: How many label combinations one metric currently has.

entries.name: totalOf
doc: Everything a distribution's observations added up to.

entries.name: Unit
doc: What a measurement is in.
Declared with the metric rather than left to its name. The commonest
failure with measurements is not a wrong number but a right one in a unit
nobody wrote down, found during an incident when two dashboards disagree.

entries.name: valueOf
doc: What a series holds, or nothing when it was never measured.

entries.name: valueOr
doc: What a series holds, or zero.

entries.name: Configuring
doc: Where an exporter sends, what it carries, and how long it may take.
Wiring a collector up means saying two or three of these at once, and as
methods they read down the page in the order they are decided: the address
first, then what travels with every export, then how long to wait.

entries.name: document
doc: The document a collector is sent.
Built and answered rather than only sent, because the first thing anyone
debugging a trace pipeline wants is to see exactly what was going to be
sent — and because a service that writes its spans to a file instead of a
collector needs the same document.

entries.name: explain
doc: Why an export failed, written for a person to read.

entries.name: exportable
doc: The spans that have finished, which are the ones worth sending.

entries.name: exporter
doc: An exporter pointed at a collector running beside the service.
The default endpoint is the one the specification names, so a collector run
with its own defaults needs nothing said about it here.

entries.name: Exporter
doc: Where finished spans are sent, and what to call the service that made them.
A trace is only worth recording if somebody can read it, and nothing in
`Std.App.Trace` sends one anywhere: it decides what a span is and how a
trace travels between services, which is the hard half, and leaves the
spans in the program that made them.
This is the other half. Spans are sent to a collector in the format every
collector accepts, so what receives them is a choice made in a
configuration file rather than in the program: an OpenTelemetry collector,
or anything that has agreed to look like one.
JSON over HTTP rather than protocol buffers over gRPC. Both are defined by
the same specification and every collector reads both; the difference is
that one of them can be read by a person looking at a request, which
matters far more while a service is being wired up than the bytes it saves
afterwards.

entries.name: ExportError
doc: Why an export did not arrive.

entries.name: render
doc: The document as the text that goes on the wire.

entries.name: send
doc: Send finished spans to the collector.
Spans that have not finished are left out rather than sent with an ending
they do not have: a span whose end is guessed is worse than a span that is
missing, because it will be read as a measurement.
Answers how many were sent, so a caller can tell an export that carried
nothing from one that carried everything.

entries.name: algorithmOf
doc: Which algorithm made it.

entries.name: currentRounds
doc: How much work a password stored now costs to prove.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says.

entries.name: matches
doc: Whether a password is the one a stored form was made from.
The comparison takes the same time whatever it is given. One that returned
as soon as two bytes differed would take a length of time that says how
much of the digest was right, which is enough to find the rest a byte at a
time.

entries.name: needsRemaking
doc: Whether a stored form was made with weaker settings than are used now.
Asked after a password has been proved, because that is the only moment the
password is in hand to remake it with.

entries.name: parse
doc: A stored form read back from that text.
A form that cannot be read is a failure rather than a form that matches
nothing: a password that silently never verifies looks exactly like a
person who forgot theirs, and the two need different answers.

entries.name: PasswordError
doc: Why a password could not be stored or checked.

entries.name: render
doc: A stored form as one piece of text, for a column or a file.

entries.name: roundsOf
doc: How much work the stored form was made with.

entries.name: store
doc: A password in the form that proves it later without holding it.
Every password gets its own salt from the machine's own entropy. A shared
salt means two people who chose the same password have the same digest,
which turns one guess into a list of accounts.

entries.name: Stored
doc: What a stored form was made with.
Carried with the digest rather than held in a setting, which is the
decision everything else rests on: a work factor kept elsewhere cannot be
raised without invalidating every password already stored, so it is never
raised, and the number chosen at the beginning is the one still in use when
it is no longer enough.

entries.name: storeWith
doc: The same, with the salt and work factor given.
For a program checking that two passwords stored the same way agree, and
for the re-derivation that verifying is. Not for storing a password with a
salt somebody chose.

entries.name: constantTimeEquals
doc: Compares two secrets in constant time to prevent side-channel timing attacks.

entries.name: redact
doc: Returns a redacted placeholder for safe inclusion in logs, traces, and errors.

entries.name: redactKey
doc: Partially masks a secret key for audit trails, revealing at most `visibleSuffix` characters.

entries.name: reveal
doc: Unveils the inner sensitive string for authorized operations.

entries.name: secret
doc: Wraps a plain string as a protected secret.

entries.name: Secret
doc: A sensitive string wrapped in an opaque container to prevent accidental disclosure.

entries.name: anonymous
doc: A session belonging to nobody in particular.
What a visitor gets before they say who they are: somewhere to keep a
basket or a chosen language. It carries no identity, and gaining one is the
thing that issues a new name.

entries.name: boundedBy
doc: Bounds a program chose.

entries.name: bounds
doc: The bounds a session has when nobody chose.

entries.name: Bounds
doc: How long a session may live, and how long it may sit unused.

entries.name: cookieFor
doc: The cookie a session travels in.
Only the name. Secure and unreadable by script, and refused on a request
that came from another site — which is what stops a session being used by a
page the reader did not open.

entries.name: cookieName
doc: What the cookie is called, for a program that writes its own.

entries.name: count
doc: How many sessions are held.

entries.name: endingCookie
doc: The cookie that ends a session in the reader's browser.

entries.name: expiry
doc: Whether a session is still good, and if not, which bound it passed.

entries.name: Expiry
doc: Why a session is no longer good.
The two are separate answers because they mean different things to whoever
is asking: one says the session lived long enough, the other says nobody
has been there.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says.

entries.name: explainExpiry
doc: What an expiry says.

entries.name: find
doc: The session a name refers to, if it is one that is held and still good.
Expiry is asked here rather than left to the caller, because a caller that
forgot would have a session that works forever and nothing would say so.

entries.name: forgetting
doc: The sessions with one forgotten.
What signing out does to the store, since the session that replaced it has
a different name and the old one must stop working.

entries.name: identified
doc: Whether a session belongs to somebody.

entries.name: identityOf
doc: Who it belongs to, or nobody.

entries.name: keeping
doc: The sessions with one more kept.

entries.name: live
doc: Whether a session may still be used.

entries.name: nameFrom
doc: The session name a request carried, if it carried one.

entries.name: nameOf
doc: What the session is called.

entries.name: none
doc: No sessions at all.

entries.name: Session
doc: Somebody remembered between requests.
The name is what travels; everything else stays where the program put it.
A cookie carrying the contents is a session whose contents the holder can
edit.

entries.name: SessionError
doc: Why a session could not be started or continued.

entries.name: Sessions
doc: The sessions a program is holding.

entries.name: signedIn
doc: The session somebody has after signing in.
Always a new name. There is no call that changes who a session belongs to
while keeping the name it had, and that absence is what closes the oldest
attack against sessions: somebody arranges for a victim's browser to hold a
name they already know, waits for the victim to sign in, then presents the
same name. Every defence amounts to issuing a new name at this moment, so
here it is not a step to remember.

entries.name: signedOut
doc: The session somebody has after signing out.
A new name again, so a name seen while signed in is worth nothing
afterwards.

entries.name: started
doc: A session for somebody who has just proved who they are, with nothing
before it.

entries.name: touched
doc: The same session, seen now.
What makes an idle bound measure from the last request rather than the
first. The name does not change, because being used is not a change of
privilege.

entries.name: withoutExpired
doc: The sessions with every expired one forgotten.
Worth doing on a schedule rather than only on lookup: a session nobody
looks up again is one that stays in the store forever, and a store that
only grows is a leak that takes a month to notice.

entries.name: create
entries.signature: Str -> fn() -> Result[(), Str] -> fn() -> Result[(), Str] -> Std.App.Stage.Stage
doc: A stage from its name and the two actions.

entries.name: Stage
doc: A named part of an application's life: how it starts and how it stops.

entries.name: Admission
doc: The result of an admission check for a tenant request.

entries.name: admit
doc: Atomically check admission bounds for an incoming tenant request.

entries.name: enterpriseQuota
doc: Standard quota for enterprise-tier accounts.

entries.name: freeQuota
doc: Standard quota for free-tier accounts: tight concurrency and rate bounds.

entries.name: get
doc: Look up a tenant by ID.

entries.name: guard
entries.signature: &Std.App.Tenant.TenantRegistry -> fn(&Std.Http.Server.Route.Request) -> Option[Str] -> fn(Std.Http.Server.Route.Request, fn(Std.Http.Server.Route.Request) -> Std.Http.Response) -> Std.Http.Response
doc: HTTP middleware enforcing tenant admission, concurrency bounds, and account status.

entries.name: Quota
doc: Resource bounds allocated to a tenant.

entries.name: register
doc: Register a new tenant or update an existing tenant's specification.

entries.name: registry
doc: Initialize an empty synchronized tenant registry.

entries.name: release
doc: Atomically release a concurrent in-flight request slot for a tenant.

entries.name: resolveFromHeader
doc: Tenant resolver extracting tenant identifier from an HTTP header.

entries.name: scopedKey
doc: Construct a tenant-scoped resource key preventing cross-tenant data collisions.

entries.name: setActive
doc: Enable or suspend a tenant account.

entries.name: setQuota
doc: Dynamically update resource quotas for a tenant.

entries.name: standardQuota
doc: Standard quota for standard-tier accounts.

entries.name: tenant
doc: Construct a tenant with default active status.

entries.name: Tenant
doc: A registered tenant with identity, tier, and resource bounds.

entries.name: TenantRegistry
doc: A thread-safe synchronized tenant store coordinating tenant bounds and admission.

entries.name: TenantState
doc: Dynamic runtime state tracking concurrent and rate metrics for a tenant.

entries.name: Tier
doc: Service tier determining default resource quotas.

entries.name: config
doc: Initializes standard TOTP configuration with 6 digits, 30-second interval, and 1-step skew tolerance.

entries.name: Configuring
doc: The three numbers a code's shape is decided by, set one call at a time.
A configuration is built by naming the secret and who it belongs to, and
then saying which of these three differ from the defaults. As methods they
read down the page in the order they are decided, which is also the order an
authenticator app's settings screen lists them.

entries.name: decodeBase32
doc: RFC 4648 Base32 decoder with whitespace stripping and case normalization.

entries.name: encodeBase32
doc: RFC 4648 Base32 encoder converting binary secrets into uppercase strings without padding.

entries.name: generate
doc: Computes the canonical time-based OTP code for the given epoch timestamp using HMAC-SHA256.

entries.name: provisioningUri
doc: Builds the standard otpauth URI for authenticator app enrollment.

entries.name: state
doc: Constructs replay prevention tracking state.

entries.name: TotpConfig
doc: Immutable parameters for RFC 6238 TOTP generation and validation.

entries.name: TotpState
doc: Stateful replay prevention tracking the highest authenticated time counter step.

entries.name: verify
doc: Validates a user-submitted code against all allowed steps in [C - skew, C + skew]
using constant-time string comparison and atomically guards against replay attacks.

entries.name: asHeader
doc: The header as a name and a value, for adding to a request.

entries.name: childOf
doc: A step within the same piece of work, for what this service hands on.
The recording decision is carried rather than retaken.

entries.name: complete
doc: Whether a stretch has finished.

entries.name: continuing
doc: The trace a request carried, or a new one when it carried nothing this can
read.
A header that is nonsense, truncated, or from a version this does not know
is treated as no header at all. Everywhere else here something unreadable
is refused; this is the one place it is not, because a service that fails a
request over a malformed diagnostic has made the diagnosis into the outage.

entries.name: fieldsOf
doc: A span as the fields a log line carries, so one line ties to one trace.

entries.name: finished
doc: The same stretch, finished.

entries.name: headerName
doc: What the header is called, for a program writing its own.

entries.name: isRecorded
doc: Whether it is being recorded.

entries.name: noteOf
doc: What was noted under a name.

entries.name: noting
doc: The same stretch with something noted about it.
What a program put there, and only that. Nothing is noted automatically,
because a field added automatically is a field nobody chose — which is how
a trace comes to carry a password.

entries.name: parse
doc: The trace a header names, or nothing when it names none.

entries.name: recording
doc: The same trace, recorded or not.
For the one service that decides, which is the one the work entered at.
Every service after it carries what it was told.

entries.name: render
doc: The header this trace travels in.

entries.name: span
doc: A stretch of work beginning now.

entries.name: Span
doc: A named stretch of work within a trace.

entries.name: starting
doc: A new piece of work, recorded or not as the caller says.

entries.name: stepOf
doc: What this step in it is called.

entries.name: took
doc: How long a finished stretch took, or nothing while it is still running.

entries.name: Trace
doc: One piece of work, and this service's step in it.
`recorded` travels rather than being decided again: a piece of work
recorded by one service and not the next is missing its middle, which reads
as a service that stopped answering rather than as a choice.

entries.name: Trace
doc: One piece of work, and this service's step in it.
`recorded` travels rather than being decided again: a piece of work
recorded by one service and not the next is missing its middle, which reads
as a service that stopped answering rather than as a choice.

entries.name: traced
doc: Whether a trace is one anything can follow.

entries.name: untraced
doc: A trace that follows nothing and is not recorded.
What a piece of work has when entropy could not be reached. Not a failure:
tracing exists to explain what happened, and it must not be able to stop
the work it is explaining.

entries.name: workOf
doc: What the whole piece of work is called.

entries.name: Due
doc: When a job is due again.
The two intervals are both here because they answer different needs, and a
scheduler offering one is wrong for half the jobs it is given. Measured
from the end, a job that overruns simply runs less often; measured from the
start, it keeps its cadence and the skipped turns absorb the overrun.

entries.name: dueAt
doc: The names of the jobs due at a moment.
A pure function of the schedule and the moment, so an hourly job is checked
in a millisecond rather than in an hour.

entries.name: everFailed
doc: Whether a job has ever failed.

entries.name: failuresOf
doc: How many of those failed.

entries.name: isDue
doc: Whether one job is due.
A job that has never run is due once its first delay has passed, measured
from the start of time the caller is counting from — which for a service is
when it started.

entries.name: job
entries.signature: Str -> Std.App.Work.Due -> fn() -> Result[(), Str] -> Std.App.Work.Job
doc: A job from its parts.

entries.name: Job
doc: One thing a service does when nobody asked.

entries.name: jobsOf
doc: What the schedule holds.

entries.name: lastFailureOf
doc: What it last said when it failed, or nothing when it has not.

entries.name: lastTookOf
doc: How long the last run took.

entries.name: names
doc: The names of the jobs, so a program can report what it does unasked.

entries.name: nothing
doc: Nothing scheduled.

entries.name: nothingYet
doc: Nothing recorded yet.

entries.name: Record
doc: What a job has done so far.
Kept beside the job rather than somewhere else, so asking what a schedule
has been doing is reading a value rather than correlating two.

entries.name: recordOf
doc: What one job has done.

entries.name: render
doc: What a schedule has been doing, one line per job.

entries.name: runDue
doc: The schedule after running everything due at a moment.
A job already running does not start a second: two runs of a job that
writes is a race nobody designed, and it shows up as duplicated work rather
than as an error. The skipped turn is counted, so a job that never finishes
in time is visible rather than merely slow.

entries.name: runsOf
doc: How many times a job ran.

entries.name: schedule
doc: A schedule of jobs.

entries.name: Schedule
doc: The work a service does on its own.

entries.name: Scheduling
doc: What a schedule holds and which of its jobs are in flight.
A service adds its jobs one at a time and, when it drives them on workers of
its own, marks each as it starts and finishes. Both are several calls over
the same schedule, so as methods they read in the order the service makes
them rather than inside out.

entries.name: skipsOf
doc: How many turns were skipped because the last run had not finished.

entries.name: directory
doc: Convenience constructor for a directory entry.

entries.name: entry
doc: Convenience constructor for a regular file entry.

entries.name: extractFile
doc: Searches entries for a regular file matching the exact relative path.

entries.name: readArchive
doc: Decodes all TarEntries from a POSIX USTAR archive byte stream.

entries.name: TarEntry
doc: A single file, directory, or link stored within a USTAR archive.

entries.name: TarError
doc: Structured failure conditions encountered while reading a tar stream.

entries.name: TarType
doc: Classification of a filesystem entry stored in a tar archive.

entries.name: writeArchive
doc: Encodes an array of tar entries into a complete POSIX USTAR byte archive.

entries.name: Entry
doc: One file in an archive.
`stored` says whether the bytes were kept as they are or compressed. It is
read back rather than chosen by a reader, because an archive written
elsewhere decides it per entry: a JPEG compresses to nothing, so most
writers store it, and a reader that assumed either would be wrong half the
time.

entries.name: entryLimit
doc: What this reads and writes.
The zip format as it is used for the things that arrive: a document from a
spreadsheet program, a deployment bundle, an upload from a browser. Entries
are stored or deflated, which is what every writer produces; the archive's
directory is at the end, which is what every reader looks for first.
It does not read encrypted entries, spanned archives, or the 64-bit
extensions. Each is refused rather than half-read: an encrypted entry read
as though it were not is a file of noise, and a reader that ignored the
64-bit fields would answer with the low half of a size.
How large a single entry may be when read, in bytes.
A compressed entry can claim to expand to any size at all, and a reader
that believed it would allocate whatever an archive asked for. This is what
makes a hostile archive a refusal rather than a memory exhaustion.

entries.name: explain
doc: Why an archive was refused, written for a person to read.

entries.name: file
doc: A file to be written into an archive, compressed.

entries.name: find
doc: One named file out of an archive's entries.

entries.name: names
doc: Every name an archive holds, in the order its directory lists them.

entries.name: readArchive
doc: Read an archive.
The directory at the end is read rather than the entries walked from the
front. That is the format's own answer to what an archive holds — a writer
that appended to an existing archive leaves the superseded entries in
place, and only the directory says which ones count.

entries.name: stored
doc: A file to be written as it is.
For bytes that are already compressed, where deflating again costs time and
gains nothing.

entries.name: writeArchive
doc: Write an archive.

entries.name: ZipError
doc: Why bytes do not make an archive.

entries.name: allOf
doc: Every value a repeated option was given, in the order they were written.

entries.name: Args
doc: What a command line turned out to say.
Answers are held by kind rather than in one table of text, because the
question a caller asks differs by kind: a flag is asked whether it is
there, a value what it is, a repeated option for all of them. One table
would answer all three with text and leave every caller to tell "absent"
from "present and empty".

entries.name: ArgsError
doc: Why a command line was refused.

entries.name: Arity
doc: How many values an option takes.

entries.name: explain
doc: Why a command line was refused, written for a person to read.

entries.name: flag
doc: An option that is either present or absent.

entries.name: fromCommandLine
doc: Read the command line this program was given.

entries.name: isSet
doc: Whether a flag was given.

entries.name: numberChecked
doc: The value an option was given as a number, refusing text that is not one.

entries.name: numberOf
doc: The value an option was given, read as a whole number.
Answers nothing both when the option was absent and when what it was given
is not a number, because a caller with a fallback wants the fallback in
either case. `numberOr` is the form that says which happened.

entries.name: Opt
doc: One option a program accepts.

entries.name: parse
doc: Read arguments against a spec, in one pass.
The forms accepted are the ones people write: `--name value`, `--name=value`,
`-n value`, `-nvalue`, and `-abc` for three flags at once. A bare `--` ends
the options, so a value that looks like one — a file called `-`, a pattern
beginning with a dash — can still be given.

entries.name: repeated
doc: An option that may be given several times, keeping each value.

entries.name: required
doc: An option that takes a value and must be given.

entries.name: rest
doc: Everything that was not an option or an option's value.

entries.name: spec
doc: A program that accepts nothing yet.

entries.name: Spec
doc: What a program accepts, and the index that makes reading it one lookup.
Reading arguments by scanning for each one in turn — which is what asking
"was `--verbose` given?" separately from "what is `--out`?" amounts to —
walks the whole command line once per question. Ten options is ten passes,
and each pass compares every argument against a name.
So the names are indexed once, when the spec is built, and the command line
is then read in a single pass: every argument is one lookup rather than a
search. What that costs is one map per spec, built at startup; what it buys
is that adding an option to a program does not make reading its arguments
slower.
The difference is the shape of the growth rather than a constant. Reading
every option of a command line that gives all of them, measured at 25, 50,
100 and 200 options: scanning takes 9ms, 34ms, 134ms and 530ms — four times
the work for twice the options — while one pass and a lookup each takes
6ms, 11ms, 22ms and 43ms, which is twice for twice. A tool with a handful
of options would not notice either; the point is that one of them stops
being usable as the tool grows and the other does not.
`byLong` and `byShort` hold positions into `opts` rather than the options
themselves, so an option is stored once however many ways it can be
written.

entries.name: usage
doc: The usage text a program prints when asked, or when refusing.
Built from the same spec the parsing reads, so a program cannot document an
option it does not accept or accept one it does not document.

entries.name: value
doc: An option that takes a value.

entries.name: valueOf
doc: The value an option was given.

entries.name: valueOr
doc: The value an option was given, or one to use when it was not.

entries.name: compare
doc: Two measurements written as a line saying which won and by how much.

entries.name: fasterThan
doc: Whether a candidate is faster than a baseline by more than a stated margin.
The margin is why this takes one: two measurements of the same code differ
from one run to the next, and a comparison that called any difference a
change would report a result every time it was asked.

entries.name: measure
doc: Run an action and answer how long each batch of it took.
The clock counts whole milliseconds, so an operation faster than that reads
as taking no time at all. `batch` is the answer: the action is run that
many times between two clock readings, and the report divides. A batch that
leaves the best reading at zero has not been made large enough, and
`tooFast` says so rather than letting a reader believe the zero.
The first batch is run and discarded. A first run pays for whatever the
program had not done yet, and including it would make every measurement a
measurement of that instead.

entries.name: ratio
doc: How one measurement compares with another, in hundredths.
A hundred means the two took the same time, two hundred means the
candidate took twice as long. Reported as a whole number of hundredths
rather than as a ratio, because these are counts of milliseconds and a
floating quotient would suggest a precision the clock does not have.

entries.name: render
doc: One report written as a line.
The best reading leads, because it is the one with the least of the
machine's other work in it: a run cannot go faster than the operation, but
it can go slower for reasons that have nothing to do with the code.

entries.name: renderAll
doc: Every report written, one to a line.

entries.name: Report
doc: What a sample says once it has been read.
`perRun` is in microseconds because the clock counts milliseconds: an
operation worth measuring is usually faster than the clock can see, and a
figure per batch would be a number about the batch rather than about the
operation.

entries.name: run
doc: Measure and read in one step.

entries.name: Sample
doc: The timings one measurement collected.
The times are kept rather than reduced as they arrive, because a single
number cannot say whether a run was steady or whether one reading in ten
took twenty times as long, and that difference is usually the finding.

entries.name: slowerThan
doc: Whether a candidate is slower than a baseline by more than a stated margin.

entries.name: summarize
doc: What a sample says.
The median is reported beside the mean because they answer different
questions: a machine that paused once during the run moves the mean and
leaves the median where it was, and the gap between them is the evidence
that it happened.

entries.name: tooFast
doc: Whether the batch was too small for the clock to see.
A best reading of zero means the whole batch finished inside one tick, so
every figure derived from it is a claim the measurement cannot support.

entries.name: all
doc: Whether every pair satisfies the predicate. True for an empty map.

entries.name: any
doc: Whether any pair satisfies the predicate. False for an empty map.

entries.name: BiMap
doc: A map that can be read from either side.
A currency code and its symbol, a user and their session, a variant and its
wire spelling: the pairing is the fact, and which side is the key depends on
which way the program happens to be going. An ordinary `Map` answers one of
those questions and makes the other a scan of everything it holds.
Keeping a second map by hand answers both, and is two writes that must not
come apart. This does that keeping, so a caller cannot forget half of it.
The part that is not symmetric with `Map`: a value can collide the way a key
can. Binding `a` to `1` and then `b` to `1` cannot leave both, because
looking up `1` would then have two answers and the reverse direction would
no longer be a map at all. The later binding wins and the earlier one is
removed entirely — `insert` can therefore make the map smaller, which is the
one surprise here and the reason `insertChecked` exists beside it.

entries.name: containsLeft
doc: Whether a left value is paired with anything.

entries.name: containsRight
doc: Whether a right value is paired with anything.

entries.name: empty
doc: A map with no pairs.

entries.name: filter
entries.signature: &Std.BiMap.BiMap[L, R] -> fn(L, R) -> Bool -> Std.BiMap.BiMap[L, R]
doc: Only the pairs the predicate accepts.

entries.name: flipped
doc: The map with its two sides exchanged.
Free, because both directions are already held. This is the operation an
ordinary map cannot offer without rebuilding, and the reason to reach for
this type when a program reads a pairing both ways.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: &Std.BiMap.BiMap[L, R] -> fn(A, L, R) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every pair combined into one value, in the order of the left values.

entries.name: fromPairs
doc: A map built from pairs.
A later pair displaces any earlier one sharing either side, so the result is
always a bijection and may hold fewer pairs than it was given.

entries.name: fromPairsChecked
doc: A map built from pairs, or `None` if any side repeats.
The form to use when the input is meant to already be a bijection and a
repeat means the data is wrong.

entries.name: getLeft
doc: The left value paired with a right one, or `None`.

entries.name: getRight
doc: The right value paired with a left one, or `None`.

entries.name: insert
doc: The map with a pair added, displacing whatever either side was paired with.
Both sides are removed from their old pairings first, so the two directions
cannot end up disagreeing. Adding `b -> 1` to a map already holding `a -> 1`
leaves only `b -> 1`: the map has the same number of pairs it started with
rather than one more.

entries.name: insertChecked
doc: The map with a pair added, or `None` when either side is already paired.
For callers building a map that is supposed to be a bijection already — a
table of unique codes, a registry of names — where a collision means the
input was wrong rather than that the caller meant to replace something.
`insert` silently displaces; this reports.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the map holds nothing.

entries.name: lefts
doc: Every left value, in order.

entries.name: merge
doc: Two maps combined, with the second map's pairs displacing the first's.

entries.name: pairs
doc: Every pair, in the order of its left value.

entries.name: removeLeft
doc: The map with a left value's pair removed, or unchanged when it has none.

entries.name: removeRight
doc: The map with a right value's pair removed, or unchanged when it has none.

entries.name: rights
doc: Every right value, in order.

entries.name: size
doc: How many pairs the map holds.

entries.name: toMap
doc: The left-to-right direction as an ordinary map.

entries.name: and
doc: Both values' bits, kept where both are set.

entries.name: bit
doc: A value with only the bit at a position set, or nought when the position is
outside the type.

entries.name: bits
doc: The bits of a value, lowest position first, over the type's own width.

entries.name: Bits
doc: A type whose values are bit patterns.
`width` comes from the type rather than being assumed. This module used to
say "the low sixty-four positions" while taking an `Int`, whose width is the
target's; a value now answers for its own. `BigInt` has no implementation,
because it has no width and every operation here needs one.

entries.name: clearBit
doc: The value with one bit cleared.

entries.name: complement
doc: Every bit inverted, over the type's own width.

entries.name: countLeadingZeros
doc: How many high positions are clear before the first set bit. A value with no
bits set has the whole width.

entries.name: countTrailingZeros
doc: How many low positions are clear before the first set bit.

entries.name: extract
entries.signature: &T -> Int -> Int -> T where T: Bits
doc: The bits at positions `from` up to but not including `to`, moved down.

entries.name: flipBit
doc: The value with one bit inverted.

entries.name: highestSetBit
doc: The position of the highest set bit, or `None` when no bit is set.

entries.name: isSingleBit
doc: Whether a value has exactly one bit set, which is what a power of two is.
Nought has none; a negative value has its sign bit, so it never has one.

entries.name: lowestSetBit
doc: The position of the lowest set bit, or `None` when no bit is set.

entries.name: mask
doc: The value with its low `width` bits kept and the rest cleared.

entries.name: nextPowerOfTwo
doc: The smallest power of two that is not below the value.
A value at or below one answers with one, the smallest power of two there
is. A value whose next power does not fit the type answers with the largest
power that does, because there is no other value it could name.

entries.name: ones
doc: A value with every bit set, of the same type as the example given.

entries.name: or
doc: Both values' bits, kept where either is set.

entries.name: popCount
doc: How many bits are set, counted over the type's own width.

entries.name: rotateLeft
doc: The bits moved toward the high end, with the ones that leave reappearing at
the low end. Rotation is over the type's own width.

entries.name: rotateRight
doc: The bits moved toward the low end, with the ones that leave reappearing at
the high end.

entries.name: setBit
doc: The value with one bit set.

entries.name: shiftLeft
doc: The bits moved toward the high end, filling with noughts.
A count that is negative or not below the width has no defined answer and is
refused by the operator itself.

entries.name: shiftRight
doc: The bits moved toward the low end. A signed type keeps its sign; an unsigned
one brings in noughts.

entries.name: testBit
doc: Whether the bit at a position is set. A position outside the type is not.

entries.name: toBinary
doc: The value written in binary, without a sign or a prefix, over the type's own
width. Nought is a single nought rather than empty text.

entries.name: toHex
doc: The value written in lower-case hexadecimal, without a prefix.

entries.name: width
doc: How many bits a value's type has.

entries.name: width
doc: One implementation per integer width, each reporting its own. `Int` and

entries.name: width
doc: Return the fixed number of bits stored by this integer type.

doc: Both values' bits, kept where exactly one is set.

entries.name: BitSet
doc: Sparse blocks of 64 IDs. Construct through this module to preserve block invariants.

entries.name: blocks
doc: The words the set is stored as, keyed by where each begins.

entries.name: contains
doc: Whether a number is in the set.

entries.name: difference

entries.name: empty

doc: The set with a number added. Adding one already there changes nothing.

entries.name: intersection
doc: Every number in both sets.

doc: Whether the two sets share no number.

entries.name: isEmpty

entries.name: singleton

doc: UInt128 can count even the entire UInt64 ID domain.

entries.name: symmetricDifference
doc: Every number in one set but not the other.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Materialize members in ascending order.

entries.name: union
doc: Every number in either set.

entries.name: bitAnd
doc: Parallel 64-bit hardware bitwise AND.

entries.name: bitNot
doc: Parallel 64-bit hardware bitwise NOT with trailing bit masking.

entries.name: bitOr
doc: Parallel 64-bit hardware bitwise OR.

entries.name: BitVector
doc: A dense contiguous sequence of bits backed by unboxed 64-bit words.

entries.name: bitXor
doc: Parallel 64-bit hardware bitwise XOR.

entries.name: countZeros
doc: Total count of clear bits (0s).

doc: Allocates a bit-vector of exact bit length initialized to false (0) or true (1).

entries.name: findFirstSet
doc: Finds the index of the lowest set bit using hardware trailing-zero scan.

entries.name: findFirstZero
doc: Finds the index of the lowest clear bit.

entries.name: flip
doc: Inverts the bit at the given index.

entries.name: fromBits

doc: Reads the bit at the given index.

entries.name: isOnes
