entries.name: create
doc: Allocates a disjoint-set forest of `totalElements` singleton components.

entries.name: DisjointSet
doc: A low-level, flat-array Disjoint-Set (Union-Find) with path halving and union-by-rank.

entries.name: elementCount
doc: Returns the total number of elements tracked.

entries.name: find
doc: Finds the root representative of element `x` using iterative path halving.

entries.name: union
doc: Merges the sets containing elements `x` and `y` using union-by-rank.

entries.name: adjust
entries.signature: &Std.EnumMap.EnumMap[K, V] -> K -> fn(V) -> V -> Std.EnumMap.EnumMap[K, V]
doc: A key's value transformed, unchanged when the key is outside the domain.

entries.name: all
doc: Whether every entry satisfies the predicate. True over an empty domain.

entries.name: any
doc: Whether any entry satisfies the predicate. False over an empty domain.

entries.name: containsKey
doc: Whether a key is in the domain.

entries.name: countValues
doc: How many values the predicate accepts.

entries.name: EnumMap
doc: A map over a fixed set of keys, where every key has a value.
The days of a week, the variants of a status, the levels of a log: the keys
are known when the program is written, and every one of them has an entry.
Asking an ordinary `Map` for one still answers `Option[V]`, so the caller
unwraps a value they already knew was there, and picks a fallback that can
never be used — a decision they had to make and a reader has to read past.
This removes that, in the way `NonEmpty` removes the `Option` from `first`:
by making the map total when it is built. `get` answers `V`. The cost is
paid once, at the boundary, where the caller says which keys exist and what
each one starts as.
Keys are held in the order the domain names them, not sorted, because a
domain is usually written in an order that means something — Monday first,
Debug below Error — and sorting it would replace the author's order with the
spelling of the names.

entries.name: filled
doc: A map giving every key in the domain the same starting value.
A key repeated in the domain is kept once, at its first position, so a
caller who lists one twice gets a map rather than a structure with two slots
for the same key and no way to say which is meant.

entries.name: find
doc: The value stored under a key, or `None` when the key is outside the domain.
For a key that arrived from outside the program — parsed from a file, read
off a request — where being outside the domain is an input to handle rather
than a defect to stop for.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: &Std.EnumMap.EnumMap[K, V] -> fn(A, K, V) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every entry combined into one value, in domain order.

entries.name: from
doc: A map giving every key in the domain the value a function computes for it.

entries.name: get
doc: The value stored under a key.
Total for any key the domain holds, which is what this module exists to
give. A key from outside the domain has no value to answer with and no
honest one to invent, so it panics: that is a defect in the caller's own
code — they named the domain — rather than an input a program could receive.
`find` is the form to reach for when the key came from outside the program.

entries.name: getOr
doc: The value stored under a key, or the given fallback when the key is not in
the domain.
The fallback is not the "missing value" case an ordinary map has — every key
in the domain has a value. It is for a key from outside the domain
altogether, which is a different mistake and one the caller can usually rule
out. `get` is the total form for when they can.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the domain names any key at all.
A map over an empty domain is legal and holds nothing. It is the one case
where there is no key to ask about, which is why `get` still needs a domain
that contains its key.

entries.name: keys
doc: Every key, in the order the domain named them.

entries.name: keysWhere
doc: The keys whose values the predicate accepts.
Answers keys rather than a smaller map, because a map with keys removed is
no longer total over the domain it claims, and quietly returning one would
give back the `Option` this module exists to remove.

entries.name: mapValues
doc: Every value transformed, keeping the domain and its order.

entries.name: mergeWith
entries.signature: &Std.EnumMap.EnumMap[K, V] -> &Std.EnumMap.EnumMap[K, V] -> fn(V, V) -> V -> Std.EnumMap.EnumMap[K, V]
doc: Two maps over the same domain combined value by value.
The domain is the first map's. A key the second map lacks keeps the first
map's value untouched, so combining a full week with a partial one leaves
the untouched days alone rather than reporting a domain mismatch the caller
would have to handle on every call.

entries.name: pairs
doc: Every entry as a pair, in domain order.

entries.name: set
doc: The map with a key's value replaced, unchanged when the key is outside the
domain.
The domain does not grow. A map whose keys could be added to is an ordinary
map, and the totality of `get` rests on the domain being settled when the
map was built.

entries.name: size
doc: How many keys the domain holds.

entries.name: toMap
doc: The map as an ordinary map, losing the promise that every key has a value.

entries.name: values
doc: Every value, in the order of its key.

entries.name: all
doc: The arguments the program was started with, without the program's own name.

entries.name: at
doc: The argument at a position, or `None` when there is none.

entries.name: count
doc: The number of arguments given.

entries.name: elapsedMilliseconds
doc: Milliseconds on a clock that only moves forward.
Two readings may be subtracted; one alone means nothing, which is why this
is not called the time.

entries.name: fail
doc: Stop the program reporting failure, after writing a message.

entries.name: hasFlag
doc: Whether an argument was given, matched exactly.

entries.name: homeDirectory
doc: The directory this machine calls the reader's own, when it has one.
Asked of the machine rather than of one variable. `HOME` is the name one
family of operating system uses and `USERPROFILE` is the other's, and a
program that asked only for the first answered `None` on a machine that has
a home directory and a different word for it.

entries.name: isSet
doc: Whether an environment variable is set at all, whatever its value.

entries.name: option
doc: The value given after a named argument, or `None`.
`--out file` and `--out=file` are both read, because both are written.

entries.name: positional
doc: Every argument that is not a flag or a flag's value.

entries.name: searchPath
doc: The program's search path, split on the separator its platform uses.
The separator is asked for rather than written down: it is a colon on one
family of operating system and a semicolon on the other, so a program that
splits on a colon reads the whole of `PATH` as a single entry everywhere
else.

entries.name: stop
doc: Stop the program with a status. Nought means it succeeded.

entries.name: succeed
doc: Stop the program reporting success.

entries.name: temporaryDirectory
doc: Where this machine says a program may put a file it does not intend to keep.
The answer is the machine's, not the program's: it honours `TMPDIR` where
that is set, and names the system's own directory where it is not. A program
that writes `/tmp` directly has stated one machine's answer as though it
were every machine's, and will not run where that path does not exist.
The directory is where a file may go, not a file — a caller that needs one
joins a name it chose onto it, and one that may run twice at once chooses a
name that cannot collide.

entries.name: variable
doc: One environment variable, or `None` when it is not set.

entries.name: variableOr
doc: One environment variable, or a fallback when it is not set.

entries.name: variables
doc: Every environment variable as a name and a value.

entries.name: add
doc: Adds `delta` to the 1-based element at `index` in O(log n) time.

entries.name: create
doc: Allocates a zero-initialized Fenwick tree for sequence length `elementCount`.

entries.name: FenwickTree
doc: A low-level Binary Indexed Tree for O(log n) prefix sums and point updates.

entries.name: findPrefix
doc: Finds the smallest 1-based index whose prefix sum is >= `targetSum` in O(log n) time.

entries.name: fromArray
doc: Builds a Fenwick tree in strict O(n) linear time from an array of initial values.

entries.name: get
doc: Retrieves the single value at 1-based `index` in O(log n) time.

entries.name: prefixSum
doc: Computes the prefix sum up to 1-based `index` in O(log n) time.

entries.name: rangeSum
doc: Computes the range sum [left, right] inclusive in O(log n) time.

entries.name: set
doc: Sets the 1-based element at `index` to `value`.

entries.name: size
doc: Returns the number of elements in the tree.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Materializes the tree values into a standard 0-indexed array.

entries.name: containsKey
doc: Whether the table contains an entry for the specified 64-bit key.

entries.name: empty
doc: Creates an empty flat hash table with the requested minimum capacity.
Capacity is rounded up to the nearest power of two (minimum 16 slots).

entries.name: entries
doc: Extracts all active key-value pairings as an array in slot order.

entries.name: FlatMap
doc: A high-performance flat hash table specialized for 64-bit unsigned keys.
Slots are indexed using 1-byte control metadata with 7-bit hash fingerprints
to eliminate pointer chasing and false key equality comparisons. Collisions
are resolved via linear probing, and tables automatically rehash at 75% load factor.

entries.name: get
doc: Looks up a value by its 64-bit unsigned key.
Probes control metadata using the 7-bit fingerprint (H2); returns `None`
immediately without dereferencing slot memory if an empty slot is encountered.

entries.name: getOr
doc: Looks up a value by its key, returning `fallback` if the key is absent.

entries.name: insert
doc: Inserts or replaces a key-value pairing in the table.
If the addition causes the load factor to exceed 75%, the table automatically
doubles in capacity and rehashes all active entries.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the table contains zero entries.

entries.name: remove
doc: Removes a key-value pairing from the table.
Marks the deleted slot with a tombstone control tag to preserve linear probing
chains for subsequent lookups.

entries.name: size
doc: The number of live key-value pairings currently stored in the table.

entries.name: Align
doc: Where the content sits when it is narrower than the width asked for.

entries.name: alignOf
doc: Where a spec places its content.

entries.name: binary
doc: A whole number in base two, shaped by the spec.

entries.name: columns
doc: Rows laid out in columns, each column as wide as its widest entry.
The widths are measured from the rows themselves, so a caller does not
declare what they cannot know until every row is in hand. A short row is
padded with empty cells rather than refused, since a table with a ragged
edge is still a table.

entries.name: fillOf
doc: The character a spec fills with.

entries.name: fixed
doc: An exact fraction shaped by the spec, shown to a fixed number of places.
A `Decimal` rather than a `Float`, because a figure shown to two places is
almost always money or a measurement, and a float cannot hold those exactly
— a total that renders as `0.30` after adding `0.10` three times is the
error this avoids by not admitting the type that causes it.
Rounding is half away from zero, which is the rounding a reader does by
hand. Asking for more places than the value carries pads with zeros, so a
column of figures lines up on its point.

entries.name: hex
doc: A whole number in base sixteen, shaped by the spec.

entries.name: int
doc: A whole number shaped by the spec.

entries.name: list
doc: Every value in an array shaped alike and joined.

entries.name: octal
doc: A whole number in base eight, shaped by the spec.

entries.name: radix
doc: A whole number in a base the caller names, shaped by the spec.

entries.name: Shaping
doc: A spec with one decision changed, each answering a spec rather than taking
one apart.
Methods, so that a spec asking for three things is written down the page.
As functions taking the spec first, each call had to be wrapped in the next
and the spec a reader looks for first ended up furthest in.

entries.name: spec
doc: A spec that shapes nothing.

entries.name: Spec
doc: The decisions about how a value is shaped, held as a value.
`Std.Out` settles how output is written; this settles what it is written
from. The two are the same idea applied twice: the decisions are made once,
given a name, and handed to whatever does the work, rather than assembled at
each call out of padding helpers.
There is no format string here and nothing is parsed at run time. A spec is
a value the checker sees, so a width that is not a number or an alignment
that is not one of the three is a type error rather than a line that comes
out wrong.
The defaults shape nothing: a width of zero, left alignment, a space to fill
with, no forced sign, and no grouping. Every builder answers a new spec and
leaves the one it was given alone.

entries.name: text
doc: Text placed within the spec's width.
Content at least as wide as the width is answered unchanged, so shaping a
column never costs a character that was there.

entries.name: truncated
doc: Text cut to a width, ending in a marker when anything was removed.
The marker is counted inside the width, so the answer is never wider than
asked for. A width too small to hold the marker answers the marker cut to
the width, because a caller who asked for three columns gets three.

entries.name: widthOf
doc: The width a spec asks for.

entries.name: zeroPadded
doc: A number filled to its width with zeros between the sign and the digits.
Padding with a zero through `filledWith` would put it before the sign and
answer `00-42`, which is not a number. This keeps the sign leading.

entries.name: apply
doc: A function applied to a value, for the places where a function is a value
and applying it needs to be one too.

entries.name: applyTo
doc: A value passed to a function, reading left to right.
The counterpart to `apply`, for when the value is what the reader has in
hand and the function is what they are choosing.

entries.name: compose
entries.signature: fn(B) -> C -> fn(A) -> B -> A -> C
doc: One function after another: `compose(f, g, x)` is `f(g(x))`.
The outer function is written first, which is the order it is applied last.

entries.name: constant
doc: A function that ignores its argument and answers with a fixed value.

entries.name: fixpoint
doc: A function applied to itself's result until it stops changing.
The step count is bounded: a strict language cannot recover from a function
with no fixed point, and exhausting the bound answers with what it had.

entries.name: flip
entries.signature: fn(A, B) -> C -> B -> A -> C
doc: A function with its two arguments exchanged.

entries.name: identity
doc: The value itself. Useful wherever a transformation is required and none is
wanted, such as `flatten` written as `flatMap(items, identity)`.

entries.name: on
entries.signature: fn(B, B) -> C -> fn(A) -> B -> A -> A -> C
doc: Two values compared after the same transformation is applied to each.
`on(compare, key, left, right)` compares by key, which is how a comparison on
one field is built from a comparison on its type.

entries.name: partial
entries.signature: fn(A, B) -> C -> A -> B -> C
doc: A two-argument function with its first argument fixed.

entries.name: pipe
entries.signature: fn(A) -> B -> fn(B) -> C -> A -> C
doc: One function after another, reading left to right.
`pipe(f, g, x)` is `g(f(x))`, which is the order a reader follows data.

entries.name: pipe3
entries.signature: fn(A) -> B -> fn(B) -> C -> fn(C) -> D -> A -> D
doc: Three functions in a row, reading left to right.

entries.name: times
doc: A function applied a number of times. A count below one is the value itself.

entries.name: twice
doc: A function applied twice.

entries.name: until
entries.signature: Int -> fn(T) -> Bool -> fn(T) -> T -> T -> T
doc: A function applied until a condition holds.
The step count is bounded because a strict language cannot recover from a
condition that never holds; exhausting the bound answers with what it had.

entries.name: isLiteral
doc: Whether a pattern has anything in it that varies.
A pattern with nothing to match is a name, and a caller can look it up
directly rather than walking a tree to compare every path against it.

entries.name: literalPrefix
doc: The longest leading run of a pattern that varies in no way.
What a caller walking a directory tree starts from: everything the pattern
can match is under this, so nothing above it needs to be looked at.

entries.name: matches
doc: Whether a path matches a pattern written the way a shell writes one.
The vocabulary is small and fixed, which is the point: a glob is written by
a person into a configuration file — files to include, paths to ignore,
routes to match — and every piece of it has to be guessable without a
reference.
- `?` matches one character, but never a separator.
- `*` matches any run of characters within one segment, never a separator.
- `**` matches whole segments, separators and all.
- `[abc]` and `[a-z]` match one of a set, `[!abc]` one outside it.
- `\` makes the next character ordinary.
The separator rule is what makes a glob a path pattern rather than a text
pattern: `src/*.pudu` names files in one directory and `src/**/*.pudu`
names them at any depth. A `*` that crossed separators would make the two
the same, and there would be no way to write the first.
For matching text rather than paths, use `Std.Regex`.
Whether a path matches a pattern.

entries.name: matchesAny
doc: Whether any of several patterns matches, which is how an include list reads.

entries.name: reject
doc: The paths left after removing everything an ignore list names.

entries.name: select
doc: The paths a pattern selects, out of the ones given.

entries.name: addEdge
entries.signature: &Std.Graph.Graph[N] -> N -> N -> Std.Graph.Graph[N] where N: Ord
doc: The graph with an edge from one node to another.
Both ends are added as nodes. An edge to a node the caller never mentioned
is still a statement that the node exists, and requiring it to be declared
first would only make callers write it twice.

entries.name: addNode
doc: The graph with a node in it, whether or not it has any edges.

entries.name: components
doc: The groups of nodes joined to each other when direction is ignored.

entries.name: empty
doc: A graph with nothing in it.

entries.name: fromEdges
doc: A graph built from a list of edges.

entries.name: Graph
doc: A directed graph: nodes, and the edges leading out of each one.
Held as a map from a node to the nodes it points at, because that is the
question every walk over a graph asks — given where I am, where may I go.
A node with no outgoing edges still belongs, so membership is kept apart
from the edge map rather than inferred from it; a graph that forgot its
leaves would report a shorter topological order than it has nodes.
The edges are a `MultiMap`, which is what several values under one key are.
That keeps the rule about a node whose last edge is removed in one place
rather than here, and it fits because membership is already held separately:
such a node leaves the edges and stays a node.

entries.name: hasCycle
doc: Whether following edges can lead back to where it started.

entries.name: hasEdge
entries.signature: &Std.Graph.Graph[N] -> N -> N -> Bool where N: Ord
doc: Whether there is an edge from one node to another.

entries.name: hasNode
doc: Whether the node is in the graph.

entries.name: inDegree
doc: How many edges lead into a node.

entries.name: leaves
doc: The nodes that point at nothing.

entries.name: neighbours
doc: The nodes an edge leads to from here.

entries.name: nodes
doc: Every node.

entries.name: order
doc: How many nodes there are.

entries.name: outDegree
doc: How many edges lead out of a node.

entries.name: reachableFrom
doc: Every node reachable from a starting node, nearest first.
Breadth first, so the order says something: a node listed earlier is no
further away than one listed later. The queue is a deque because the walk
takes from the front on every step, which is the one thing an array is bad
at.

entries.name: reaches
entries.signature: &Std.Graph.Graph[N] -> N -> N -> Bool where N: Ord
doc: Whether one node can be reached from another by following edges.

entries.name: reversed
doc: The graph with every edge turned around.

entries.name: roots
doc: The nodes that nothing points at, which is where a topological walk begins.

entries.name: shortestPath
entries.signature: &Std.Graph.Graph[N] -> N -> N -> Option[Array[N]] where N: Ord
doc: The shortest path from one node to another counted in edges, or `None` when
there is no way through.

entries.name: stronglyConnected
doc: The groups of nodes that can all reach each other.
A node reaches every node in its own group and they all reach it back, so a
group of more than one is a cycle and the groups themselves, taken as
units, have none. This is what turns a circular dependency graph into
something that can be ordered: the cycles become single items.

entries.name: topologicalOrder
doc: The nodes in an order where every node comes before the ones it points at,
or `None` when there is no such order.
`None` means a cycle. That is the honest answer rather than a partial list
or an arbitrary tie-break: a caller ordering build steps or resolving
declarations needs to know its input is circular, not to receive an order
that quietly is not one.
Nodes with nothing pointing at them are taken first, and removing them
exposes the next such nodes. If nodes remain when none are left exposed,
every remaining node has something pointing at it, which is a cycle.

entries.name: bucketCount
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Int where K: Eq + Hash
doc: How many buckets the map is currently spread across.
For a program measuring how well its keys distribute, not for one deciding
what to do: a bucket count is a fact about the seed and the keys together,
and it changes between runs even for the same keys.

entries.name: containsKey
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> &K -> Bool where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Whether a key is present.

entries.name: empty
entries.signature: Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map holding nothing.

entries.name: entries
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Array[(K, V)] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Every pairing, in the order the keys were first put in.
Order is what the entries record rather than where the buckets put them, so
two programs that inserted the same keys in the same order enumerate them
the same way — even though the seed makes their buckets differ.

entries.name: Entry
doc: One pairing, with the position it was first put in.
The position is kept beside the pairing rather than in a list of its own,
because a list would have to be searched and rewritten on every removal.
Carrying it here makes a removal cost what removing from one bucket costs,
and makes enumeration a sort of what the buckets already hold.

entries.name: equals
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Bool where K: Eq + Hash, V: Eq
doc: Whether two maps hold the same pairings.
Order is not part of it. Two maps built by inserting the same pairs in
different orders hold the same thing, and a comparison that said otherwise
would make equality depend on history rather than on contents.

entries.name: filter
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> fn(K, V) -> Bool -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map holding only the pairings a test accepts.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> A -> fn(A, K, V) -> A -> A where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Every pairing combined into one value, in insertion order.

entries.name: fromArray
entries.signature: &Array[(K, V)] -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map built from pairings, later ones replacing earlier ones.

entries.name: get
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> &K -> Option[V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: The value under a key, or nothing when the map does not hold it.

entries.name: getOr
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> &K -> V -> V where K: Eq + Hash
doc: The value under a key, or a fallback when the map does not hold it.

entries.name: HashMap
doc: A map that finds a key by hashing it rather than by comparing it.
The ordered `Map` reaches a key by comparison, so a lookup walks a tree
whose depth grows with the collection. This reaches a bucket by a number,
which costs the same at any size; what it gives up is that keys come back
in insertion order rather than sorted, and that a key must be able to hash
as well as compare equal.
`placed` counts upwards and is never reused. Two entries can therefore
never claim one position, which is what makes enumeration a total order
rather than an order with ties the sort would break arbitrarily.

entries.name: insert
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> K -> V -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map with a pairing added, replacing any value already under the key.
Replacing keeps the position the key already had, so a value corrected
after the fact does not move to the end of what enumeration reports. A key
removed and put back is a new pairing and does take a new position.

entries.name: insertWith
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> K -> V -> fn(V, V) -> V -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map with a pairing added, combining with any value already there.
The value already present is given first, so a caller writing an addition
or an append does not have to remember which way round the arguments came.

entries.name: isEmpty
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Bool where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Whether a map holds nothing.

entries.name: keys
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Array[K] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Every key, in the order they were first put in.

entries.name: map
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> fn(V) -> W -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, W] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map with every value transformed, keeping keys and their order.

entries.name: merge
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Two maps joined, the second's value winning where both hold a key.

entries.name: mergeWith
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> fn(V, V) -> V -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Two maps joined, a rule deciding where both hold a key.

entries.name: remove
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> &K -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map with a key removed, or the same map when it held none.

entries.name: singleton
entries.signature: K -> V -> Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: A map holding one pairing.

entries.name: size
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Int where K: Eq + Hash
doc: How many pairings a map holds.

entries.name: values
entries.signature: &Std.HashMap.HashMap[K, V] -> Array[V] where K: Eq + Hash
doc: Every value, in the order their keys were first put in.

entries.name: contains
doc: Whether an element is present.

entries.name: dropMin
doc: The heap without its smallest element, unchanged when it is empty.

entries.name: empty
doc: A heap with nothing in it.

entries.name: filter
entries.signature: &Std.Heap.Heap[T] -> fn(T) -> Bool -> Std.Heap.Heap[T] where T: Ord
doc: A heap of every element that satisfies a test.

entries.name: fromArray
doc: A heap holding every element of an array.

entries.name: Heap
doc: A collection that always knows its smallest element.
A sorted array knows its smallest too, but paying to keep everything in
order is paying for an answer nobody asked for: a scheduler wants the next
task, not the whole schedule. Sorting the array again after each insertion
costs far more than this, and scanning an unsorted one for the minimum
costs more on every read.
The shape is a tree whose every node is smaller than the nodes beneath it,
so the smallest element is the root and reading it is immediate. Adding is
one comparison. Removing the root leaves its children loose, and they are
rejoined in two passes — pairing them up, then folding the pairs together —
which is what keeps the tree from degenerating into a list under repeated
removal.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the heap holds nothing.

entries.name: map
entries.signature: &Std.Heap.Heap[A] -> fn(A) -> B -> Std.Heap.Heap[B] where B: Ord
doc: A heap of every element transformed.
The order is rebuilt rather than carried over, because a transform may not
respect the ordering the old heap was arranged by.

entries.name: merge
doc: Two heaps joined into one.
The root of the result is whichever root is smaller; the other heap becomes
its child. This is the single operation the rest is built from — adding is
joining a heap of one, and removing is joining what the root left behind.

entries.name: one
doc: A heap of one element.

entries.name: peek
doc: The smallest element, or `None` for an empty heap.

entries.name: pop
doc: The smallest element and the heap without it, or `None` when empty.
Both together, because a caller taking the next item almost always wants
the rest as well, and rejoining the children is work worth doing once.

entries.name: push
doc: The heap with an element added.

entries.name: size
doc: How many elements the heap holds.

entries.name: smallest
doc: The smallest few elements, in order.
The reason to reach for a heap over a sort: finding the ten smallest of a
million does not require putting the million in order.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Every element, in no particular order beyond the smallest being reachable.

entries.name: toSortedArray
doc: Every element, smallest first.
Taking the whole heap apart in order, which is a sort — and a reasonable
one, though `List.sorted` is the better answer when order is all that is
wanted and the heap was built only to get it.

entries.name: union
doc: Two heaps' elements in one heap.

entries.name: asciiToNibble
doc: Converts an ASCII character byte to its 4-bit numeric nibble value (0..15).

entries.name: byteToHex
doc: Splits a byte into two ASCII hex character bytes (high nibble, low nibble).

entries.name: decode
doc: Decodes an even-length hexadecimal string into an array of bytes.

entries.name: decodeWithPrefix
doc: Decodes a hexadecimal string, skipping an optional leading '0x' or '0X' prefix.

entries.name: encode
doc: Encodes an array of bytes into a lowercase hexadecimal string.

entries.name: encodeUpper
doc: Encodes an array of bytes into an uppercase hexadecimal string.

entries.name: isValid
doc: Checks whether `hexStr` consists of an even number of valid hex digits.

entries.name: nibbleToAscii
doc: Converts a 4-bit numeric nibble (0..15) into an ASCII character byte.

entries.name: anchor
doc: A link to a destination, with attributes and children.

entries.name: attribute
doc: An attribute, checked.
An attribute whose name begins the way a handler's does is refused
outright: its value is a program, not text, and no amount of escaping makes
a program safe. A page needing behaviour attaches it from a script the page
loaded, which is what a policy permitting only the page's own origin is
for.

entries.name: body
doc: The rendered section, with attributes and children.

entries.name: button
doc: A button, with attributes and children.

entries.name: cell
doc: One table cell. A header cell when the first argument holds.

entries.name: classes
doc: The class attribute, from the classes rather than from their spelling, so a
caller adding one does not also maintain the separators.

entries.name: destination
doc: A destination, checked, or the reason it is refused.
A path within this site is always admitted. Anything naming a scheme must
name one of the few that carry a destination rather than a program. Nothing
is unescaped first: what arrives is what was written, and undoing an
encoding before checking is how a check is bypassed.

entries.name: Destination
doc: A destination an attribute may carry.
There is no way to make one except through a call that checked it, which is
the same arrangement text has and for the same reason. Escaping text does
nothing for a destination: `href="javascript:..."` contains no character
that escaping touches, and it runs. A page builder that escapes text and
takes any string as a destination has closed one door and left the other
open — which is where the established template engines are.

entries.name: destinationText
doc: How a destination is written.

entries.name: div
doc: A grouping with no meaning of its own.

entries.name: document
doc: A whole document, with the declaration that says which one it is.

entries.name: each
doc: A view for each item of a list.

entries.name: element
doc: An element with a name, attributes, and children.

entries.name: empty
doc: An element with attributes and nothing inside it.

entries.name: escape
doc: Text with the characters that would otherwise start markup written as
themselves.

entries.name: explainUnsafe
doc: What a refusal says.

entries.name: flag
doc: An attribute whose presence is its meaning, written as its own name.

entries.name: form
doc: A form posting to a destination by the given method.

entries.name: fragment
doc: Several views with no element around them.

entries.name: head
doc: The metadata section, holding the given children.

entries.name: heading
doc: A heading of the given level, from 1 to 6.

entries.name: here
doc: A destination within this site, which names no scheme and so needs no
scheme check.

entries.name: html
doc: The root element, with attributes and children.

entries.name: Html
doc: A page, as a value.
Text and markup are different things here, and the only way to obtain the
second is to build a node. A template language solves escaping repeatedly
and gets it wrong at each new context because it lets a string become markup
by being interpolated; a string cannot become markup at all, so the failure
has no way to occur rather than being prevented by a rule to remember.
`Trusted` is the one exception, named so it cannot be reached by accident
and cannot be missed in review. A caller who genuinely holds markup — the
output of a document converter, a fragment from elsewhere — says so, and the
word appears where they said it.

entries.name: image
doc: An image from a destination, with the description screen readers read.

entries.name: input
doc: A form control, from its attributes alone.

entries.name: isHandler
doc: Whether an attribute name is one whose value would be a program.

entries.name: link
doc: A relationship to another resource, from its attributes alone.

entries.name: list
doc: A list. Ordered when the first argument holds, unordered when it does not.

entries.name: meta
doc: A metadata element, from its attributes alone.

entries.name: nothing
doc: Nothing, for a branch that renders no view.

entries.name: paragraph
doc: A paragraph, with attributes and children.

entries.name: render
doc: A view as markup.
The only thing here that produces text. It reads nothing outside the value
it was given, so two renders of equal views are equal and a page can be
compared in a test rather than matched against a pattern.

entries.name: renderChunks
doc: Buffered output fragments, in document order, without joining child subtrees.

entries.name: row
doc: One table row, holding the given cells.

entries.name: span
doc: A run of inline content with no meaning of its own.

entries.name: style
doc: The style attribute, from its declarations.

entries.name: table
doc: A table, with attributes and children.

entries.name: tag
doc: An element with children and no attributes, which most elements are.

entries.name: text
doc: Text, which is text: whatever it holds, it renders as that and not as
markup.

entries.name: title
doc: The document title, from its text.

entries.name: trusted
doc: Markup the caller has taken responsibility for.
The only way text becomes markup. Named rather than convenient on purpose:
an escape hatch that is easy to reach is the same as no escaping, while one
that must be named is a decision somebody made and a reviewer can find.

entries.name: trustedDestination
doc: A destination the caller has taken responsibility for.
The only way an unchecked destination is written, named so it cannot be
reached by accident and appears in the source where somebody chose it.

entries.name: Unsafe
doc: Why a destination or an attribute was refused.

entries.name: when
doc: One view or the other, for a branch that renders either.

entries.name: BytePlan
doc: A pre-compiled immutable byte plan with static size metadata.

entries.name: coalesceToMss
doc: Batches streaming chunks up to the TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) boundary.
Prevents small-packet amplification on mobile cellular networks and minimizes
OS socket transmission syscalls.

entries.name: compile
doc: Pre-compiles a list of chunks, aggregating static byte metrics.

entries.name: formatHexChunkHeader
doc: Formats an HTTP/1.1 chunk length into a hex frame header `<hex>\r\n` without string heap allocation.

entries.name: frameChunk
doc: Frames a byte payload as an HTTP/1.1 chunk: `<hex-length>\r\n<payload>\r\n`.

entries.name: RawChunk
doc: A chunk of an HTML template: either pre-baked static bytes or a named dynamic slot.

entries.name: renderToBytes
doc: Assembles the byte plan and runtime slot values directly into a contiguous unboxed buffer.
Pre-computes exact capacity to perform a single contiguous allocation followed by
vectorized memory block copies (`Buffer.copy`), avoiding string reallocations.

entries.name: a
doc: A link, whose destination is set with `href`.

entries.name: article
doc: Content that stands on its own, such as a post or a comment.

entries.name: aside
doc: Content related to what surrounds it but separable from it.

entries.name: blockquote
doc: A quotation from another source.

entries.name: body
doc: The document's rendered content.

entries.name: br
doc: A line break.

entries.name: Building
doc: The attributes and content a node accepts.
Common attributes have a method of their own; `at` sets any other.

entries.name: button
doc: A button. Use `submit` to make it submit its form.

entries.name: code
doc: A fragment of code.

entries.name: dd
doc: The description of the term before it.

entries.name: details
doc: A disclosure that a reader can open and close.

entries.name: dialog
doc: A dialogue box or other interactive component.

entries.name: div
doc: A grouping with no meaning of its own, for layout or styling.

entries.name: dl
doc: A list of terms and their descriptions.

entries.name: document
doc: Renders a node as a whole document, prefixed with `<!DOCTYPE html>`.

entries.name: dt
doc: A term in a description list.

entries.name: em
doc: Content with stress emphasis.

entries.name: fieldset
doc: A group of related controls within a form.

entries.name: figcaption
doc: The caption for a figure.

entries.name: figure
doc: Self-contained content with an optional caption.

entries.name: footer
doc: Closing content for the page or the section around it.

entries.name: form
doc: A group of controls submitted together.

entries.name: h1
doc: A first-level heading.

entries.name: h2
doc: A second-level heading.

entries.name: h3
doc: A third-level heading.

entries.name: h4
doc: A fourth-level heading.

entries.name: h5
doc: A fifth-level heading.

entries.name: h6
doc: A sixth-level heading.

entries.name: head
doc: The document's metadata, which is not rendered.

entries.name: header
doc: Introductory content for the page or the section around it.

entries.name: hr
doc: A thematic break between sections of content.

entries.name: html
doc: The root element of a document.

entries.name: html
doc: A node with no tag name renders as its children alone, with no element
around them. That is what `words` and `nothing` produce.

entries.name: html
doc: The view this node describes.

entries.name: img
doc: An image, whose source is set with `src` and description with `alt`.

entries.name: input
doc: A form control. Its kind is set with `kind`.

entries.name: labelFor
doc: A caption for a control. Named `labelFor` because `label` sets an attribute.

entries.name: legend
doc: The caption for a fieldset.

entries.name: li
doc: One item of a list.

entries.name: link
doc: A relationship to another resource, such as a stylesheet.

entries.name: main
doc: The content particular to this page.

entries.name: meta
doc: A piece of document metadata, such as the character set.

entries.name: nav
doc: A group of navigation links.

entries.name: Node
doc: Builds HTML by naming a tag as a function and its attributes as methods.
button().class("send").submit().says("Post")
renders `<button class="send" type="submit">Post</button>`.
A node holds a tag name, its attributes in the order they were given, and
its children. Every method answers a new node, so a partly built node may
be kept and finished more than once.

entries.name: nothing
doc: A node that renders nothing.

entries.name: ol
doc: A list whose order carries meaning.

entries.name: option
doc: One choice within a select.

entries.name: p
doc: A paragraph.

entries.name: pre
doc: Text whose whitespace and line breaks are kept as written.

entries.name: progress
doc: The progress of a task.

entries.name: render
doc: Renders a node on its own, without a doctype.

entries.name: script
doc: A script written into the document, or a reference to one.

entries.name: section
doc: A themed grouping of content, usually with a heading.

entries.name: select
doc: A control offering a list of options.

entries.name: small
doc: Side comments such as small print.

entries.name: span
doc: A run of inline content with no meaning of its own.

entries.name: strong
doc: Content with strong importance.

entries.name: style
doc: A stylesheet written into the document.

entries.name: summary
doc: The visible heading of a disclosure.

entries.name: table
doc: A table of rows and columns.

entries.name: tag
doc: An element with the given tag name, for tags without a function here.

entries.name: tbody
doc: The group of rows that make up a table's body.

entries.name: td
doc: A data cell.

entries.name: textarea
doc: A control for text of more than one line.

entries.name: tfoot
doc: The group of rows that summarise a table.

entries.name: th
doc: A header cell, naming a row or a column.

entries.name: thead
doc: The group of rows that head a table.

entries.name: time
doc: A time or a date, machine-readable through `at("datetime", ...)`.

entries.name: tr
doc: One row of a table.

entries.name: ul
doc: A list whose order carries no meaning.

entries.name: words
doc: Text as a node, so it can appear in a list beside elements. Escaped.

entries.name: Composition
doc: Content reads top to bottom; every adding method returns the next value.

entries.name: content
doc: Content holding nothing, to be added to.

entries.name: Content
doc: An ordered, persistent sequence of typed views.

entries.name: document
doc: A whole page with the given title and body.

entries.name: documentIn
doc: A whole page, declaring the language it is written in.

entries.name: adaptiveImage
entries.signature: &Std.Http.Server.Resilience.NetworkProfile -> Str -> Str -> Int -> Int -> Std.Html.Media.Priority -> Str -> Bytes
doc: Renders a network-adaptive `` tag tuned for device telemetry and network bandwidth.
On poor networks (2G/3G) or `Save-Data: on`:
- If `lqipDataUri` is provided, it is used directly as the `src` to avoid round-trips.
- Enforces `loading="lazy"`, `decoding="async"`, and `fetchpriority="low"`.
On high-speed networks:
- With `Priority.Critical`, enforces `loading="eager"`, `decoding="sync"`, and `fetchpriority="high"`.

entries.name: adaptivePicture
entries.signature: &Std.Http.Server.Resilience.NetworkProfile -> Str -> Str -> Int -> Int -> &Array[Std.Html.Media.SourceRule] -> Std.Html.Media.Priority -> Bytes
doc: Renders a network-adaptive `<picture>` container.
Filters out bandwidth-heavy and desktop-only sources (`minWidth > 800`) on constrained
mobile connections, drastically reducing payload sizes over 2G/3G links.

entries.name: Priority
doc: Rendering priority for responsive media.

entries.name: SourceRule
doc: Specification for a responsive source candidate within a `<picture>` element.

entries.name: chunks
doc: The page as its pieces, in order, so a caller may write them as they come.

entries.name: document
doc: A whole view rendered with its length, without a plan.

entries.name: finish
doc: The page with its length in bytes, which is what a response header needs.

entries.name: fragment
doc: A view rendered with its length, without a plan.

entries.name: Piece
doc: Part of a page: either fixed markup or a named hole.

entries.name: Plan
doc: A page prepared once, ready to be filled and rendered many times.

entries.name: prepare
doc: Render static sections once; the plan never stores request-specific slots.

entries.name: Prepared
doc: A piece after preparing: rendered text, or the hole still to fill.

entries.name: render
doc: The page as one piece of text.

entries.name: Rendered
doc: A rendered page and its length in bytes.

entries.name: RenderError
doc: Why a prepared page could not be rendered.

entries.name: renderWithin
doc: The page, refused if it would exceed the given number of bytes.

entries.name: documentHead
doc: Generates the early flush HTML document head strictly bounded for 1-RTT delivery.

entries.name: documentTail
doc: Generates closing markup for the document stream.

entries.name: renderSuspended
doc: Paired helper generating both initial fallback and deferred replacement chunks.

entries.name: suspenseError
doc: Generates the out-of-order error template and inline resolution script.
Replaces the placeholder contents with the error fallback without crashing the HTTP stream.

entries.name: suspensePlaceholder
doc: Generates the initial placeholder container for a Suspense boundary.

entries.name: suspenseReplacement
doc: Generates the out-of-order replacement template and inline resolution script.
Executes immediately upon stream receipt in the browser, swapping the placeholder
contents synchronously without an external client framework runtime.

entries.name: allowsBody
doc: Whether a status is defined to carry no body, whatever the headers say.

entries.name: base64
doc: Text encoded as base64, without line breaks.

entries.name: basicAuth
doc: A user name and password written as a basic authorization value.
The credentials are encoded, not protected: basic authorization is only safe
over a secured connection, and this function cannot check that it is on one.

entries.name: bearerAuth
doc: A bearer token written as an authorization value.

entries.name: contentLength
doc: The length a `content-length` header reports, or `None`.

entries.name: Cookie
doc: A cookie as a request carries it: a name and a value.

entries.name: endToEnd
doc: The headers a proxy may forward, with the connection's own removed.

entries.name: expectsBody
doc: Whether a method carries a body describing what to do.
A query must carry one and must say what it is: a server is required to
refuse a query whose content type is missing or does not match its body,
because the body is the request and a body it cannot read is a request it
cannot answer.

entries.name: hasHeader
doc: Whether a header is present.

entries.name: header
doc: The first value given for a header, matched without regard to case.

entries.name: headerAccept
doc: The header names the protocol defines, so a caller never spells one wrong.
Lower case throughout, because header names are compared without regard to
case and one spelling is easier to compare than two.

entries.name: headerAcceptCharset
doc: The character sets a client will accept.

entries.name: headerAcceptEncoding
doc: The content codings a client will accept, such as gzip.

entries.name: headerAcceptLanguage
doc: The languages a client prefers.

entries.name: headerAcceptRanges
doc: The range units a server accepts, or `none`.

entries.name: headerAge
doc: How long a cached response has been held, in seconds.

entries.name: headerAllow
doc: The methods a resource supports.

entries.name: headerAuthorization
doc: The client's credentials for the request.

entries.name: headerCacheControl
doc: How the response may be cached, and for how long.

entries.name: headerConnection
doc: Options for this connection only, such as `close`.

entries.name: headerContentEncoding
doc: The codings applied to the body, in the order applied.

entries.name: headerContentLanguage
doc: The languages the body is intended for.

entries.name: headerContentLength
doc: The length of the body in bytes.

entries.name: headerContentLocation
doc: Where the body can be found on its own.

entries.name: headerContentRange
doc: Which part of the whole this body is.

entries.name: headerContentType
doc: The media type of the body, and its character set.

entries.name: headerCookie
doc: Cookies the client is sending back.

entries.name: headerDate
doc: When the message was produced.

entries.name: headerETag
doc: A tag identifying this version of the resource.

entries.name: headerExpect
doc: What the client requires the server to support.

entries.name: headerExpires
doc: When the response stops being fresh.

entries.name: headerHost
doc: The host and port the request is addressed to.

entries.name: headerIfMatch
doc: Act only if the resource matches one of these tags.

entries.name: headerIfModifiedSince
doc: Act only if the resource changed after this time.

entries.name: headerIfNoneMatch
doc: Act only if the resource matches none of these tags.

entries.name: headerIfRange
doc: Send the range only if the resource is unchanged.

entries.name: headerIfUnmodifiedSince
doc: Act only if the resource has not changed since this time.

entries.name: headerLastModified
doc: When the resource last changed.

entries.name: headerLocation
doc: Where to go instead, or where a new resource was created.

entries.name: headerOrigin
doc: The origin the request was made from.

entries.name: headerPragma
doc: Directives kept for caches that predate `cache-control`.

entries.name: headerRange
doc: The part of the resource the client is asking for.

entries.name: headerReferer
doc: The page the request was made from.

entries.name: headerRetryAfter
doc: How long to wait before asking again.

entries.name: headerServer
doc: What software answered the request.

entries.name: headerSetCookie
doc: A cookie for the client to store and send back.

entries.name: headerTransferEncoding
doc: The codings applied for transfer, such as `chunked`.

entries.name: headerUpgrade
doc: Other protocols the sender would rather speak.

entries.name: headerUserAgent
doc: What software made the request.

entries.name: headerValues
doc: Every value given for a header.

entries.name: headerVary
doc: Which request headers a cached response depends on.

entries.name: headerWwwAuthenticate
doc: How the client should authenticate.

entries.name: isCacheable
doc: Whether a response to a method may be kept and used again.
A query is cacheable, which is the reason it exists rather than being a
post with a different name. What a cache stores it under has to take in the
request's body, since that is where the terms are: two queries to one
target asking different things are different requests, and a cache keyed on
the target alone would answer the second with the first's result.

entries.name: isChunked
doc: Whether a message says its body is sent in chunks.

entries.name: isClientError
doc: Whether a status blames the caller.

entries.name: isError
doc: Whether a status reports any kind of failure.

entries.name: isHopByHop
doc: Whether a header belongs to one connection rather than to the message.
A proxy must not pass these on.

entries.name: isIdempotent
doc: Whether repeating a method has the same effect as sending it once.

entries.name: isInformational
doc: Whether a status reports a provisional response.

entries.name: isRedirect
doc: Whether a status asks the caller to look elsewhere.

entries.name: isSafe
doc: Whether a method is defined to have no effect on the server.
A caller retrying a failed request needs this and nothing else.

entries.name: isServerError
doc: Whether a status blames the server.

entries.name: isSuccess
doc: Whether a status reports success.

entries.name: keepsAlive
doc: Whether a version keeps the connection open unless told otherwise.

entries.name: keepsMethodOnRedirect
doc: The status a redirect answers with, and whether the method must be kept.
A 301, 302, or 303 historically became a `GET`; 307 and 308 do not, which is
the whole reason those two exist.

entries.name: mediaType
doc: The media type a `content-type` header names, without its parameters.

entries.name: Method
doc: A request method.
The closed set the protocol defines, plus `Other` for a method a server
accepts that this list does not name: refusing to represent one would make
the type useless for the servers that have them.
`Query` carries its terms in the request's own body rather than in the
target. A search whose terms do not fit a target — because they are long,
deeply structured, or should not sit in a log or a history — was otherwise
sent as a post, which says the request changes something and so may be
neither cached nor retried. This says what such a request actually is: safe,
idempotent, and cacheable, with the terms in the body.

entries.name: methodFrom
doc: The method a name stands for, or the fallback when it names none.

entries.name: methodName
doc: A method written the way the protocol writes it.

entries.name: negotiate
doc: The first offered choice the caller will accept, or `None`.
A weight of nought is a refusal, not a low preference, so it never matches.

entries.name: parseAuth
doc: The scheme and the credentials an authorization header carries.

entries.name: parseCookies
doc: Every cookie a `cookie` header carries.

entries.name: parseForm
doc: A form body read back into fields.

entries.name: parsePreferences
doc: An `accept`-style header read into choices, best first.
Weights are read in thousandths so they can be compared as whole numbers; a
choice with no weight is worth one, as the protocol says.

entries.name: parseRanges
doc: The ranges a `range` header asks for, or nothing when it asks for none.

entries.name: Preference
doc: One offered choice and the weight the caller gave it.

entries.name: Range
doc: A byte range a request asked for: a first position and an optional last.

entries.name: reasonFor
doc: The reason phrase that goes with a status code.

entries.name: redirectTarget
doc: The target a redirect names, or `None` when the response is not one.

entries.name: renderChunked
doc: A body written as one chunk followed by the terminator.

entries.name: renderContentRange
doc: A `content-range` header value for a range of a known total length.

entries.name: renderCookies
doc: Cookies written as a `cookie` header value.

entries.name: renderForm
doc: A form body written as `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.

entries.name: renderHead
doc: A request written as the protocol writes it, without a body.
Enough to inspect, log, or compare a request without sending one.

entries.name: renderSetCookie
doc: A cookie written as a `set-cookie` header value.

entries.name: renderStatusLine
doc: A response's first line, as the protocol writes it.

entries.name: request
doc: A request with a method and a target and nothing else.

entries.name: Request
doc: A request, with nothing about how it will be sent.
Transport is not here because it needs the foreign interface; everything a
caller decides before sending is, so a request can be built, inspected, and
tested without one.

entries.name: Response
doc: A response, with nothing about how it arrived.

entries.name: responseBytes
doc: The body as bytes, with a binary body taking precedence over the text one.
The body alone, not the status line and headers: this is what a
`Content-Length` counts and what `Std.Http.Message` puts after the head it
renders separately.

entries.name: setCookie
doc: A cookie with only a name and a value, and the safe attributes set.
Secure and http-only default to on: a cookie that does not need them can
turn them off deliberately, and one that does need them will otherwise
forget.

entries.name: SetCookie
doc: The attributes a response attaches when it sets a cookie.

entries.name: setHeader
doc: Headers with every value for a name removed, then one added.

entries.name: status
doc: A status built from its number, with the reason the protocol gives.

entries.name: Status
doc: A response status: its number and the reason given with it.

entries.name: Version
doc: The protocol version a message was written in.

entries.name: versionFrom
doc: The protocol version a name stands for.

entries.name: versionName
doc: A version written the way the protocol writes it.

entries.name: withBody
doc: A request with a body, and the length header that goes with it.

entries.name: withForm
doc: A request with a form body and the headers that describe it.

entries.name: withHeader
doc: A request with one header added, keeping any it already had.

entries.name: withJson
doc: A request with a JSON body and the headers that describe it.
The body is taken as written: encoding a value is `Std.Json`'s work, and
doing it here would make this module depend on that one for no gain.

entries.name: ClientError
doc: Why a request did not answer.

entries.name: explain
doc: What went wrong, in words for a person.

entries.name: fetch
doc: Request a URL, within the given limits.

entries.name: isRedirect
doc: Whether a status code asks the client to go elsewhere.

entries.name: Limiting
doc: What a request is allowed to cost and where it is allowed to go.
A caller bounding a request says two or three of these at once — how long,
how much, how far — and as methods they read down the page in the order the
decisions are made rather than wrapped inside one another.

entries.name: limits
doc: The bounds a request has when the caller does not say.

entries.name: Limits
doc: What a request may cost, and where it may go.
Bounds rather than none: an unbounded client is a way to exhaust the memory
of the program that made the request rather than of the one that answered.

entries.name: originsMatch
doc: Whether two URLs share a scheme, host and port.

entries.name: resolved
doc: An address resolved against the one it was found on.

entries.name: send
doc: Send a request and read what comes back.
Every hop is checked against the address rules as though it were the first,
because a redirect is a new request to a new place and treating it as a
continuation is how the checks get skipped.

entries.name: checkLength
doc: Whether a message's declared length matches the body it carried.
A short body is how a truncated read shows itself, and a caller reading from
a connection needs to tell that from a complete message.

entries.name: decodeChunked
doc: A chunked body read back into the bytes it framed.
Stops at the terminating chunk, ignoring any trailer, which is what a reader
that only wants the body should do.

entries.name: decodeChunkedBytes
doc: Remove chunk framing in octets, refusing truncated or malformed data.

entries.name: explain
doc: A reader's failure explained in the terms a caller can report.

entries.name: MessageError
doc: What stopped a message from being read.

entries.name: parseHead
doc: A request read from text where the head has already been separated from the body.

entries.name: parseRequest
doc: A request read from the text a connection carried.
Line endings are accepted as `\r\n` or `\n`, because a message written by
hand for a test is worth reading and refusing it teaches nothing.

entries.name: parseResponse
doc: A response read from the text a connection carried.

entries.name: redirect
doc: A redirect to a target, with the status a caller chooses.

entries.name: renderRequest
doc: A request written as the protocol writes it, head and body together.

entries.name: renderResponse
doc: A response written as the protocol writes it.

entries.name: renderResponseBytes
doc: Serialize binary payloads without a text or base64 conversion.

entries.name: respond
doc: A response built from a status and a body, with the headers that describe it.

entries.name: respondBytes
doc: A response carrying bytes, with a status and a media type.

entries.name: respondEmpty
doc: A response with no body, for the statuses that carry none.

entries.name: responseComplete
doc: Whether a complete response has arrived without waiting for its connection to close.
A declared length and a terminating chunk frame are message boundaries. `HEAD` and statuses
that never carry a body end at the blank line after their headers. A response without one of
those boundaries remains incomplete until its transport reports closure.

entries.name: accepting
doc: Bounds a program chose.

entries.name: allNamed
doc: Every part sent under a field, for a form that repeated one.

entries.name: boundaryOf
doc: The boundary a content type names, or nothing when it names none.

entries.name: declaredTypeOf
doc: What the sender said the file is.
Carried because a program may want it, and never treated as a fact about
the bytes: it is a claim by whoever sent them, and a program that decides
what to do from this alone has let the sender choose.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says.

entries.name: explainName
doc: What a refusal about a name says.

entries.name: field
doc: The part sent under a field, if the form carried one.

entries.name: fields
doc: The fields a form carried, each once, in the order they arrived.

entries.name: isFile
doc: Whether a part was sent as a file rather than as a value.

entries.name: limits
doc: What a read accepts when nobody says otherwise.

entries.name: Limits
doc: How much a read will accept.
Bounds rather than none: a body announcing ten thousand parts is not a
form, it is a way to exhaust the memory of whatever reads it.

entries.name: MultipartError
doc: Why a body could not be read.

entries.name: NameError
doc: Why a name cannot be written to disk.

entries.name: Part
doc: One thing a form carried.
`filename` is what the sender called it, kept as what it is. It is not a
path and this module will not make one from it: see `safeName`.

entries.name: read
doc: The parts a body carried.
The bounds are applied while reading rather than afterwards, because a
bound checked afterwards is a bound checked once the memory is gone.

entries.name: safeName
doc: A name safe to write to disk, or the reason there is none.
Only what follows the last separator of either kind survives, so a name
carrying a directory carries nothing after this. Nothing is decoded first:
what arrived is what was sent, and undoing an encoding before checking is
how a check is bypassed.

entries.name: safeNameOf
doc: The same, for a name a caller already holds.

entries.name: senderName
doc: What the sender called the file.
What the sender called it, and nothing more. It is not a path and must not
be joined to one: a file uploaded as `../../etc/passwd` has that as its
name, and a program that joins it to a directory has been told where to
write by whoever sent it. Ask `safeName` for something that may be written.

entries.name: sizeOf
doc: How large a part is.

entries.name: textOf
doc: A part's content as text, for the fields that are text.

entries.name: Adjusting
doc: A policy with one part changed, each answering the policy rather than
taking it apart.
Methods, so a policy that differs from the starting point in three ways
reads down the page rather than wrapping each call in the next.

entries.name: backoff
doc: A starting point that suits a call between services.
Three attempts rather than more: a fault that survives two retries is
usually not the kind that a third fixes, and the caller is waiting.

entries.name: Backoff
doc: How many times to try, and how long to wait between attempts.
A service that calls another over a network will meet a failure that would
have succeeded a moment later: a connection reset while an instance
restarts, a gateway between deployments, a rate limit that clears. Trying
again is the whole answer, and doing it without these three rules is worse
than not doing it at all.
**Wait longer each time.** Retrying immediately turns one failure into
several, and every caller retrying at once at the moment a service comes
back is what stops it coming back.
**Wait a random amount.** Every caller backing off by the same doubling
arrives together anyway, one step later. The spread is what breaks that up,
and it is why `jitter` is not a refinement to add afterwards.
**Give up.** A budget bounds the total wait, so a request cannot sit for
minutes behind a service that is simply down while whoever asked for it
waits.

entries.name: describe
doc: How many attempts a plan makes, and how long it may spend waiting.
For a caller deciding whether a retry plan fits inside its own deadline: a
retry that outlives the request it belongs to is a retry nobody is waiting
for.

entries.name: fetch
doc: Fetch a page, trying again when trying again could help.

entries.name: repeatable
doc: Whether a request may be sent twice without meaning something different.
The question a retry actually turns on, and the one that is usually skipped.
Reading the same thing twice is reading it; charging a card twice is
charging it twice. A `POST` is therefore not retried here unless the caller
says it carries a key that makes a repeat harmless.

entries.name: send
doc: Send a request, trying again when trying again could help.
A request that cannot be repeated safely is sent once whatever the backoff
says, because the alternative is a duplicate order rather than a slow one.
Mark such a request with an idempotency key if the service accepts one, and
it will be retried.

entries.name: waitFor
doc: How long to wait before attempt `attempt`, counting the first as zero.
Doubling from the first wait, capped, then reduced by up to the jitter
proportion. Reduced rather than increased so the cap stays a cap.

entries.name: worthRetrying
doc: Whether a failure is worth trying again.
A request is retried when nothing says it was received and acted on: a
connection that failed, a deadline that passed, a gateway that had nothing
behind it. It is not retried when the answer says the request itself was
wrong — a 400 sent twice is wrong twice — nor on a 500, which says the
request was received and something went wrong while acting on it, and which
may well have half-happened.
The exception is 429 and 503, which are a service asking to be asked later.

entries.name: bodyLength
doc: How long a body a message says is coming.

entries.name: changeAllowed
doc: Whether a request may change something.
A method that changes nothing is always allowed. One that does must have
come from this site, and a request that stated nothing is treated as
though it came from elsewhere — an old client and a hostile one look the
same, and only one reading is safe for both.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says.

entries.name: framing
doc: How long a body a message says is coming.
A message that says it two ways is refused rather than resolved. There is
no precedence rule here because a rule only helps when everything in the
chain shares it, and a message framed two ways exists precisely because
they do not.
How long a body a message says is coming, and whether it is chunked.

entries.name: headersWritable
doc: Every header, checked, so a message is refused before any of it is written
rather than after some of it has been.

entries.name: headerWritable
doc: Whether a header may be written as it stands.
A carriage return or line feed would end the header and begin whatever
followed it, which is a response the sender did not write. Refused rather
than escaped: escaping guesses at an intent, and no legitimate value
contains one.

entries.name: isChunked
doc: Whether a message says its body is chunked, which is a separate question
from how long it is.

entries.name: originOf
doc: The scheme and host a URL names, which is what an origin comparison is
between — a path or a query never makes two targets different origins.

entries.name: outboundHost
doc: An address a request named, refused when it is one the network trusts.

entries.name: Provenance
doc: Where a request says it came from.
Read from what the browser states and a page cannot forge. `Unstated` is
its own answer rather than being folded into one of the others, because a
caller decides what silence means and that decision differs by method.

entries.name: provenanceOf
doc: Where the request says it came from.

entries.name: redirectTarget
doc: A redirect target the program named, or a refusal.
A path within this site is always allowed. An absolute target must name an
origin on the list the program gave. A target taken from a request and used
unchecked is how a trusted name is borrowed to make a link look real.

entries.name: reservedHost
doc: Whether a host is one the network trusts and a request should not be able
to make a server reach.
A server that fetches what it was told to fetch is a way to reach what only
the server can reach: the machine itself, the network it sits on, and the
address that answers with the credentials of the environment it runs in.

entries.name: resolveUnder
doc: A path resolved under a root it cannot leave.
Segments are consumed one at a time and an ascent past the root refuses.
Nothing looks for the shape of an escaping path: every filter of that kind
has an encoding that gets past it, and by the time a segment exists the
encoding has already been undone.

entries.name: Unsafe
doc: Why a request or a value was refused.
Each names what was wrong rather than saying that something was, because
these are the failures an operator reads in a log and has to act on.

entries.name: Configuring
doc: A server with one decision changed, each answering the server rather than
taking it apart.
Methods, so a server that differs from the default in four ways reads down
the page in the order the decisions are made. As functions taking the
server first, each call had to be wrapped in the next and the server a
reader looks for first ended up furthest in.

entries.name: handlerOf
doc: The handler a server presents, with every step wrapped around it.
Built once rather than per request: the chain is the same for every
request, and rebuilding it on each one would put the whole of the server's
configuration inside its hot path.

entries.name: listenAndServe
doc: Start, serve, and stop, for a caller that wants one call.

entries.name: logging
doc: A step that writes a line about every request once its answer is known.
Given as an example of the shape as much as for its own sake: it calls on,
times what it wrapped, and reports afterwards, which is what a step that
only ran before could not do.

entries.name: portOf
doc: Which port a running server is on.
Worth asking even when a port was named, because a server started on port
zero was given one by the machine and this is the only way to learn it.

entries.name: run
doc: Accept connections into a bounded queue consumed by a fixed worker pool.
A connection is handled on its own thread, so one slow request does not
hold up every other client. That is the difference between a server and a
queue: without it, a handler that waits on a database stops the whole
program for as long as it waits.
`limit` bounds how many connections are accepted before the loop ends, so a
caller wanting one does not have to arrange to stop the server. A limit of
zero or less accepts until the server is stopped.

entries.name: Running
doc: A running server, and the switch that stops it.

entries.name: serveConnection
doc: Serve one connection: read a request, answer it, and say whether the
connection may carry another.
A connection is kept open unless something said otherwise, because opening
one costs a round trip and a client fetching a page makes many requests.
The response always states its own length, so the client knows where the
body ends without the connection closing to tell it.

entries.name: server
doc: A server over a router, with no middleware and the default limits.

entries.name: Server
doc: A server, ready to be given an address.

entries.name: ServerError
doc: Why a server could not start or could not keep serving.

entries.name: start
doc: Start listening, and answer what is needed to stop.

entries.name: stop
doc: Ask a server to stop.
Closing the listener is what ends the accept loop, because accepting does
not answer until a connection arrives and a flag alone would not be read
until one did. The flag is what tells the loop the failure was asked for
rather than a fault.

entries.name: stopOnSignal
doc: Stop the server when the supervisor asks the program to stop.
The drain below is careful and, until something calls `stop`, unreachable
in the one case it exists for: a deployment, where the request to stop
arrives as a signal. This is the wire between the two.
A thread does the waiting because accepting blocks: the loop is inside
`accept` when the signal arrives, and only closing the listener brings it
out. Closing is what `stop` already does, so the drain that follows is the
ordinary one and nothing here has to know how it works.
Answers whether the program can hear the request at all. `false` means this
platform has no such signal and the server will run until something else
stops it — worth reporting rather than assuming a drain that cannot happen.

entries.name: allowing
doc: The same, permitting different methods.

entries.name: audited
doc: Audit logging middleware recording security outcomes in the tamper-evident audit ledger.

entries.name: boundedConcurrency
doc: Bounded concurrent request admission middleware enforcing backpressure.
When active inflight requests reach `maxInflight`, excess requests are shed immediately
with status 503 Service Unavailable and `Retry-After: 1`, preventing memory starvation.

entries.name: circuitBreaker
entries.signature: Int -> Int -> fn(Std.Http.Server.Route.Request, fn(Std.Http.Server.Route.Request) -> Std.Http.Response) -> Std.Http.Response
doc: Circuit breaker middleware protecting downstream dependencies from cascading failure.
Trips open when consecutive 5xx errors reach `failureThreshold`, fast-failing with 503
for `resetTimeoutSeconds` before permitting a half-open probe request.

entries.name: identified
doc: A request identity, carried into the answer.
Taken from the request when it brought one, so a value that entered at a
proxy stays the same value across every service it reaches. Made from what
this program can see when it did not.

entries.name: identityOf
doc: The identity a request carries, or one made for it.

entries.name: protectedHeaders
doc: The protective headers, added to whatever the answer was.
Added rather than replaced where a handler already set one, because a
handler that set a policy meant it and this step is a floor rather than a
ceiling.

entries.name: quiet
doc: A step that answers a refusal the same way whatever caused it.
What crosses the network is a status and a sentence; the identity in the
answer is what ties it to the detail recorded elsewhere. An error that
explains itself tells a stranger about the program.

entries.name: rateLimited
entries.signature: Int -> Int -> fn(Std.Http.Server.Route.Request, fn(Std.Http.Server.Route.Request) -> Std.Http.Response) -> Std.Http.Response
doc: A rate limiting middleware that restricts requests per peer within a moving window.
Refuses requests exceeding `maxRequests` per `windowSeconds` with RFC 6585 status 429
and sets the `Retry-After` header.

entries.name: redirect
doc: A redirect to somewhere the program named, or a refusal.
A target taken from a request and used unchecked is how a trusted name is
borrowed to make a link look real, so the check is here rather than left to
each handler.

entries.name: sameSiteOnly
doc: A refusal of state-changing requests that came from another site.
The browser states where a request came from in a header a page cannot
forge, which makes this stronger than a token a page has to carry: it
cannot be forgotten by the author of a form. A token remains available for
what the header does not cover.

entries.name: shared
doc: The cross-origin permission, from the allowlist and only from it.

entries.name: shareNothing
doc: A service that permits no other origin to read its answers.

entries.name: shareWith
doc: A service that permits the named origins, and nothing else.

entries.name: Sharing
doc: Which origins a service permits to read its answers.
An allowlist and nothing else. Reflecting back whichever origin asked is
indistinguishable from permitting everything, and is what a
misconfiguration produces; a wildcard alongside credentials is refused by
browsers anyway and states an intention nobody has.

entries.name: standard
doc: Every protection, in the order they belong.
The outermost is applied first, so the identity is attached before anything
can fail and the headers are added to whatever answer comes back, including
a refusal. A program that needs one of these to differ writes that one step
itself rather than turning this off.

entries.name: strict
doc: Every protection for a service nothing shares with, which is most of them.

entries.name: timeout
doc: Request deadline middleware enforcing an execution time budget.
If the wrapped handler does not produce a response within `timeoutMs`,
RFC 7231 status 504 Gateway Timeout is returned immediately to the client.

entries.name: traced
doc: A step that answers with the trace the request belongs to.
So a caller holding an answer can find the record of what produced it, and
a service handing work on has the header to hand on.

entries.name: traceOf
doc: The trace a request belongs to, continued from what it carried.
Read here rather than in each handler, so every service in a chain agrees
about what piece of work a request is part of. A request that carried
nothing readable begins a new one rather than being refused: the header is
a diagnostic, and refusing over a malformed diagnostic makes the diagnosis
into the outage.

entries.name: withCredentials
doc: The same, for a caller that also sends credentials. A wildcard is not
reachable from here, which is why credentials can be permitted at all.

entries.name: answer
doc: Post an answer for one invocation.

entries.name: explain
doc: Why a loop ended, in words a deployment log can be read by.

entries.name: fail
doc: Say an invocation could not be answered.
Reported rather than left unanswered. An invocation nothing answers is
retried, and a request that fails the same way every time is retried until
the platform stops — so a failure said once costs one invocation, and a
failure not said costs every retry the platform is willing to make.

entries.name: failedToStart
doc: Say the program could not start at all.
Said before any invocation is taken, so the platform stops rather than
sending work to a process that cannot do it. Without it a function whose
configuration is wrong answers every request with the same failure, and the
platform reports a service that is failing rather than one that never began.
