entries.name: fromEnvironment
doc: The interface this process was started under, when it was started under one.
Absent everywhere else, which is how a program tells the two apart: serve the
loop when there is an interface to ask, and open a listener when there is
not. The same program then runs under a platform and on a developer's machine
without being built differently for each.

entries.name: Invocation
doc: One invocation, as the platform hands it over.

entries.name: LambdaError
doc: Serving a platform that invokes a program instead of connecting to it.
A serverless platform does not open a socket to a service. It starts a
process, hands it one request at a time, and freezes it in between — so a
program written as a listener has nothing to listen to, and the usual answer
is a wrapper in whatever language the platform runs natively. That wrapper
then holds a second copy of whatever it had to do to answer, which is a
second copy that can disagree with the first.
This is the other answer: the program asks the platform for work rather than
waiting to be connected to. What it serves is an ordinary handler — the same
one a listener serves — so nothing about a service has to be written twice.
The loop is the one AWS Lambda defines and every platform built on it
speaks. It is written here rather than in the compiler because it is a use of
the library rather than a property of the language: a request is fetched, a
handler answers it, the answer is posted back, and none of that needs the
evaluator's help.
Why a run of the loop ended.
A loop that ends is worth telling apart from one that was stopped. The
platform is entitled to freeze a process between requests and to end it
whenever it likes, so ending is ordinary — but ending because the address of
the runtime was never set is a program started outside a platform, and that
is a mistake in how it was deployed rather than a shutdown.

entries.name: nextInvocation
doc: Ask for the next invocation, waiting until there is one.
The identifier comes back in a header rather than in the body, so a reader
that only decoded the body would answer every invocation against nothing.

entries.name: Runtime
doc: The interface a platform offers, and the version of it being spoken.
A value rather than something read from the environment at each call. The
address and the version are the whole of what identifies an interface, and
holding them lets a program point at one this module did not assume: another
platform implementing the same protocol, a local one during development, or a
version after the one below.
It is also what makes this testable. A module that reached for the
environment inside every call could only be checked by setting environment
variables around it; a value can be pointed at a server written in a fixture.

entries.name: RUNTIME_ADDRESS_VARIABLE
doc: The variable a platform announces its runtime interface in.
Exported because a platform that sets a different one is a platform this
still works with: read that variable and hand the address to `runtimeAt`.

entries.name: RUNTIME_VERSION
doc: The version of the interface this module was written against.
A version identifier rather than a date, in the way `HTTP/1.1` is a version:
it names the shape of the paths, and AWS has published no other. Exported so
a program that meets another can say so rather than reimplement the module.

entries.name: runtimeAt
doc: An interface at a stated address, speaking the version this was written for.

entries.name: runtimePath
doc: Where the interface serves one of its paths.

entries.name: serve
doc: Take invocations and answer them until the platform stops the process.
The handler is given the event and answers the body to post back. It is the
caller's, so what a function does with an event — decode it as a request,
read a field, ignore it — stays in the program rather than here.
A handler that fails is reported against the invocation it failed on and the
loop continues. One request that cannot be answered is not a reason to stop
answering the next, and a process that ended on one bad request would be
started again to meet the same one.

entries.name: serveEnvironment
doc: Serve the interface this process was started under.
What a program written only for a platform calls. A program that also runs as
a listener asks `fromEnvironment` itself and decides.

entries.name: speaking
doc: The same interface, speaking a different version of the protocol.

entries.name: underARuntime
doc: Whether this program was started by a platform that invokes it.

entries.name: acceptQuery
doc: The media types a resource accepts for a request that carries its terms in
its body, as the header that advertises them.
Sent with the refusal a resource gives a body it cannot read, so a client
told its request was unreadable is also told what would be readable. A
refusal that only said no would leave the client guessing.

entries.name: bytes
doc: A response carrying arbitrary bytes with an explicit media type.

entries.name: computeEtag
doc: Computes a fast hex ETag hash from body content.

entries.name: conditional
doc: Evaluates If-None-Match in the request; answers 304 Not Modified on match or attaches ETag on miss.

entries.name: empty
doc: A response with a status and nothing else.

entries.name: gatewayTimeout
doc: A 504 Gateway Timeout response.

entries.name: html
doc: A response carrying HTML.

entries.name: json
doc: A response carrying JSON, already encoded.

entries.name: jsonValue
doc: Encode the standard JSON model at the response boundary.

entries.name: notModified
doc: A 304 Not Modified response with an ETag and empty body.

entries.name: page
doc: Render a complete HTML document, including its doctype.

entries.name: rendered
doc: Reuse server-rendered output and its UTF-8 length without rendering again.

entries.name: serviceUnavailable
doc: A 503 Service Unavailable response with a Retry-After directive in seconds.

entries.name: text
doc: The answers a handler gives, apart from the routing that chose it and the
connection that carries it.
Separated because a reply is the one part of serving that a program builds
without a request in hand: a test naming an expected response, a middleware
refusing one, and a handler answering one all want these and none of them
wants a server.
A response carrying text.

entries.name: tooManyRequests
doc: A 429 Too Many Requests response with a Retry-After directive in seconds.

entries.name: unprocessable
doc: The refusal a body the resource could read but could not act on receives.
Distinct from a body it could not read at all: one says the type was wrong,
the other says the content was, and a client can act on the difference.

entries.name: unsupportedMediaType
doc: The refusal a body in a type the resource cannot read receives.

entries.name: view
doc: Render a typed fragment using the standard HTML escaping rules.

entries.name: withEtag
doc: Attaches an ETag entity tag validator header to a response.

entries.name: enforceInitcwndBudget
doc: Enforces that an early flush payload fits strictly within the TCP initial congestion window (initcwnd).
Standard OS kernel `initcwnd` is 10 segments (~14,600 bytes). Staying below `maxBytes`
(default 14,000 bytes) ensures delivery to the client NIC in a single round-trip (1-RTT).

entries.name: inspectClientNetwork
doc: Inspects request headers for Client Hints and data-saving directives.

entries.name: NetworkProfile
doc: Classification of client connection constraints.

entries.name: selectAdaptivePayload
doc: Selects lightweight minimal markup on poor connections and full markup on broadband.

entries.name: swrHeaders
doc: Constructs RFC 5861 `stale-while-revalidate` Cache-Control directives and optional cache tags.

entries.name: adding
doc: A router with one more route after the ones it has.
For a program building its routes from something it read rather than from a
list written in the source.

entries.name: body
doc: The body a request carried.

entries.name: carriesFields
doc: Whether a request carried fields in the ordinary encoding.

entries.name: carriesForm
doc: Whether a request carried a form with files in it.

entries.name: delete
doc: A route answering DELETE on a path.

entries.name: dispatch
doc: Send a request through a router.
A path that matches a route written for another method answers that the
method is not allowed rather than that the path is not there. The two are
different to a client: one is a mistake in the request, and the other says
the thing does not exist.

entries.name: fieldsOf
doc: The fields an ordinary form posted.
A form without a file in it is sent as a query string in the body, which is
what every browser does for a `<form method="post">` unless it is told
otherwise. `formOf` reads the other shape — the multipart one a form uses
once it carries a file — and a program that only wants a title and a
checkbox should not have to reach for a parser built for uploads.
The body is read with the same decoder a query string is read with, because
it is the same encoding: `+` is a space, `%41` is an `A`, and a field
written twice keeps the last of them.

entries.name: formOf
doc: The form a request carried, when it carried one.
The seam between a handler and an uploaded form: a handler holds a request
and should not have to know how the parts were framed, or find the header
that says what separates them. What comes back keeps the sender's filename
as what it is — see [[Std Http Multipart]] for why that is never a path.

entries.name: get
doc: A route answering GET on a path.

entries.name: Handler
doc: What a handler is: a request in, a response out, and nothing else.
A handler cannot reach the connection, which is what makes it testable
without one. Every check over a handler in this module's own fixture calls
it directly, and a program's tests can do the same.

entries.name: header
doc: A header, found without regard to the case it was written in.
The protocol says a header name means the same thing however it is spelled,
and a client that wrote one differently from the server's expectation is
not making a mistake.

entries.name: joining
doc: Two routers joined, the first tried before the second.
This is how a group of routes written elsewhere is mounted: a module
exports its own router, and the program joins it to the rest.

entries.name: Middleware
doc: A step that wraps a handler.
It is given the request and the rest of the chain, so it decides whether
to call on at all: that is what lets one refuse a request outright, and it
is why this shape is used rather than a pair of before and after hooks. A
hook that ran before could only edit the request, never stop it.

entries.name: notFoundHandler
doc: The response a request nothing matched receives.

entries.name: on
doc: One route, as a value.
A route is built on its own rather than by adding to a router, so a list of
them reads down the page in the order they are tried. Building a router by
wrapping it in itself once per route puts the last route written outermost,
which reads backwards and nests one level deeper for every route added.

entries.name: param
doc: A captured piece of the path, or nothing when the pattern captured none.

entries.name: patch
doc: A route answering PATCH on a path.

entries.name: pathOf
doc: The path a target names, with its query removed.

entries.name: post
doc: A route answering POST on a path.

entries.name: put
doc: A route answering PUT on a path.

entries.name: query
doc: A route for a request carrying its terms in its own body.
Answered like any other route, and the terms are read from the body rather
than from the query. A handler for one is written against `body` where a
handler reached by a target's query is written against `queryParam`.

entries.name: queryOf
doc: The query a target carries, read once rather than by every handler.

entries.name: queryParam
doc: A query value, or nothing when the request carried none.

entries.name: Request
doc: What a request is once it has been routed, and how a router decides.
Separated from [[Std Http Server]] because routing needs no connection: a
handler is a request in and a response out, so a program checks its routes
and its chain of steps by calling them, without binding a port. The server
reads requests off sockets and hands them here.
A request as a handler sees it.
The protocol's own request is kept whole rather than taken apart, so a
handler that needs a header the router did not look at still has one. What
is added is the part routing produced: the path with its query removed, the
values a pattern captured, and the query read once rather than by every
handler that wants a parameter.

entries.name: Route
doc: One route: a method, a pattern, and what answers it.

entries.name: router
doc: A router with nothing in it, answering everything as not found.

entries.name: Router
doc: Where requests are sent, and what answers the ones nothing matched.

entries.name: routing
doc: A router over a list of routes.
Routes are tried in the order given, so a pattern that could also match an
earlier one never will. That is a rule a reader applies by reading down the
list, which the alternative — the most specific pattern wins — is not: it
asks the reader to compare every pattern against every other.

entries.name: under
doc: Every route with a prefix in front of its pattern.
So a group of routes can be written without repeating where they live, and
moved by changing one line.

entries.name: withFallback
doc: A router answering unmatched requests with something of its own.

entries.name: constantTimeCompare
doc: Compares tokens in constant time to prevent side-channel timing attacks.

entries.name: generateNonce
doc: Generates a hexadecimal nonce for per-request CSP inline script/style authorization.
Uses `seed` when positive for deterministic testing; draws from OS cryptographic
entropy (`Std.Random.secureBytes`) when `seed <= 0`.

entries.name: strictSecurityHeaders
doc: Generates defense-in-depth HTTP security headers with strict CSP.

entries.name: verifyOrigin
doc: Validates that mutation requests originate from the expected host.

entries.name: accept
doc: The answer that agrees to a lasting connection, or the reason it is refused.
The permitted origins are a parameter rather than a step that can be
omitted. A lasting connection is not subject to the rule that stops one
site reading another's answers: a page on any site can open one to any
server and it carries the viewer's cookies when it does. A server that
upgrades whoever asks has given every site an authenticated connection to
it, and the viewer sees nothing.

entries.name: accepting
doc: The value that proves this end followed the protocol.

entries.name: answering
doc: The answer a check of the far end expects.

entries.name: binary
doc: Bytes to send.

entries.name: completes
doc: Whether a frame completes the message it belongs to.

entries.name: decode
doc: The frame at the start of these bytes, and how many bytes it used.
The stated length is checked against the bound before anything is read, so
a sender cannot say how much memory to allocate.

entries.name: encode
doc: A frame to send to the far end.
Never masked. What this end sends is not masked and what it receives must
be, which is what the protocol requires and what stops a crafted message
being read as a request by something between the two ends.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says.

entries.name: Frame
doc: One frame read off a connection: what it is, whether it completes a
message, and what it carried.

entries.name: goodbye
doc: A goodbye to send.

entries.name: isControl
doc: Whether a frame is one the protocol handles rather than the program.

entries.name: isUpgrade
doc: Whether a request is asking for a lasting connection.

entries.name: Message
doc: What a message is.

entries.name: messageLimit
doc: How large a message this module reads when nothing said otherwise.

entries.name: messageOf
doc: What a frame means, once it is whole.

entries.name: SocketError
doc: Why a connection was refused or a frame would not be read.

entries.name: text
doc: Text to send.

entries.name: finishChunked
doc: Emits the HTTP/1.1 chunked terminator frame `0\r\n\r\n`.

entries.name: sendChunk
doc: Sends a single chunk framed as `<hex-length>\r\n<data>\r\n`.

entries.name: sendHead
doc: Sends HTTP status and headers immediately with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`.

entries.name: streamChunks
doc: Coordinates complete chunked response delivery over the socket.

entries.name: empty
doc: A pool holding no text.

entries.name: intern
doc: Preserve an existing ID or append the spelling and return the updated pool.

entries.name: internAll
doc: Intern in input order, preserving one ID per input occurrence.

entries.name: lookup
doc: Look up a spelling and check that the indexed ID still names that spelling.

entries.name: Pool
doc: A persistent, session-local spelling table. Thread returned pools forward.

entries.name: resolve
doc: Resolve a pool-local ID, refusing negative and out-of-range values.

entries.name: size
doc: How many distinct pieces of text the pool holds.

entries.name: empty
doc: Creates an empty interval tree.

entries.name: findOverlaps
doc: Finds all intervals in the tree that overlap with the query interval.

entries.name: fromIntervals
doc: Builds a balanced interval tree from an array of intervals in O(n log n) time.

entries.name: hasOverlap
doc: Tests whether any interval in the tree overlaps with the query interval.

entries.name: insert
doc: Inserts an interval into the tree and updates subtree maximum endpoints.

entries.name: interval
doc: Validates and constructs an interval where low <= high.

entries.name: Interval
doc: Closed 1D interval where low <= high.

entries.name: IntervalNode
doc: Internal interval tree node storing subtree maximum endpoint.

entries.name: IntervalTree
doc: Augmented Interval Tree indexing closed 1D intervals with O(log n + k) queries.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Returns whether the tree contains no intervals.

entries.name: pointQuery
doc: Stabbing query finding all intervals containing the given point.

entries.name: size
doc: Returns the number of intervals stored in the tree.

entries.name: toIntervals
doc: Materializes all intervals sorted by low endpoint in O(n) time.

entries.name: adjust
doc: Updates the value at key if present using function f.

entries.name: delete
doc: Deletes the entry for key if present in the map.

entries.name: difference
doc: Computes the difference of two maps (entries in left whose keys are not in right).

entries.name: empty
doc: Constructs an empty integer map.

entries.name: entries
doc: Returns an array of all key-value entries in key order.

entries.name: get
doc: Looks up the value associated with key in the map.

entries.name: getOr
doc: Looks up the value associated with key, returning fallback if absent.

entries.name: insert
doc: Inserts or replaces a key-value pairing in the map.

entries.name: intersection
doc: Computes the intersection of two maps, keeping values from the left map.

entries.name: IntMap
doc: A purely functional bitwise integer Patricia Trie mapping 64-bit integer keys to values.

entries.name: IntMapEntry
doc: A key-value pairing retrieved from an IntMap.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the map contains no entries.

entries.name: keys
doc: Returns an array of all keys in ascending order.

entries.name: mapValues
doc: Transforms all values in the map using function f.

entries.name: maxKey
doc: Returns the largest key present in the map, or None if empty.

entries.name: member
doc: Whether the map contains an entry for key.

entries.name: minKey
doc: Returns the smallest key present in the map, or None if empty.

entries.name: singleton
doc: Constructs an integer map with a single key-value pairing.

entries.name: size
doc: The number of entries contained in the map.

entries.name: union
doc: Computes the union of two maps, preferring values in left on duplicate keys.

entries.name: values
doc: Returns an array of all values in key order.

entries.name: delete
doc: Deletes an integer element from the set if present.

entries.name: deleteMax
doc: Deletes the maximum element from the set.

entries.name: deleteMin
doc: Deletes the minimum element from the set.

entries.name: difference
doc: Computes the set difference (elements in left not present in right).

entries.name: disjoint
doc: Tests whether the two sets share no common elements.

entries.name: empty
doc: Constructs an empty integer set.

entries.name: filter
doc: Filters the set, retaining only elements satisfying the predicate.

entries.name: findMax
doc: Returns the maximum element present in the set, or None if empty.

entries.name: findMin
doc: Returns the minimum element present in the set, or None if empty.

entries.name: fromArray
doc: Constructs a set from an array of integers.

entries.name: insert
doc: Inserts an integer element into the set.

entries.name: intersection
doc: Computes the intersection of two integer sets.

entries.name: IntSet
doc: A purely functional bitwise integer Patricia Trie storing 64-bit integer elements.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the set contains no elements.

entries.name: isSubsetOf
doc: Tests whether every element of subset is in superset.

entries.name: member
doc: Tests whether element is present in the set.

entries.name: singleton
doc: Constructs a set with a single element.

entries.name: size
doc: The number of elements contained in the set.

entries.name: split
doc: Partitions elements into strictly smaller and strictly greater than pivot.

entries.name: splitMember
doc: Partitions into strictly smaller, presence boolean, and strictly greater.

entries.name: symmetricDifference
doc: Computes the symmetric difference of two sets.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Returns an array of all elements in ascending order.

entries.name: union
doc: Computes the union of two integer sets.

entries.name: append
doc: Contents added to the end of a file, creating it when it is absent.

entries.name: appendAllBytes
doc: Add bytes after what a file already holds.

entries.name: appendLine
doc: A line added to the end of a file.

entries.name: copy
doc: A file copied, or a report of what stopped it.

entries.name: countBytes
doc: How many bytes a file holds, without holding any of them.

entries.name: directoryOf
doc: A path without its last piece, or `.` when it has only one.

entries.name: exists
doc: Whether a path names something that exists.

entries.name: extensionOf
doc: A path's extension, without its dot, or nothing when it has none.

entries.name: foldChunks
entries.signature: &Std.Io.Reader -> T -> fn(T, Bytes) -> T -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError]
doc: Combine every chunk of a file into one value, holding one chunk at a time.
What it costs to run does not depend on how large the file is, which is the
whole of what streaming buys: a file larger than memory is folded here and
cannot be read by anything that materialises it first.

entries.name: foldLines
entries.signature: Str -> T -> fn(T, Str) -> T -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError]
doc: Combine every line of a file into one value, holding one chunk at a time.
A line is split on the newline wherever it falls, including across the
boundary between two chunks, so what a caller sees does not depend on how
the file happened to be divided. Text that is not a valid encoding is
reported rather than replaced: a substituted character would make a broken
file look like a readable one.
The value is threaded rather than gathered by the step function, for the
same reason a sequence passes its state: a function literal carries a copy
of what it captured, so a step that assigned to a variable outside itself
would leave that variable as it found it.

entries.name: forEachChunk
doc: Run an action for every chunk, keeping nothing.

entries.name: forEachLine
doc: Run an action for every line of a file, keeping nothing.
For an action that only reaches outside the program — printing a line,
writing it elsewhere. A caller gathering the lines wants `foldLines`,
because what this action assigns to a variable outside itself does not
leave the action.

entries.name: IoError
doc: Why an operation over a file did not do what it was asked.
One variant per cause a caller can act on differently: a missing file is
created, a refused one is reported to a person, and a caller handed one
message for both could do neither. `Other` carries what the operating
system said, unchanged, for the causes this list does not name.

entries.name: isSeparator
doc: Whether a character ends a piece of a path on this machine.

entries.name: join
doc: Two path pieces joined with a separator, without doubling one.

entries.name: list
doc: The names a directory holds, without their paths.

entries.name: listPaths
doc: The paths a directory holds, each joined to the directory.

entries.name: makeDirectory
doc: A directory created along with every parent it needs.

entries.name: move
doc: A file moved, which is a copy followed by removing the original.

entries.name: nameOf
doc: The last piece of a path.

entries.name: read
doc: A file's whole contents.

entries.name: readAllBytes
doc: Every byte of a file, joined once rather than once per chunk.
Named so its cost is visible: this is the wrapper that decides the memory
profile of the program using it, and `foldChunks` is the one that does not.

entries.name: readAllLines
doc: Every remaining line of input.

entries.name: readAllLinesOf
doc: Every line of a file, in order.
Named so its cost is visible: this holds every line at once, and
`foldLines` is the one that does not.

entries.name: Reader
doc: A file open for reading, named by a token the runtime gave out.
The token is meaningless outside the bracket that produced it, and there is
no way to write one down, so a reader cannot outlive the file it names.

entries.name: readFrom
doc: The next bytes from a reader, or nothing when the input has ended.
Nothing is a different answer from an empty sequence: a reader that could
not tell them apart would either stop early or never stop.

entries.name: readLineOrEnd
doc: One line of input, or `None` at the end of it.
The end of input is not a failure: a program reading until there is no more
is doing the ordinary thing.

entries.name: readLines
doc: A file's contents in lines.

entries.name: remove
doc: A file removed, or a report of why it could not be.

entries.name: removeIfPresent
doc: A file removed if it is there, and nothing done if it is not.
Removing something that is already gone is what the caller wanted.

entries.name: separator
doc: The path vocabulary, so a program reaching for it through `Std.Io` finds
the same answers `Std.Path` gives. The work is written once, there, and
these carry it: two implementations of `normalize` would eventually
disagree about a path holding a climb, and only one of them would be the
one a caller checked against before writing.
The character this machine writes between the pieces of a path.

entries.name: withAppender
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Std.Io.Writer) -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError] -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError]
doc: Write after what the file already holds.

entries.name: withExtension
doc: A path carrying the given extension, replacing any it had.

entries.name: withoutExtension
doc: A path with its extension removed.

entries.name: withReader
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Std.Io.Reader) -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError] -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError]
doc: Read a file through a handle the runtime owns for the length of the call.
There is no `close` a caller can forget, because there is no `close`: the
bracket opened the file and the bracket closes it, on the path where the
action answered and on the path where it failed.

entries.name: withWriter
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Std.Io.Writer) -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError] -> Result[T, Std.Io.IoError]
doc: Write a file the same way, replacing whatever it held.
The bracket flushes before it closes and reports a failing flush rather
than discarding it: bytes that never reached the file are not written, and
a caller told the write succeeded would have no way to find out.

entries.name: write
doc: A file replaced with the given contents.

entries.name: writeAllBytes
doc: Write bytes to a file, replacing what it held.

entries.name: writeErrorLine
doc: A line written to the program's error output.

entries.name: writeFileLines
doc: Lines written to a file, each followed by a newline.

entries.name: writeLine
doc: A line written to the program's output.
The output is flushed, so a program that prints and then waits for input has
already shown what it printed.

entries.name: writeLines
doc: Every line written in order, stopping at the first that fails.

entries.name: Writer
doc: A file open for writing.

entries.name: writeTextTo
doc: Write text through a writer, as its UTF-8 encoding.

entries.name: writeTo
doc: Write bytes through a writer.

entries.name: writeValue
doc: Any value rendered and written as a line.

entries.name: count
doc: How many items a sequence yields.

entries.name: drop
doc: Everything after the first `skip` items.

entries.name: Dropped
doc: A sequence of another's items past the first `skip`.

entries.name: empty
doc: The sequence with no items.

entries.name: Empty
doc: A walk that yields nothing.

entries.name: filter
doc: Keep only the items a test accepts.

entries.name: Filtered
doc: A sequence of another's items that satisfy a test.

entries.name: indexed
doc: Pair each of an array's items with its position.

entries.name: Indexed
doc: A walk over an array's items paired with their positions.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether a sequence yields nothing.

entries.name: items
doc: Walk an array's items.

entries.name: Items
doc: A walk over an array's items.
The element type is the array's own. Fixing it to one type would make the
whole module useless for every array that is not of that type, which is the
mistake this type exists to avoid.

entries.name: map
entries.signature: Q -> fn(A) -> B -> Std.Iter.Mapped[Q, A, B]
doc: Transform each item of a sequence as it is produced.

entries.name: Mapped
doc: A sequence whose items are another's, transformed.
Nothing is computed until the walk asks for it: `advance` transforms one
item and returns. Building a `Mapped` over a sequence of a million does no
work at all, which is what "lazy" has to mean to be worth having.

entries.name: range
doc: The numbers from `first` up to but not including `last`.

entries.name: Range
doc: A half-open range of whole numbers, from `first` up to but not including
`last`.
Generic over the integer family rather than fixed to `Int`: a range of
`UInt8` indices is a range, and a caller working in one width should not
have to leave it to count.

entries.name: repeat
doc: The same value, `count` times.

entries.name: Repeated
doc: A walk that yields the same item a fixed number of times.

entries.name: Sequence
doc: A value that produces a sequence of items.
`S` is the state the walk carries and `T` is what it yields. `begin` answers
the state to start from; `advance` answers the next item and the state after
it, or `None` when the sequence is finished.
The state is passed rather than mutated, so a sequence is an ordinary value:
it can be held, copied, and started again without anything having changed
underneath. Two walks of the same value see the same items.
`for item in value` uses this. A type implementing it is iterable with no
further ceremony, and a type that is not says so at the `for` rather than
part way through one.

entries.name: sum
entries.signature: &Q -> Option[N] where N: Add, Q: Sequence
doc: The sum of a sequence's items, or `None` when it has no first value.

entries.name: take
doc: The first `limit` items, or all of them if there are fewer.
This is what makes an endless sequence usable: the source is never asked
for an item past the limit, so a walk of `take(naturals(), 5)` ends.

entries.name: Taken
doc: A sequence of at most the first `limit` items of another.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Collect a sequence into an array.
Bounded by `Sequence` rather than written for one type, so it works for any
sequence a program declares as well as for the ones here.

entries.name: zip
entries.signature: P -> Q -> Std.Iter.Zipped[P, Q, A, B]
doc: Pair two sequences, ending when either does.

entries.name: Zipped
doc: A sequence pairing two others item by item.

entries.name: asBool
doc: The truth value a value holds, or `None`.

entries.name: asInt
doc: The whole number a value holds, or `None`.

entries.name: asList
doc: The members a list holds, or `None`.

entries.name: asObject
doc: The entries an object holds, or `None`.

entries.name: asText
doc: The text a value holds, or `None` when it holds something else.

entries.name: at
doc: The value at a position in a list, or `None`.

entries.name: decode
doc: A value read from text, or what stopped the reader.

entries.name: encode
doc: A value written as compact text, with no spaces between its parts.

entries.name: encodePretty
doc: A value written across lines, each level indented by two spaces.

entries.name: explain
doc: A reader's failure explained in the terms a caller can report.

entries.name: field
doc: The value stored under a key, or `None` when the value is not an object or
has no such key.

entries.name: isNull
doc: Whether a value is null.

entries.name: Json
doc: A JSON value.
Numbers are whole here: the language's floating types exist, but a decoder
that silently turned `1` into a float would lose the distinction a caller
cares about. A fractional literal decodes as `Fractional`, keeping its text
so nothing is rounded on the way through.

entries.name: JsonError
doc: What went wrong while reading JSON.

entries.name: keys
doc: Every key an object has, in the order they were written.

entries.name: list
doc: A list built from values.

entries.name: object
doc: An object built from key and value pairs.

entries.name: path
doc: The value reached by following a path of object keys.

entries.name: withField
doc: An object with one key added or replaced.

entries.name: all
doc: Whether every entry satisfies the predicate. True for an empty map.

entries.name: any
doc: Whether any entry satisfies the predicate. False for an empty map.

entries.name: containsKey
doc: Whether a key has an entry.

entries.name: empty
doc: A map with no entries.

entries.name: filter
entries.signature: &Std.LinkedMap.LinkedMap[K, V] -> fn(K, V) -> Bool -> Std.LinkedMap.LinkedMap[K, V]
doc: Only the entries the predicate accepts, in the order they were put in.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: &Std.LinkedMap.LinkedMap[K, V] -> fn(A, K, V) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every entry combined into one value, in insertion order.

entries.name: fromPairs
doc: A map built from pairs, in the order they are given.
A later pair replaces an earlier one's value and keeps its position.

entries.name: get
doc: The value stored under a key, or `None`.

entries.name: getOr
doc: The value stored under a key, or a fallback.

entries.name: insert
doc: The map with an entry added or replaced.
A key already here keeps its place. Only a key that is new joins the end of
the order, so the order stays a record of when each key first appeared
rather than of when it was last written.

entries.name: insertIfAbsent
doc: An entry added only when its key has none.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the map holds nothing.

entries.name: keys
doc: Every key, in insertion order.

entries.name: LinkedMap
doc: A map that also remembers the order its keys were first put in.
`Map` deliberately does not. Two maps with the same entries are the same
map there, however they were built, and that is what makes them compare and
print alike — a promise worth more than insertion order for the map every
program reaches for first.
It is worth less than insertion order for the programs that have to give
something back to a person. Configuration written to a file, a request log,
the columns of a report, the fields of a form: each is read in an order
somebody chose, and handing it back sorted silently discards that choice.
Today those programs keep an array of keys alongside a map and are careful
to update both, which is a bug waiting for the one place they forget.
The order is of *first* insertion. Writing to a key that is already here
changes its value and leaves it where it is. That is what separates this
from a recency order, and it is the one a person means: a setting does not
move to the bottom of the file because it was edited.

entries.name: mapValues
doc: Every value transformed, keeping the keys and their order.

entries.name: merge
doc: Two maps combined, with the second map's entries winning.
Keys the second map introduces join the end of the order in its order.

entries.name: newest
doc: The most recently added entry, or `None`.

entries.name: oldest
doc: The first entry put in that is still here, or `None`.

entries.name: pairs
doc: Every entry as a pair, in insertion order.

entries.name: remove
doc: The map with a key's entry removed, or unchanged when there is none.

entries.name: removeOldest
doc: The map without its oldest entry, unchanged when it is empty.

entries.name: reversed
doc: The entries in the reverse of the order they were put in.

entries.name: size
doc: How many entries the map holds.

entries.name: toMap
doc: The map with its order forgotten, as an ordinary map.
Named rather than automatic, because the entries are the same and only the
promise about their order differs; a conversion a reader cannot see is a
promise dropped silently.

entries.name: touch
doc: The map with an entry moved to the end of the order, added if it is new.
The recency order `insert` deliberately does not keep. A cache deciding what
to discard, or a list of recently opened files, wants the key it just
touched to be last; both are asking a different question from "when did this
first appear", so both are spelled differently.

entries.name: upsert
entries.signature: &Std.LinkedMap.LinkedMap[K, V] -> K -> V -> fn(V) -> V -> Std.LinkedMap.LinkedMap[K, V]
doc: An entry's value transformed, inserting a starting value when it is absent.

entries.name: values
doc: Every value, in the insertion order of its key.

entries.name: all
doc: Whether every element satisfies the predicate. True for an empty array.

entries.name: any
doc: Whether any element satisfies the predicate. False for an empty array.

entries.name: breakWhen
doc: The longest leading run the predicate *rejects*, and the rest.
This is `span` with the predicate negated: `span` keeps while it holds, and
this one keeps until it does.

entries.name: cartesian
doc: Every pairing of one array's elements with the other's.

entries.name: chunksOf
doc: The array in pieces of at most `size` elements.

entries.name: concat
doc: One array followed by another.

entries.name: contains
doc: Whether any element equals the given value.
Equality is structural, which is what the runtime compares; there is no
`Eq` bound to write until the language has one.

entries.name: count
doc: How many elements equal the given value.

entries.name: countWhere
doc: How many elements the predicate accepts.

entries.name: cycle
doc: The array repeated end to end a number of times.

entries.name: difference
doc: Every element of the first array that is not in the second.

entries.name: distinct
doc: The elements with later duplicates removed, keeping the first of each.

entries.name: distinctBy
doc: The elements with later duplicates removed under a comparison.

entries.name: drop
doc: Every element after the first `skipped`.

entries.name: dropEnd
doc: Every element but the last `skipped`.

entries.name: dropWhile
doc: Everything after the longest leading run the predicate accepts.

entries.name: dropWhileEnd
doc: The array with trailing elements the predicate accepts removed.

entries.name: enumerate
doc: Every element paired with its position.

entries.name: filter
doc: Every element the predicate accepts.

entries.name: find
doc: The first element the predicate accepts, or `None`.

entries.name: findIndex
doc: The position of the first element the predicate accepts, or `None`.

entries.name: findIndices
doc: Every position whose element the predicate accepts.

entries.name: first
doc: The first element, or `None` for an empty array.
Nothing in `Std` is partial: this is why there is no `head` that panics.

entries.name: flatMap
doc: Every element transformed into an array, and those arrays joined.

entries.name: flatten
doc: Every array joined end to end.

entries.name: fold
doc: Combine every element into one, left to right.

entries.name: foldRight
doc: Combine every element into one, right to left.

entries.name: get
doc: The element at a position, or `None` when there is none.

entries.name: group
doc: Runs of adjacent equal elements.

entries.name: groupBy
doc: Runs of adjacent elements that a comparison calls equivalent.

entries.name: indexOf
doc: The position of the first element equal to the given value.
The runtime answers `-1` for absent; this is the form a caller can match on
without remembering which sentinel means absent.

entries.name: indicesOf
doc: Every position holding the given value.

entries.name: initial
doc: Every element but the last, or an empty array when there is none.

entries.name: insertBy
doc: A value placed into an array ordered by a comparison, keeping it in order.

entries.name: insertOrdered
doc: A value placed into an array that is already in ascending order, keeping it
in order. Placed after equal elements, so repeated insertion is stable.

entries.name: intercalate
doc: Every array joined with a separator array between them.

entries.name: intersection
doc: Every element of the first array that is also in the second.

entries.name: intersperse
doc: A separator placed between every pair of elements.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the array has no elements.

entries.name: isInfixOf
doc: Whether one array appears inside another as a contiguous run.

entries.name: isPrefixOf
doc: Whether one array begins with another.

entries.name: isSuffixOf
doc: Whether one array ends with another.

entries.name: iterate
doc: Repeated application of a function, starting from a seed.
The count is required: Pudu evaluates strictly and has no infinite arrays,
so a repeated application must be told when to stop.

entries.name: last
doc: The last element, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: length
doc: The number of elements.

entries.name: lookup
doc: The value paired with the first matching key, or `None`.

entries.name: map
doc: Every element transformed.

entries.name: mapAccum
doc: A fold that also collects what each step produced, left to right.

entries.name: maximum
doc: The largest element, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: maximumBy
doc: The element a comparison ranks last, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: maximumOn
entries.signature: &Array[T] -> fn(T) -> K -> Option[T] where K: Ord
doc: The element whose key is largest, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: merge
doc: Two ascending arrays interleaved into one.
Exported because merging already-sorted input is worth doing without sorting
it again, which is the whole reason a merge sort has this step.

entries.name: mergeBy
doc: Two arrays ordered by the same comparison interleaved into one.

entries.name: minimum
doc: The smallest element, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: minimumBy
doc: The element a comparison ranks first, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: minimumOn
entries.signature: &Array[T] -> fn(T) -> K -> Option[T] where K: Ord
doc: The element whose key is smallest, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: modify
doc: The array with one position transformed, or unchanged when it has none.

entries.name: notContains
doc: Whether no element equals the given value.

entries.name: partition
doc: The elements the predicate accepts, and the elements it rejects.

entries.name: permutations
doc: Every ordering of the elements. The count is the factorial of the length,
so this is for small inputs by nature rather than by choice.

entries.name: pick
doc: The elements at the given positions, skipping positions the array lacks.

entries.name: prefixes
doc: Every prefix, shortest first, including the empty one and the whole array.

entries.name: product
doc: The product of every element, or `None` for an empty array.

entries.name: productOr
entries.signature: &Array[T] -> T -> T where T: One + Mul
doc: Every element multiplied together, with a caller-supplied value for empty.

entries.name: range
doc: The whole numbers from `from` up to but not including `to`.

entries.name: removeFirst
doc: The first occurrence of a value removed, if it is there.

entries.name: replicate
doc: A value repeated a number of times. A count below one produces nothing.

entries.name: rest
doc: Every element but the first, or an empty array when there is none.
Named for what it is rather than for the position it drops, because the
partial version other languages call `tail` is not offered here at all.

entries.name: reversed
doc: The elements in reverse order.

entries.name: scan
doc: Every running total, starting from the initial value.
The result is one longer than the input, because the initial value is a
running total too.

entries.name: scanRight
doc: Every running total, from the right.

entries.name: set
doc: The array with one position replaced, or unchanged when it has none.

entries.name: slice
doc: The elements from `from` up to but not including `to`.

entries.name: sortBy
doc: The elements ordered by a comparison the caller supplies.
`before` answers whether its first argument sorts before its second; a
comparison that is not a total order produces an unspecified order rather
than a failure, which is the same promise every comparison sort makes.

entries.name: sorted
doc: The elements in ascending order, under the type's own ordering.
Merge sort: the input is halved with `slice` and rejoined with `concat`,
both of which the runtime does on the structure rather than by rebuilding.

entries.name: sortOn
entries.signature: &Array[T] -> fn(T) -> K -> Array[T] where K: Ord
doc: The elements ordered by a key drawn from each one.
The key may be of any ordered type, not only a number: sorting people by
name is the same operation as sorting them by age.

entries.name: span
doc: The longest leading run the predicate accepts, and the rest.

entries.name: splitAt
doc: The array split at a position: the first `at` elements, then the rest.

entries.name: stripPrefix
doc: The remainder after a prefix, or `None` when the prefix is not there.

entries.name: stripSuffix
doc: The remainder before a suffix, or `None` when the suffix is not there.

entries.name: subsequences
doc: Every subsequence, including the empty one and the whole array.
The count doubles with each element, so this is for small inputs by nature
rather than by choice.

entries.name: suffixes
doc: Every suffix, longest first, including the whole array and the empty one.

entries.name: sum
doc: The sum of every element, or `None` for an empty array.
Generic over any type with an additive identity and an addition, which is
every integer width and both floating widths.

entries.name: sumOr
entries.signature: &Array[T] -> T -> T where T: Zero + Add
doc: Every element added together, with a caller-supplied value for empty.
The form to reach for when nought is the right answer for nothing; `sum`
keeps the distinction for callers that need it.

entries.name: take
doc: The first `wanted` elements, or every element when the array is shorter.
A negative count takes nothing.

entries.name: takeEnd
doc: The last `wanted` elements, or every element when the array is shorter.

entries.name: takeWhile
doc: The longest leading run of elements the predicate accepts.

entries.name: transpose
doc: The rows and columns exchanged. Rows of unequal length contribute only the
positions they have, so no element is invented to fill a gap.

entries.name: unfold
entries.signature: Int -> S -> fn(S) -> Option[(T, S)] -> Array[T]
doc: An array grown from a seed until the step answers `None`.
The step count is bounded because a strict language cannot recover from a
step that never stops; exhausting the bound answers with what it had.

entries.name: union
doc: The first array followed by every element of the second it does not contain.

entries.name: unzip
doc: Pairs separated back into two arrays.

entries.name: unzip3
doc: Triples separated back into three arrays.

entries.name: windows
doc: Every contiguous run of `size` elements, one position apart.
Nothing at all when the array is shorter than the window.

entries.name: zip
doc: Corresponding elements paired, stopping at the shorter array.

entries.name: zip3
doc: Three arrays' corresponding elements gathered, stopping at the shortest.

entries.name: zipWith
doc: Corresponding elements combined, stopping at the shorter array.

entries.name: zipWith3
doc: Three arrays' corresponding elements combined, stopping at the shortest.

entries.name: Adjusting
doc: A logger with one decision changed, each answering a logger rather than
taking one apart.
Methods, so that a logger that differs from the default in three ways is
written down the page rather than with each call wrapped in the next, where
the base a reader looks for first ends up furthest in.
Each answers a new logger, which is what makes carrying a field safe: a
request identifier is attached once where the request is known, and the
logger it was attached to is unchanged for everything else.

entries.name: at
doc: Write a line, or nothing when the level is below what the logger keeps.
Nothing rather than an empty line: a filtered line that still moved the
cursor would make a quiet log look busy.

entries.name: atMoment
doc: Write a stamped line, or nothing when the level is below what is kept.

entries.name: carryingValue
doc: The same logger carrying a rendered value as a field.
A free function rather than a method, because it is generic in the value it
renders and the trait is not.

entries.name: debug
doc: Write a line at `Debug`.

entries.name: error
doc: Write a line at `Error`.

entries.name: failure
doc: Write a failure's cause at `Error`, and answer the failure unchanged.
Answering it back means a caller logs on the way past rather than choosing
between reporting a failure and returning it.

entries.name: fatal
doc: Write a line at `Fatal`.

entries.name: field
entries.signature: &Std.Log.Logger -> Std.Log.Level -> Str -> Str -> Str -> Result[(), Str]
doc: Write a line carrying one further field, without keeping it on the logger.
For the field that belongs to one line rather than to everything after it,
which is most of them.

entries.name: Field
doc: One named value carried alongside a message.

entries.name: fieldsOf
doc: The fields a logger carries, in the order they were added.

entries.name: Format
doc: How a line becomes text.

entries.name: info
doc: Write a line at `Info`.

entries.name: json
doc: A line written as a JSON object, for whatever collects it.
Every value is written as a string, including one that looks like a number,
because a field holding `00123` or a version is not a number and a reader
that guesses will eventually guess wrong.

entries.name: keeps
doc: Whether a logger would keep a line at this level.
Worth asking before building a line whose message is expensive to produce:
the check is a comparison, and the message is not built if it is not kept.

entries.name: leastOf
doc: The level a logger keeps from.

entries.name: Level
doc: How much a line matters, from most detail to least.
Ordered so a threshold is a comparison rather than a set: a logger keeping
`Warn` keeps `Error` too, because a program turned down to its warnings has
not asked to stop hearing about failures.
`Silent` names a threshold rather than a line. Nothing is written at it, so a
logger keeping `Silent` keeps nothing — which is how a program is quietened
without a separate switch to forget to check.

entries.name: levelFrom
doc: A level read from its name, or `None` for anything else.
For a program taking its level from a setting or an argument, where the text
arrived from outside and being unrecognised is an input rather than a defect.

entries.name: levelName
doc: How a level is written.

entries.name: Line
doc: Everything one line knows, before anything decides how it should read.
Held apart from the writing so a format is a function on this rather than a
set of options on the logger. A format nobody anticipated is then a function
a program writes, not a change to this module.

entries.name: lineOf
doc: The line a logger would make, before anything writes it.
For a program that hands its lines somewhere other than a stream, and for
checking what a logger produces by comparing values rather than by capturing
output — the same reason [[Std Out]] keeps `rendered` apart from `write`.

entries.name: logfmt
doc: Every part of a line written as a `key=value` pair, message included.
The shape a log ends up in whenever anything other than a person reads it. A
message left outside the pairs is the one part a reader has to find by
position, and position is what breaks when a field is added:
timestamp=2026-08-31T12:00:00Z level=INFO logger=checkout order=A17 message=captured
Parts that are empty are left out rather than written as nothing, so a line
with no name carries no `logger=`.

entries.name: Logger
doc: What a program says, held as a value.
`print` is enough for a script and not enough for anything unattended: no
level, so nothing can be turned down; no name, so nothing can be told apart;
no fields, so nothing can be searched. A logger carries those, and a line
built from it inherits them.
Building a line is separate from writing it, as shaping is separate from
writing in [[Std Fmt]] and [[Std Out]]. A library that logs should be able to
hand a line to whatever its caller chose rather than write to a stream the
caller did not pick.

entries.name: nameOf
doc: The name a logger speaks under.

entries.name: pretty
doc: A line written for someone reading it as it happens.
The parts a person scans for come first and unlabelled — when, how bad, and
who — because at a terminal the position is the label. The message ends the
line so the eye can run down the right of the output and read what happened:
2026-08-31T12:00:00Z INFO checkout order=A17 captured

entries.name: quoted
doc: A field's value written so the pair it belongs to can be read back.
A value with nothing in it to confuse a reader is written bare, which is most
of them and keeps a line short. A value that is empty, or that carries a
space, a quote, or an equals sign, is quoted, because otherwise
`note=see below` reads as a field `note` and a stray word. A value carrying a
line break is quoted and the break written as an escape, so one line of
output stays one line of output.

entries.name: rendered
doc: A line as it would be written, without a timestamp.

entries.name: stamped
doc: A line as it would be written, stamped with a time the caller supplies.
The time is given rather than read from a clock, so a line is a pure function
of what it was told and two runs of the same program can be compared. A caller
wanting the real clock asks `Std.Time` for it and passes the answer, which is
one line at the edge of the program rather than a clock hidden in every line.

entries.name: stderr
doc: A logger to the error stream, keeping everything from `Info` up.
Where a program's diagnostics belong when its answer goes to output, so the
two can be read apart and piped apart.

entries.name: stdout
doc: A logger to the output stream, keeping everything from `Info` up.
`Info` rather than `Debug`, because a default that says everything trains a
reader to ignore the output, and the one thing a log must not be is ignored.

entries.name: warn
doc: Write a line at `Warn`.

entries.name: capacity
doc: How many entries the cache will hold before it starts discarding.

entries.name: cleared
doc: The cache holding nothing, keeping its capacity.

entries.name: containsKey
doc: Whether a key is held, without marking it as used.

entries.name: evict
doc: The cache with its next entry discarded, unchanged when it is empty.

entries.name: fromPairs
doc: A cache of the given capacity holding these pairs, in the order given.
A later pair counts as more recent, so giving more pairs than the capacity
keeps the last ones.

entries.name: get
doc: The value stored under a key, and the cache with that key marked as used.
Both, because a read is what a recency order is about: taking the value
without recording that it was taken would let an entry the program relies on
be discarded as unused. A caller that genuinely only wants to look — a
diagnostic, a report — should use `peek`.

entries.name: getOrCompute
entries.signature: &Std.LruCache.LruCache[K, V] -> K -> fn(K) -> V -> (V, Std.LruCache.LruCache[K, V])
doc: The value under a key, computing and storing it when it is absent.
The reason a cache exists, in one call: the caller says what the value would
be if it had to be made, and gets back the value and the cache that now
holds it. The function is not called when the key is already present, which
is the saving being asked for.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the cache is holding nothing.

entries.name: isFull
doc: Whether the cache is holding as much as it can.

entries.name: keys
doc: Every key, least recently used first.
The order entries would be discarded in, which is the useful direction to
read a cache in when deciding whether its capacity is right.

entries.name: LruCache
doc: A map that holds only so much, and gives up what has gone longest unused.
A cache without a bound is a map that only grows, which is a leak with a
helpful name. The bound is the whole point: memoised results, parsed files,
recently opened documents all want to keep what is being used and let go of
what is not, and none of them can afford to keep everything.
Least recently *used*, not least recently written — so reading an entry
keeps it alive. That is what separates a cache from a queue, and it is why
`get` answers both the value and a cache: the read changed which entry is
next to go, and hiding that would make the order depend on reads a caller
could not see.
The recency order comes from `LinkedMap.touch`, which already exists to move
a key to the end of an order. Nothing here re-implements it.

entries.name: newest
doc: The most recently used entry, or `None` when the cache is empty.

entries.name: oldest
doc: The entry that will be discarded next, or `None` when the cache is empty.

entries.name: pairs
doc: Every entry as a pair, least recently used first.

entries.name: peek
doc: The value stored under a key, without marking it as used.
For looking at a cache rather than using it. A program that reads through
`peek` alone has a cache that evicts by write order, which is not what it
asked for — so this exists for reports and assertions, not for the hot path.

entries.name: put
doc: The cache with an entry added or replaced, and marked as the most recently
used.
Writing is using, so an existing key moves to the end of the order rather
than staying where it was — which is the opposite of `LinkedMap.insert` and
the reason this is a different type rather than a wrapper.

entries.name: remove
doc: The cache with a key's entry removed, or unchanged when there is none.

entries.name: resized
doc: The cache with a new capacity, discarding the oldest entries if it shrank.

entries.name: size
doc: How many entries the cache is holding.

entries.name: toMap
doc: The entries as an ordinary map, losing the recency order and the bound.

entries.name: values
doc: Every value, least recently used first.

entries.name: withCapacity
doc: A cache holding at most `capacity` entries.
A capacity below one is kept as zero, and such a cache stores nothing: every
write is immediately evicted. That is a legal and occasionally useful thing
to configure — a cache turned off without the calling code changing shape —
so it is allowed rather than refused.

entries.name: address
doc: An address, checked.
A break here lets whoever supplied it write headers of their own — another
recipient, another sender, or a whole second message. Refused rather than
stripped, because stripping guesses at what was meant and hands back
something the caller believes carries what they gave it.

entries.name: Address
doc: Somewhere a message goes, checked.
There is no way to make one except through a call that looked at it, which
is the arrangement the rest of this library uses wherever text from outside
reaches a format with structure.

entries.name: addressText
doc: How an address is written.

entries.name: andTo
doc: The same, with one more recipient.

entries.name: copying
doc: The same, copying somebody the others can see.

entries.name: copyingBlind
doc: The same, copying somebody the others cannot see.
This one reaches the envelope and never the headers, which is what stops
the list being disclosed.

entries.name: envelope
doc: Every address a server must be given, which is not the same list the
headers name.

entries.name: explain
doc: What a refusal says.
A refusal never repeats what it refused, for the same reason a validation
failure does not: the sender knows what they gave, and repeating it carries
whatever was in it somewhere else.

entries.name: hasBlindCopies
doc: Whether anybody is copied without the others knowing.

entries.name: headers
doc: The headers a message carries.
Built from the visible recipients only. A program cannot write the blind
list here by forgetting something, because nothing it can call does that.

entries.name: MailError
doc: Why something could not be sent.

entries.name: message
doc: A message from somebody to somebody, about something.

entries.name: Message
doc: A message a program sends.
The blind list is kept apart from the others rather than marked within one
list, so nothing that builds headers has to remember to filter it. That is
the failure worth designing out: every recipient seeing who else was
copied is not noticed until after it has happened.

entries.name: recipientCount
doc: How many people a message reaches.

entries.name: render
doc: What goes on the wire.
A line of the body that is a lone full stop would end the message, so every
such line gains a second stop, which the receiving end removes. That is a
property of the format rather than of the message, and a caller who has not
read the format has no reason to know it.

entries.name: renderChecked
doc: Validate public records again at the outbound boundary.

entries.name: sendable
doc: Whether a message can be sent at all.

entries.name: stuffed
doc: A body with the lines that would end it escaped.

entries.name: authLoginPassword
doc: Formats the password challenge response for `AUTH LOGIN`.

entries.name: authLoginUsername
doc: Formats the username challenge response for `AUTH LOGIN`.

entries.name: authPlainPayload
doc: Formats the single-line payload for `AUTH PLAIN`.

entries.name: client
doc: Configure the relay destination and the application-supplied EHLO identity.

entries.name: Configuring
doc: Who the client says it is, how it proves it, how long it waits, and how the
connection is protected.
A submission host usually needs three of these said at once, and as methods
they read down the page in the order a connection makes them: the name sent
first, then the proof, then the limits the socket is held to.

entries.name: dataCommand
doc: Generates the canonical `DATA` command.

entries.name: deliver
doc: Delivers a message to the target SMTP relay and returns the count of accepted envelope recipients.

entries.name: ehloCommand
doc: Generates the canonical `EHLO` command line.

entries.name: mailFromCommand
doc: Generates the canonical `MAIL FROM` envelope command.

entries.name: parseReply
doc: Parses an RFC 5321 server response string into a structured status code and message lines.

entries.name: quitCommand
doc: Generates the canonical `QUIT` command.

entries.name: rcptToCommand
doc: Generates the canonical `RCPT TO` recipient command.

entries.name: SmtpAuth
doc: Authentication mechanism variants supported by the SMTP transport.

entries.name: SmtpClient
doc: Configuration parameters for connecting to an SMTP submission or relay host.

entries.name: SmtpError
doc: Structured failure conditions encountered during SMTP transmission.

entries.name: SmtpReply
doc: A parsed RFC 5321 server reply containing a status code and message lines.

entries.name: SmtpSecurity
doc: How a connection to the server is protected.

entries.name: notContainsKey
doc: Whether a key has no entry.

entries.name: toArray

entries.name: update

entries.name: upsert
entries.signature: &Map[K, V] -> K -> V -> fn(V) -> V -> Map[K, V]

This is how a counter or an accumulator is kept in a map without the caller
writing the same two-case match every time.

doc: Only the keys the first map has and the second does not.

entries.name: filled
doc: Every value in a container replaced by one value.
Written once against the trait rather than once per container, which is the

entries.name: Mappable
doc: Something that holds values and can have every one of them transformed
without changing its shape.
Every collection here already has a `map`, and until parameters could stand
for a constructor the five of them could not be related: `Array`, `Option`,
`Tree` and the rest each named the same operation and no function could take
"some container" and transform what it held.
`F` stands for the constructor, not for a type. `F[_]` says it takes one
argument, so a member may write `F[A]` and `F[B]` and mean the same
container holding different things.
The law this asks of an implementation, and does not check: transforming by
a function that answers what it was given must leave the container as it
was. A `mapped` that reordered, dropped, or duplicated would satisfy the
type and break every caller that relied on the shape surviving.

entries.name: over
entries.signature: &F[A] -> fn(A) -> B -> F[B] where F: Mappable

The function that could not be written before: it takes the container it is
given rather than one container it was written for.

rather than merely defined for one.

entries.name: clamp

A negative exponent yields one, matching integer exponentiation everywhere

doc: A map built from triples of first part, second part, and value.

doc: The value under both parts of a key, or `None`.

entries.name: getOr
entries.signature: &Std.MultiKeyMap.MultiKeyMap[A, B, V] -> A -> B -> V -> V
doc: The value under both parts of a key, or a fallback.

entries.name: insert
entries.signature: &Std.MultiKeyMap.MultiKeyMap[A, B, V] -> A -> B -> V -> Std.MultiKeyMap.MultiKeyMap[A, B, V]
doc: The map with an entry added or replaced.
The indexes only gain an entry when the key is new. Replacing a value leaves
them alone, because the pair they record is unchanged — recording it twice
would make a later removal drop only one of the copies and leave the index
claiming a key the entries no longer hold.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the map holds nothing.

entries.name: MultiKeyMap
doc: A map keyed by two things, which can also be asked about either one alone.
The composite key by itself is not why this exists: `Map[(A, B), V]` already
works, because the runtime's order handles tuples, and a caller wanting only
"the value under this pair" should write that and stop here.
What a pair-keyed `Map` cannot do is answer about *part* of the key. Every
permission for one user, whatever the resource; every reading from one
sensor, whatever the hour; every override for one environment, whatever the
setting. Against `Map[(A, B), V]` each of those reads every entry and throws
most of them away, and the map gets slower at exactly the rate the data
grows.
So this keeps two indexes beside the entries — one grouping the pairs by
their first part, one by their second — and a partial lookup reads the group
it wants instead of the whole map. That is the cost too: three structures
updated on every write, in exchange for the two questions. A caller who never
asks a partial question is paying for indexes they do not read, and should
use a pair-keyed `Map` instead. This is written on the module because it is
the whole decision of whether to reach for it.

entries.signature: &Std.MultiKeyMap.MultiKeyMap[A, B, V] -> A -> B -> Std.MultiKeyMap.MultiKeyMap[A, B, V]
doc: The map with an entry removed, or unchanged when there is none.
A part of the key left naming nothing is dropped from its index, so a
partial lookup never reports a key with no entries behind it.

doc: The map with every entry whose key begins with this first part removed.

indexes would be carried and never read.

doc: A map with no entries.

entries.name: filterKeys
doc: Only the keys the predicate accepts.

entries.name: filterValues
doc: Only the values the predicate accepts, dropping keys left with none.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: &Std.MultiMap.MultiMap[K, V] -> fn(A, K, Array[V]) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every key and all its values combined into one value, in key order.

entries.name: fromPairs
doc: A map built from pairs, collecting values under their shared keys.

entries.name: get
doc: Every value under a key, in the order they were added, or an empty array.
An empty array rather than `Option[Array[V]]`, because a key with no values
and a key that was never added are the same thing here, and offering two
spellings of one state would invite the caller to distinguish them.

entries.name: groupBy
doc: Items collected under the key each one produces.
What `Map.groupBy` answers, in the shape that can then be added to.

entries.name: groups
doc: Every key paired with all of its values, in key order.

entries.name: inverted
doc: The map with its keys and values exchanged.
Each value becomes a key holding every key it appeared under, which is the
reverse index a caller otherwise builds by hand.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the map holds nothing.

entries.name: keys
doc: Every key that has values, in order.

entries.name: mapValues
doc: Every value transformed, keeping its key and position.

entries.name: merge
doc: Two maps combined, with the second map's values added after the first's.

entries.name: MultiMap
doc: A map holding several values under one key.
Grouping is the commonest thing anyone does with a map, and `Map.groupBy`
already builds one. What it does not do is *keep* one: adding a value to a
key that may or may not already be there, taking one occurrence back out,
and having the key stop existing when its last value goes.
Written by hand that is the same three lines every time — match the key, push
onto what is there or start an array — plus a fourth that is the one people
forget: removing the key once its values run out. A key left mapped to an
empty array is a key `containsKey` then answers `true` for and `get` answers
nothing for, which is a map disagreeing with itself.
So the rule here is that **a key with no values does not exist**. Every
operation maintains it, and it is what makes `size`, `containsKey` and
`keys` mean what a reader expects.
Values under a key keep the order they were added in. Duplicates are kept:
this is a bag under each key, not a set, because the commonest use is
collecting records that genuinely repeat — two log lines at the same level,
two headers with the same name.

entries.name: pairs
doc: Every key paired with each of its values, in key order.
One pair per value, so a key with three values appears three times. This is
the flat reading, for handing to something that takes pairs.

entries.name: remove
doc: The map with one occurrence of a value removed from a key.
One occurrence, not all of them, because the values under a key are a bag:
removing every copy when the caller took one back would lose the others.
The key goes when its last value does.

entries.name: removeAll
doc: The map with every occurrence of a value removed from a key.

entries.name: removeKey
doc: The map with a key and all its values removed.

entries.name: setAll
doc: The map with a key's values replaced entirely.
Replacing with nothing removes the key, rather than leaving one with an
empty array behind it.

entries.name: size
doc: How many keys have values.
Keys, not values, matching `Map`. `total` counts the values.

entries.name: toMap
doc: The map as an ordinary map from key to its values.

entries.name: total
doc: How many values the map holds across every key.

entries.name: values
doc: Every value under every key, in key order.

entries.name: fmix32
doc: Finalization mix avalanche stage for 32-bit integers.

entries.name: fmix64
doc: Finalization mix avalanche stage for 64-bit integers.

entries.name: hash32
doc: Computes the 32-bit MurmurHash3 digest over a byte array with a given `seed`.

entries.name: hash32Int
doc: Computes the 32-bit MurmurHash3 digest directly from a 64-bit integer without byte allocations.

entries.name: hash32Text
doc: Computes the 32-bit MurmurHash3 digest directly over a UTF-8 string.

entries.name: rotL32
doc: Rotates a 32-bit unsigned integer left by `r` bits.

entries.name: accept
doc: Wait for the next connection.
This does not answer until one arrives, which is what makes a server a
loop around it rather than a poll.

entries.name: close
doc: Close a connection.

entries.name: closeListener
doc: Stop listening.

entries.name: connect
doc: Open a connection to somewhere else.

entries.name: Connection
doc: A connection, open in both directions.

entries.name: connectWithin
doc: Open a connection, waiting no longer than the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: finish
doc: Say that nothing more will be sent, while still reading what comes back.
This is how a sender marks the end of a message in a protocol that has no
length ahead of the body. Closing outright would discard the reply.

entries.name: foldChunks
entries.signature: &Std.Net.Connection -> T -> fn(T, Bytes) -> T -> Result[T, Std.Net.NetError]
doc: Combine everything a peer sends into one value, holding one chunk at a
time. What it costs does not depend on how much the peer sends.
The value is threaded rather than gathered by the step function, for the
same reason a sequence passes its state: a function literal carries a copy
of what it captured, so a step assigning to a variable outside itself would
leave that variable as it found it.

entries.name: listen
doc: Wait for connections on a port.
A port of zero asks the machine to choose one, which `portOf` then answers.
That is how a program starts a listener without picking a number something
else may already hold, and it is what a test wants.
The address is made reusable before it is bound, so a program restarted
straight after stopping can bind the port it just had rather than waiting
out the connections that may still be in flight.

entries.name: Listener
doc: An endpoint waiting for connections.

entries.name: listenLocal
doc: Wait for connections reachable only from this machine.

entries.name: NetError
doc: Why an operation over the network did not do what it was asked.
One variant per cause a caller acts on differently: a refused connection is
retried, a name that resolves to nothing is a configuration mistake, and a
peer that went away mid-message is neither.

entries.name: peerOf
doc: Who is at the other end.

entries.name: portOf
doc: Which port a listener is actually on.

entries.name: receive
doc: The next bytes, or nothing when the other end has closed.
Nothing is a different answer from an empty read: a reader that could not
tell them apart would stop on a slow peer or never stop on a finished one.

entries.name: receiveAll
doc: Everything a peer sends until it closes, joined once rather than once per
chunk. Named so its cost is visible: this holds the whole message, and
`foldChunks` is the one that does not.

entries.name: receiveExactly
doc: Read exactly the requested count of bytes, or report that the peer closed
before they arrived.
A protocol that states a length ahead of its body needs this rather than
`receive`, which is permitted to answer with fewer bytes than it was asked
for whenever that is all that has arrived so far.

entries.name: receiveUntil
doc: Read until a marker has arrived, answering what came before it and what
came after.
This is what a protocol whose messages end with a marker needs, and it is
the operation such a reader most often gets wrong: the marker can arrive
split across two reads, so a reader that looked only at the newest chunk
would miss it. The buffer is searched whole each time.
The remainder is answered rather than dropped because it is the start of
the next message: a reader that discarded it would lose the beginning of
everything that followed.

entries.name: receiveWithin
doc: Read the next bytes, waiting no longer than the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: send
doc: Send bytes, and keep sending until every one has gone.
A single write is permitted to take fewer bytes than it was offered, so
this loops underneath rather than writing once: a sender that moved on
would truncate exactly the large messages it most matters not to.

entries.name: sendText
doc: Send text, as its UTF-8 encoding.

entries.name: sendTextWithin
doc: Send text, waiting no longer than the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: sendWithin
doc: Send bytes, waiting no longer than the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: serve
doc: Wait for connections, hand each to an action, and close it however the
action ended. The listener is closed when the loop stops.
The action answers whether to keep waiting, so a server stops by saying so
rather than by a flag something else has to set. `count` bounds how many
connections are served before the loop ends whatever the action says, so a
caller that wants one connection does not have to arrange to stop itself.

entries.name: withConnection
entries.signature: Str -> Int -> fn(Std.Net.Connection) -> Result[T, Std.Net.NetError] -> Result[T, Std.Net.NetError]
doc: Open a connection, hand it to an action, and close it however the action
ended. There is no close a caller can forget, because there is no close.

entries.name: exactly
doc: Read this many bytes, or fail rather than answer fewer.

entries.name: until
doc: Read up to and including a separator, within a limit.

entries.name: all
doc: Whether every element satisfies a test.

entries.name: any
doc: Whether any element satisfies a test.

entries.name: append
doc: An element added to the end.

entries.name: concat
doc: Two sequences joined.

entries.name: contains
doc: Whether an element is present.

entries.name: filter
doc: The elements that satisfy a test, as an ordinary array — filtering can
remove every element, so what comes back may be empty.

entries.name: find
doc: The first element satisfying a test, or `None`.

entries.name: first
doc: The first element. There is always one.

entries.name: fold
doc: The elements combined from the left, starting from a value of your own.

entries.name: fromArray
doc: An array as a non-empty sequence, or `None` when it is empty.
The only way in from ordinary data, and the one place the question is
asked. Everything after it may assume the answer.

entries.name: group
doc: Adjacent equal elements gathered.

entries.name: groupBy
doc: Adjacent equal elements gathered, each group non-empty by construction.
This is what the type is for: `List.group` answers arrays that are known to
hold at least one element, and had no way to say so.

entries.name: last
doc: The last element. There is always one.

entries.name: length
doc: How many elements there are, which is never fewer than one.

entries.name: make
doc: A head and the rest.

entries.name: map
