doc: Every element transformed. A sequence that had one still has one.

entries.name: maximum
doc: The largest element. There is always one.

entries.name: maximumBy
doc: The largest element under an ordering. There is always one.

entries.name: minimum
doc: The smallest element. There is always one, so this answers a value rather
than an `Option`.

entries.name: minimumBy
doc: The smallest element under an ordering. There is always one.

entries.name: NonEmpty
doc: A sequence that has at least one element, and says so in its type.
`List.first` and `List.maximum` answer `Option` because an array may be
empty and there is nothing honest to return when it is. A caller that
already knows its data is not empty pays for that everywhere: an `Option`
unwrapped at each step, or a fallback invented for a case that cannot
happen. Stating it once, here, removes the question from every call after.

entries.name: one
doc: A sequence of one.

entries.name: prepend
doc: An element added to the front.

entries.name: reduce
doc: The elements combined from the left, starting from the first one.
No initial value is asked for, because the first element is one. This is
the fold that cannot be given the wrong starting point.

entries.name: rest
doc: Everything after the first element, which may be empty.

entries.name: reversed
doc: The elements in the opposite order.

entries.name: sortBy
doc: The elements in order under an ordering of your own.

entries.name: sorted
doc: The elements in order.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Every element, as an ordinary array.

entries.name: Add
doc: A type whose values add.

entries.name: Div
doc: A type whose values divide, answering `None` for a divisor of nought.
Total, like everything else here: division is the one arithmetic operation
with an input it has no answer for.

entries.name: Integer
doc: A whole-number type that can cross the width-independent `BigInt`
boundary without losing information.
`toBigInt` is exact. `fromBigInt` is fallible because the mathematical
value may not fit the receiver's signedness or width. The receiver is the
type witness that lets a generic algorithm preserve the caller's type.

entries.name: Mul
doc: A type whose values multiply.

entries.name: One
doc: A type with a multiplicative identity.

entries.name: product
doc: Every element multiplied together, or `None` for an empty collection.

entries.name: Rem
doc: A type whose values have a remainder, answering `None` for a divisor of
nought. Separate from `Div` because a type can divide exactly without having
one, and because asking for both when only one is used is a bound a caller
has to satisfy for nothing.

entries.name: runningSum
doc: Every running total, one longer than the input.

entries.name: small
entries.signature: &T -> Int -> T where T: Zero + One + Add
doc: A whole number of the caller's type, built by repeated addition.
Only for the small constants an algorithm needs — ten for digits, two for
halving. Building a large one this way would be a loop a caller can see.

entries.name: spread
entries.signature: &Array[T] -> T -> T -> T where T: Sub
doc: The difference between the largest and the smallest, or `None` when empty.

entries.name: Sub
doc: A type whose values subtract.

entries.name: sum
doc: Every element added together, or `None` for an empty collection.
`None` rather than the identity because a caller that wants nought for an
empty collection can say so, while one that needs to know it was empty
cannot get that back from a nought.

entries.name: sumOr
entries.signature: &Array[T] -> T -> T where T: Zero + Add
doc: Every element added together, with a caller-supplied value for empty.

entries.name: two
doc: Two, built from the identity rather than written, so it has whatever type
the caller is working in.

entries.name: Zero
doc: A type with an additive identity.
Separate from `Add` because summing an empty collection needs the identity
and nothing else, and a type can have one without the other.

entries.name: allPresent
doc: Every value if every one is present, otherwise nothing.

entries.name: andThen
doc: The value transformed into another option, flattened.

entries.name: dropIf
doc: The value if it is present, otherwise nothing, with the option discarded.
The counterpart to `keepIf`: it drops a value the predicate accepts.

entries.name: exists
doc: Whether a value is present, as a plain question about an owned value.

entries.name: firstPresent
doc: The first present value, or nothing when there is none.

entries.name: flatten
doc: A nested option flattened by one level.

entries.name: fold
doc: The result of transforming the value, or a fallback when there is none.
The arguments are in the order a reader meets them: the value, what to do
with it, and what to do without it.

entries.name: fromArray
doc: The first element of an array, as an option.
The bridge from "a collection that might be empty" to "a value that might be
absent", which is the shape the rest of this module works on.

entries.name: holds
doc: Whether the value is present and the predicate accepts it.

entries.name: isNone
doc: Whether a value is absent.

entries.name: isSome
doc: Whether a value is present.

entries.name: keepIf
doc: The value if it is present and the predicate accepts it.

entries.name: map
doc: The value transformed, if there is one.

entries.name: map2
entries.signature: Option[A] -> Option[B] -> fn(A, B) -> C -> Option[C]
doc: Both values if both are present, combined.

entries.name: mapPresent
doc: Every element transformed, keeping only the results that are present.
One pass rather than a map followed by a filter, which is why it exists.

entries.name: okOr
doc: A present value, or a declared failure when there is none.
This is the bridge from "might be absent" to "explains why", and it is the
only honest way to leave `Option` behind.

entries.name: okOrElse
doc: The value, or the failure a caller names, without discarding either.

entries.name: orElse
doc: The first value if it is present, otherwise the second.

entries.name: present
doc: Every present value, with the absent ones dropped.

entries.name: toArray
doc: The value as an array of nought or one element, which is how a caller
iterates over a maybe-absent value without matching on it.

entries.name: unwrapOr
doc: The value, or a fallback when there is none.
There is no `unwrap` that panics: nothing in `Std` is partial, and a caller
who has no fallback wants `okOr` and the failure that goes with it.

entries.name: unwrapOrElse
doc: The value, or a fallback computed only when there is none.
The fallback is a function so it runs only when it is needed, which matters
when computing it is expensive or can itself fail.

entries.name: when
doc: A value made present when a condition holds.

entries.name: zip
doc: Two options paired, present only when both are.

entries.name: ascending
entries.signature: fn(T, T) -> Std.Order.Ordering -> T -> T -> Bool
doc: A comparison turned into the predicate the sorting functions take.

entries.name: before
doc: An ordering as the "sorts before" predicate the sorting functions take.
A sort needs one answer, not three, and this is the honest conversion:
equivalent values do not sort before one another.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: before
doc: Return true when this value belongs strictly before `other` in the type's order.

entries.name: clamped
doc: A value confined to a range, under its own ordering.

entries.name: compareBool
doc: Two truth values compared, with false before true.

entries.name: compareChar
doc: Two characters compared by scalar value.

entries.name: compareInt
doc: Two whole numbers compared.

entries.name: compareText
doc: Two texts compared by their characters, in scalar order.

entries.name: descending
entries.signature: fn(T, T) -> Std.Order.Ordering -> T -> T -> Bool
doc: A comparison turned into a descending predicate.

entries.name: different
doc: Whether two values differ under their own rule.

entries.name: Eq
doc: A type whose values can be compared for equality.
Structural equality already works for every value; this trait exists so a
generic function can *say* that it compares, and so a type can give equality
a meaning of its own where structure is not it.

entries.name: equivalent
doc: Whether two values are equivalent under the ordering.
Distinct from equality: an ordering may call two values equivalent that a
type's own equality separates, which is why sorting is stable rather than
deduplicating.

entries.name: follows
doc: Whether the first value sorts after the second.

entries.name: Hash
doc: A value's number, for a collection that reaches its entries by one.
The law is one direction only: two values that are equal must hash the
same, and two values that hash the same need not be equal. A collection
built on this settles identity with `Eq` and uses the number only to decide
where to look, so a collision costs a comparison rather than an answer.
This is not a digest. A value hashed here is not hidden, and two runs of a
program are not promised the same number for the same value — a hash map
mixes the result against a value chosen when the process started, so that a
caller who can choose keys cannot choose which of them collide. Anything
that must be secret or repeatable across runs wants `Std.Crypto`.

entries.name: hashed
doc: The number a value hashes to, for a caller writing their own container.

entries.name: isEqual
doc: Whether an ordering says the two values are equivalent.

entries.name: isGreater
doc: Whether an ordering says the second value comes first.

entries.name: isLess
doc: Whether an ordering says the first value comes first.

entries.name: larger
doc: The larger of two values under their own ordering.

entries.name: max
entries.signature: T -> T -> fn(T, T) -> Std.Order.Ordering -> T
doc: The larger of two values under a comparison.

entries.name: min
entries.signature: T -> T -> fn(T, T) -> Std.Order.Ordering -> T
doc: The smaller of two values under a comparison.

entries.name: Ord
doc: A type whose values are ordered.
One method rather than three, because `before` is what a sort needs and the
rest follow from it without a type having to keep them in step.

entries.name: ordering
doc: How one value stands to another, under its own ordering.

entries.name: Ordering
doc: How one value stands to another.

entries.name: precedes
doc: Whether the first value sorts before the second.

entries.name: reverse
doc: The opposite ordering, which is how a descending sort is written from an
ascending comparison.

entries.name: same
doc: Whether two values are equal under their own rule.

entries.name: smaller
doc: The smaller of two values under their own ordering.

entries.name: thenBy
doc: The first ordering unless it is `Equal`, in which case the second.
This is how a comparison on one field falls through to the next.

entries.name: toInt
doc: An ordering as a whole number: -1, 0, or 1.

entries.name: Adjusting
doc: A printer with one decision changed, each answering a printer rather than
taking one apart.
Methods, so that setting several of them reads down the page. As functions
taking the printer first, a printer that differed from the default in three
ways had to be written with each call wrapped in the next, and the decision
a reader looks for first ended up furthest in.

entries.name: bare
doc: A printer that writes nothing between pieces and nothing at the end.
The starting point for building a line from parts written at different
times, where every separator and ending is the caller's to supply.

entries.name: blank
doc: Write the ending alone, which is a blank line for a printer ending in one.

entries.name: endingOf
doc: The ending a printer puts after the pieces.

entries.name: lines
doc: Write each piece on its own line, every line carrying the prefix.

entries.name: prefixOf
doc: The prefix a printer puts on every line.

entries.name: Printer
doc: The decisions about how something is written, held as a value.
`print` takes text and ends the line, and every choice beyond that — what
goes between the pieces, what ends the line, whether it is output or errors,
how far it is indented — has to be assembled at the call site. Assembled
there, those choices cannot be named, cannot be passed to a function, and
are rewritten at every call.
Here they are a value. A printer is built once, given a name, and handed to
whatever does the writing, so a function that reports something takes the
printer to report through rather than deciding the shape itself.
The defaults are the familiar ones: a space between pieces and a newline at
the end.

entries.name: rendered
doc: Exactly the text a write would produce.
Pure, so what a printer does can be checked by comparing values rather than
by capturing output. Every other function here is stated in terms of this
one, which is what makes the configuration testable at all.
With no pieces the answer is the ending alone: a prefix decorates a line's
content, and there is none.

entries.name: separatorOf
doc: The separator a printer puts between pieces.

entries.name: showing
doc: Each value rendered, ready to be handed to `write` beside other pieces.
The bridge for a line built from values of different types: render each one
where its type is known, and write the pieces together.

entries.name: stderr
doc: A printer to the error stream, with the same defaults.

entries.name: stdout
doc: A printer to the output stream: pieces separated by a space, line ended by a
newline.

entries.name: Stream
doc: Which of the two streams a printer writes to.
Output is what a program answers with; Errors is what it says about itself.
A program whose diagnostics go to Output cannot have its answer piped
anywhere, which is the reason the two are separate rather than a flag.

entries.name: streamOf
doc: The stream a printer writes to.

entries.name: text
doc: Write one piece of text.

entries.name: value
doc: Write any value, rendered the way the session prints it.

entries.name: values
doc: Every value in an array, rendered and separated by the printer's separator.

entries.name: write
doc: Write the pieces, and answer what went wrong if anything did.
The ending is written as part of the text rather than by the stream, so a
printer whose ending is empty really does leave the line open.

entries.name: ancestors
doc: Every directory above a path, nearest first.

entries.name: components
doc: The pieces of a path, with the separators removed.
An absolute path keeps its root as its first piece, so the components of a
path and the path itself say the same thing about where it starts.

entries.name: directoryOf
doc: A path without its last piece, or `.` when it has only one.

entries.name: extensionOf
doc: A path's extension, without its dot, or nothing when it has none.

entries.name: fromComponents
doc: The path a sequence of pieces names.

entries.name: hasExtension
doc: Whether a path carries the given extension, compared without regard to case.
File systems disagree about whether a name's case matters, and a caller
asking whether something is a text file means the question either way.

entries.name: isAbsolute
doc: Whether a path names a place from the root rather than from somewhere else.
Two shapes count. One family of operating system writes a leading
separator; the other writes a drive letter, a colon, and a separator, and
also admits the leading separator alone.

entries.name: isHidden
doc: Whether a name is one this machine's shell hides by default.

entries.name: isInside
doc: Whether one path is inside another, once both are normalized.
The question a program asks before writing somewhere a caller named: a
relative path holding `..` can leave the directory it looked like it was
under, and reading the text without normalizing first would not notice.

entries.name: isRelative
doc: Whether a path names a place from wherever the program happens to be.

entries.name: isSeparator
doc: Whether a character ends a piece of a path on this machine.
Every separator this machine accepts, not only the one it writes: a path
that arrived from somewhere else still has to come apart correctly, and one
family of operating system reads the other's separator as its own.

entries.name: join
doc: Two path pieces joined with a separator, without doubling one.

entries.name: joinAll
doc: Every piece joined in order, left to right.
A piece that is itself absolute begins the path again, which is what a
caller joining a root onto a relative fragment means.

entries.name: nameOf
doc: The last piece of a path.

entries.name: normalize
doc: A path with `.` removed and each `..` applied to the piece before it.
This is done by reading the path rather than by asking the file system, so
it does not follow links and does not need the path to exist. Where a link
is involved the two answers differ, and the one that does not touch the
disk is the one a program can rely on before creating anything.
A `..` that would climb past the root stays at the root, because there is
nothing above it; a `..` at the front of a relative path is kept, because
what it climbs to is not known until the path is resolved against
somewhere.

entries.name: parentOf
doc: The directory holding a path, or nothing when the path is a root.
Where `directoryOf` answers `.` for a bare name, this answers nothing for a
path that has nowhere above it, so a caller walking upwards is told when to
stop rather than looping on a root that is its own parent.

entries.name: relativeTo
doc: How to reach a path starting from another, or nothing when it cannot be
reached without knowing where the program is.
A relative path and an absolute one have no answer between them: reaching
one from the other depends on where the program happens to be, and that is
not something reading two strings can tell.

entries.name: resolve
doc: A path resolved against a directory, and normalized.
An absolute path answers for itself, which is what makes this safe to apply
to a path a caller may already have made absolute.

entries.name: separator
doc: The character this machine writes between the pieces of a path.
Asked of the machine rather than written down. It is a slash on one family
of operating system and a backslash on the other, and a path built with the
wrong one is not a path there. A separator spelled into the source would be
a claim about somebody else's computer.

entries.name: splitExtension
doc: A path split into the part before its extension and the extension itself.

entries.name: stemOf
doc: The last piece of a path with its extension removed.

entries.name: withExtension
doc: A path carrying the given extension, replacing any it had.
The dot is supplied here, so a caller writes `txt` rather than `.txt` and
the two spellings cannot produce two different names.

entries.name: withoutExtension
doc: A path with its extension removed.

entries.name: containsKey
doc: Whether a key has a value.

entries.name: countWithPrefix
doc: How many keys begin with the prefix.

entries.name: empty
doc: A trie with nothing in it.

entries.name: filter
doc: Only the entries the predicate accepts.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: &Std.PrefixTrie.PrefixTrie[V] -> fn(A, Str, V) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every entry combined into one value, in key order.

entries.name: fromKeys
doc: A trie of every key in an array, each holding the same value.

entries.name: fromPairs
doc: The trie with every key of an array of pairs.

entries.name: get
doc: The value stored under a key, or `None`.

entries.name: getOr
doc: The value stored under a key, or a fallback.

entries.name: hasPrefix
doc: Whether any key begins with this prefix.
Cheaper than asking for the matches and counting them: it walks the prefix
and stops, without collecting anything beneath.

entries.name: insert
doc: The trie with a key's value added or replaced.
Rebuilt down the key's path, so the nodes the key does not touch are shared
with the trie it came from rather than copied.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the trie holds no keys.

entries.name: keys
doc: Every key, in order.

entries.name: keysWithPrefix
doc: Every key beginning with the prefix, in order.

entries.name: longestPrefixOf
doc: The longest key that is a prefix of the given text, and its value.
What a routing table asks: the most specific rule that covers this path.
Every prefix of the text is on one walk, so the last match found on the way
down is the longest, and nothing needs comparing afterwards.

entries.name: mapValues
doc: Every value transformed, keeping the keys.

entries.name: merge
doc: Two tries combined, with the second's values winning.

entries.name: pairs
doc: Every key and value, in key order.

entries.name: PrefixTrie
doc: Text keys held by their characters, so a prefix can be asked about.
Autocomplete, a routing table, a dictionary, every setting under
`server.tls.`: each of these asks for the entries whose key *starts with*
something. A `Map` can only answer by reading every key and testing it, so
returning five entries costs the whole map. `SortedMap` narrows that to a
range when the keys are text, which is better, and still compares whole keys
at each step.
Here a key is a path through the characters. Walking a prefix touches one
node per character of the prefix — not per entry in the trie — and everything
under that node is the answer. A prefix shared by a thousand keys is walked
once and stored once, which is the other thing this shape buys: the common
stem of `server.tls.cert` and `server.tls.key` exists one time.
The cost is that this holds text keys and nothing else, and that a key with
no shared prefix is a node per character with one child each. It is worth
reaching for when prefixes are asked about and keys overlap, and not
otherwise.

entries.name: remove
doc: The trie with a key's value removed, or unchanged when it has none.
Nodes left holding nothing and leading nowhere are dropped on the way back
up, so removing a key gives back the path it did not share.

entries.name: size
doc: How many keys have values.

entries.name: toMap
doc: The entries as an ordinary map, losing the ability to ask about prefixes.

entries.name: under
doc: The trie of everything under a prefix, with the prefix stripped from the
keys.
The subtree as a trie in its own right, for handing a section of a
configuration or a routing table to something that should not know where it
came from.

entries.name: values
doc: Every value, in the order of its key.

entries.name: withPrefix
doc: Every entry whose key begins with the prefix, in key order.
The question the trie exists for. It walks the prefix once and then collects
what is under it, so what it costs follows the prefix and the number of
matches rather than the size of the trie.

entries.name: chunkSize
doc: How many bytes a read asks for at once.
Large enough that reading a program's whole output does not cost a call
per line, small enough that a caller watching output sees it while it is
still being produced rather than in one piece at the end.

entries.name: closeInput
doc: Tell a program there is no more input.
Not an optimisation: a program reading until its input ends waits forever
if nothing closes it, so this is the difference between a pipeline that
finishes and one that hangs.

entries.name: describe
doc: A finished program described the way an error message should say it.

entries.name: drain
doc: Everything a program writes, read until it stops writing.
The form to reach for when the output is wanted whole but the program is
long-running enough that starting it and waiting would hold its pipe until
it filled.

entries.name: Finished
doc: What a program left behind when it finished.

entries.name: isAvailable
doc: Whether a program can be found and run at all.
Asked by running it with no arguments, so a program that refuses those still
counts as present.

entries.name: isSuccess
doc: Whether a program reported success.

entries.name: lines
doc: Run a program and answer with its output in lines.

entries.name: output
doc: Run a program and answer with its output, treating a non-zero status as a
failure carrying whatever it wrote to its error stream.
The form to reach for when the program is a step that must work.

entries.name: pipe
doc: Feed one program's output into another's input, and answer what comes out.
The shape a shell writes with a vertical bar, and it is written here
because doing it by hand goes wrong in two ways that look like the program
hanging rather than like a mistake.
**Both run at once.** Reading the first program to its end before starting
the second would hold everything it wrote in memory, which is the whole
thing a pipeline exists to avoid — and for a first program that never ends
on its own, the second would never start at all. So a thread moves bytes
across while both are running, and neither waits for the other to finish.
**Each input is closed.** A program reading until its input ends waits
forever if nothing closes it: the first program's at once because nothing
is feeding it, and the second's when the first has stopped writing.

entries.name: read
doc: Read what a program has written since the last read.
`None` means its output has ended, which for a child means it has stopped
writing — usually because it has finished. An empty run of bytes is not
used for that, because a caller could not tell it from a pause.

entries.name: readErrors
doc: The same for what a program wrote to its error stream.
Kept apart from its output rather than merged, because a caller reading
output as data — a pipeline, a parser — must not find a warning in the
middle of it.

entries.name: run
doc: Run a program with arguments and no input, and collect what it produced.
A non-zero status is not a failure of this call: the program ran, and what
it decided is the answer. Only being unable to run it at all fails.

entries.name: start
doc: Start a program and answer without waiting for it.

entries.name: Started
doc: A program that was started and has not been waited for.
`run` above starts a program, waits for it, and answers everything it
wrote. That is right for a step in a script and wrong for three things a
tool has to do: show output while it is still being produced, feed one
program's output into another's input, and stop a program that is taking
too long. Each needs the program to be something the language holds rather
than a call that has already returned.
A started program is named by a token rather than carried as a value,
because a running program is not a value that may be copied: two copies
each believing they owned its output would each read half of it.

entries.name: status
doc: Run a program only for its status.

entries.name: stop
doc: Stop a program, and wait until it is actually gone.
Waiting is what makes this an answer rather than a request: a caller that
stopped a program and moved on would leave it being cleaned up at some
later moment, and anything checking it had stopped would be right only
sometimes.

entries.name: succeeded
doc: Whether a program ran and reported success.

entries.name: trimmedOutput
doc: The output with trailing whitespace removed, which is what a program that
wrote one line meant to say.

entries.name: wait
doc: Wait for a program to finish, and answer the status it left.

entries.name: waitWithin
doc: Wait a bounded time, answering nothing if the program is still running.
What a caller does about a program that is taking too long — wait again,
read more of its output, stop it — is the caller's decision, so this
reports rather than decides.

entries.name: within
doc: Run a program, and stop it if it takes longer than it is allowed.
The bounded form of `run`. A program that ran out of time is answered as
`None` rather than as a failure, because taking too long is a fact about
the program rather than about being unable to start it — and a caller
often wants what it managed to write before it was stopped.

entries.name: withInput
doc: Run a program with arguments and text on its input.

entries.name: write
doc: Write to a program's input.

entries.name: writeText
doc: Write text to a program's input.

entries.name: sortInt
doc: Sorts an array of 64-bit signed integers in linear O(N) time with sign-bit handling on the MSB pass.

entries.name: sortU64
doc: Sorts an array of 64-bit unsigned integers in linear O(N) time using 8-pass LSD radix sort.

entries.name: below
doc: A number below a bound, and the generator that follows.
The bound's own type is the answer's type: a caller drawing indices for a
`UInt8` array gets a `UInt8` back and never leaves its width. The bound is
the type witness, which is what lets one function serve the whole integer
family without a conversion the caller has to undo.
A bound of nought or less answers nought, because there is no number below
it and refusing would make every caller handle a case they can see is
impossible.

entries.name: between
entries.signature: &Std.Random.Generator -> N -> N -> (Std.Random.Generator, N) where N: Integer
doc: A number between two bounds, the lower included and the upper excluded.
Both bounds and the answer share the caller's type.

entries.name: boolean
doc: A truth value, true about half the time.

entries.name: chance
doc: A truth value true with the given chance in a hundred.

entries.name: fromClock
doc: A generator started from the clock.
Not for anything that must be unguessable: the clock is readable by anyone
who can run the program at the same moment. `Std.Crypto` is where a secret
belongs.

entries.name: fromSeed
doc: A generator started from a seed.
A seed of nought is replaced, because the algorithm below has nought as a
fixed point and would answer with it forever.

entries.name: Generator
doc: A generator's state: one number that carries everything it remembers.
A value rather than something hidden, so a program that generates the same
sequence twice does so because it asked to and not by accident. Every
operation answers with the next generator beside its value.

entries.name: identifier
doc: Text of lower-case letters and digits, for an identifier a person will read.

entries.name: next
doc: The next state and the number it produced.
Xorshift with a multiplying finish: three shifts scramble the state and the
multiply spreads the low bits, which the shifts alone leave weak.

entries.name: numbers
entries.signature: &Std.Random.Generator -> Int -> N -> (Std.Random.Generator, Array[N]) where N: Integer
doc: An array of numbers below a bound.

entries.name: pick
doc: One element of an array, or `None` when it is empty.

entries.name: sample
doc: A number of elements drawn without replacement, in a shuffled order.

entries.name: secureBytes
doc: Cryptographically strong bytes from the operating system.
This is separate from `Generator`: deterministic sequences are useful for
tests and simulation, while secrets and protocol nonces must not be
reproducible. Failure is returned and never replaced with clock-seeded
output. Requests above one mebibyte are refused at the runtime boundary.

entries.name: shuffle
doc: The elements in a shuffled order.
Fisher and Yates, walking from the end so every ordering is equally likely —
the naive version that swaps with any position is not.

entries.name: text
doc: Text of a given length drawn from an alphabet.
An empty alphabet answers with empty text, since there is nothing to draw.

entries.name: AcquireResult
doc: Result of an acquisition attempt containing the updated limiter and success status.

entries.name: availableTokens
doc: Returns the number of whole tokens currently available.

entries.name: create
doc: Creates a rate limiter with a refill rate of `ratePerSec` and capacity `burstCapacity`.

entries.name: RateLimiter
doc: A bucket is a value, so where it is kept decides what it limits.
Kept inside one process, a bucket limits what that process admits. Running
the same limit on four instances therefore admits four times the rate,
which is the direction that matters: a limit protecting something
downstream — an API quota, a database, a payment provider — is exceeded by
exactly the factor nobody counted.
A limit that must hold for the service as a whole is counted where the
whole service can see it. A limit that only protects one process from one
caller is correct here as it stands.
Fixed-point token bucket rate limiter with 64-bit integer arithmetic.

entries.name: reset
doc: Resets tokens to maximum burst capacity at the given timestamp.

entries.name: tryAcquire
doc: Attempts to acquire `tokens` at `currentMicros`.

entries.name: capture
doc: One group of a match, by number. Group 0 is the whole match.

entries.name: compile
doc: Compile a pattern, or say where it stopped making sense.
The whole pattern is read here rather than at each use, so a pattern used in
a loop is examined once. A caller holding a `Regex` holds something that is
known to be a pattern; nothing below can fail for a reason of syntax.
A pattern written as a Pudu literal meets one rule of the language first:
`{` and `}` open and close an interpolation, so a counted repetition is
written `"a\{3\}"` and a backslash the pattern should see is written `\\`.
A pattern read from a file or a form needs none of that.

entries.name: escape
doc: Text quoted so a pattern matches it exactly.
What a caller reaches for when part of a pattern comes from somewhere else —
a name typed into a form, a value read from a file — which is otherwise a
way to have someone else's text change what the pattern means.

entries.name: explain
doc: Why a pattern was refused, written for a person to read.

entries.name: find
doc: Where the pattern first matches, or nothing.
A search that gave up answers nothing, which is the safe direction: a filter
admits less rather than more. Use `search` where the difference matters.

entries.name: findAll
doc: Every match, left to right, without overlapping.
A pattern that can match nothing — `a*` against `bbb` — still advances one
character per answer, so this cannot fail to terminate.

entries.name: isExact
doc: Whether the pattern matches the whole subject, and nothing less.

entries.name: isMatch
doc: Whether the pattern matches anywhere in the subject.

entries.name: Match
doc: Where a pattern matched, and what its groups captured.
Positions are character offsets, not byte offsets: a pattern is written
against the characters a reader sees, and answering in bytes would make
every position wrong for any text outside ASCII.

entries.name: Regex
doc: A compiled pattern.
`groups` counts the capturing groups, so a caller knows how many captures a
match can carry without looking at the pattern text again.

entries.name: RegexError
doc: Why a pattern could not be compiled, or a search could not finish.

entries.name: replaceAll
doc: Every match replaced by fixed text.

entries.name: replaceAllWith
doc: Every match replaced by what a function makes of it.
The function is given the match, so a replacement can use what was
captured — which is what a fixed replacement cannot do.

entries.name: replaceFirst
doc: The first match replaced by fixed text.

entries.name: search
doc: Search from each position in turn, reporting a search that gave up.
The leftmost match wins, which is what every other tool answers and what a
reader replacing text expects: a later match that happens to be longer does
not displace an earlier one.

entries.name: split
doc: The subject cut at every match.
A match at the very start or end leaves an empty piece, which is kept: the
number of pieces is then one more than the number of separators, whatever
the subject looked like.

entries.name: stepLimit
doc: How many instructions one search may run before it gives up.
A backtracking search over a pattern like `(a+)+b` can take time
exponential in the length of the subject, and a pattern is often written by
someone other than whoever runs it — a rule in a configuration file, a
filter typed into a form. Without a bound, that is a way to stop a server
with one line of text.
The bound is on work rather than on time so that the same input decides the
same way on every machine. `search` reports reaching it; `find` and
`isMatch` answer "no match", which is the safe direction for a filter.

entries.name: unmatchable
doc: A pattern that matches nothing.
What a caller falls back to when a pattern would not compile and there is
nothing sensible to match instead. Matching nothing is the safe answer: a
filter that admits everything because its rule was malformed is the failure
worth avoiding.

entries.name: all
doc: Every success, or the first failure.
This is how a caller turns many fallible steps into one answer without
deciding, at each step, whether to keep going.

entries.name: andThen
entries.signature: Result[T, E] -> fn(T) -> Result[U, E] -> Result[U, E]
doc: The success transformed into another result, flattened.

entries.name: err
doc: The failure if there was one.

entries.name: errOr
doc: The failure, or a fallback when the operation succeeded.

entries.name: failures
doc: Every failure, with the successes dropped.

entries.name: flatten
doc: A nested result flattened by one level.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: Result[T, E] -> fn(T) -> A -> fn(E) -> A -> A
doc: One of two transformations, whichever side the result holds.
Success comes first, matching the order the cases are written everywhere
else a result is inspected.

entries.name: holds
doc: Whether the operation succeeded and the predicate accepts the value.

entries.name: isErr
doc: Whether the operation failed.

entries.name: isOk
doc: Whether the operation succeeded.

entries.name: map
entries.signature: Result[T, E] -> fn(T) -> U -> Result[U, E]
doc: The success transformed, if there was one.

entries.name: map2
entries.signature: Result[T, E] -> Result[U, E] -> fn(T, U) -> V -> Result[V, E]
doc: Both successes combined, or the first failure.

entries.name: mapErr
entries.signature: Result[T, E] -> fn(E) -> F -> Result[T, F]
doc: The failure transformed, if there was one.
This is how a caller adapts one module's failure vocabulary into its own
without discarding what went wrong.

entries.name: ok
doc: The value if there is one, forgetting why there was not.

entries.name: orElse
entries.signature: Result[T, E] -> Result[T, E] -> Result[T, E]
doc: The first result if it succeeded, otherwise the second.

entries.name: partition
doc: The two sides separated: every success, and every failure.

entries.name: require
doc: A success when a condition holds, and a named failure otherwise.

entries.name: successes
doc: Every success, with the failures dropped.

entries.name: swap
doc: The sides exchanged, so a failure becomes a success and back.

entries.name: toArray
doc: The value as an array of nought or one element.

entries.name: toOption
doc: The success, or `None` when there was a failure, keeping neither.

entries.name: traverse
doc: Every result transformed and collected, stopping at the first failure.

entries.name: unwrapOr
doc: The value, or a fallback when the operation failed.
The failure is discarded, which is why this is the only form that takes one:
a caller who needs to know why should match, or propagate with `?`.

entries.name: unwrapOrElse
doc: The success, or a fallback computed from the failure.

entries.name: capacity
doc: Returns the total power-of-two capacity of the buffer.

entries.name: clear
doc: Clears all elements from the ring buffer.

entries.name: create
doc: Creates a ring buffer whose capacity is rounded up to the nearest power of two (min 4).

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the buffer contains no elements.

entries.name: isFull
doc: Whether the buffer has reached maximum capacity.

entries.name: peek
doc: Peeks at the item at the head of the buffer without removing it.

entries.name: pop
doc: Dequeues an item from the head of the buffer. Returns None if the buffer is empty.

entries.name: PopResult
doc: The result of a successful pop operation containing the updated buffer and the dequeued item.

entries.name: push
doc: Enqueues an item at the tail of the buffer. Returns None if the buffer is full.

entries.name: RingBuffer
doc: A bounded, power-of-two circular FIFO ring buffer with branchless bitmask wrapping.

entries.name: size
doc: Returns the number of elements currently stored.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Returns the elements in FIFO order from head to tail.

entries.name: after
doc: Whether the first version comes after the second.

entries.name: before
doc: Whether the first version comes before the second.
Numbers first, then the prerelease tail. Two rules of the tail are the ones
worth stating: a version with a tail comes *before* the same version
without one, because `1.0.0-rc.1` is a run-up to `1.0.0`; and build
metadata is ignored entirely, because two builds of one version are that
version.

entries.name: best
doc: The newest of a set of versions that may stand where one was asked for.
What a resolver answers: given what is published and what was asked for,
the one to use, or nothing when none of them will do.

entries.name: explain
doc: Why text was refused, written for a person to read.

entries.name: isStable
doc: Whether a version is a release rather than a run-up to one.

entries.name: of
doc: A version with no prerelease or build, which is what most callers want.

entries.name: parse
doc: Read a version.
A leading zero is refused rather than trimmed. `01.0.0` and `1.0.0` would
otherwise be the same version written two ways, and a registry keyed by the
text would hold both.

entries.name: render
doc: A version written back out, which reads back as the same version.

entries.name: same
doc: Whether two versions are the same version, ignoring build metadata.

entries.name: satisfies
doc: Whether the second version may stand where the first was asked for.
The promise the scheme makes, written as a test: a caller that asked for
`1.2.0` accepts `1.4.1`, because a later minor version added things without
taking any away, and refuses `2.0.0`, because a new major version is
allowed to have taken something away.
Below `1.0.0` the promise does not hold — the scheme says so — and the
minor number takes the major's place, which is what every registry does in
practice.
A prerelease satisfies nothing but itself: `1.2.0-rc.1` is not `1.2.0`, and
a caller who wants it names it.

entries.name: Version
doc: A version, in the three numbers and two tails the scheme defines.
The point of the scheme is that the numbers carry a promise: a change to
`patch` fixes something, a change to `minor` adds something that does not
break what was there, and a change to `major` is allowed to break it. A
comparison that read the version as text would order `1.10.0` before
`1.9.0`, which is the one thing this exists to get right.

entries.name: VersionError
doc: Why text does not name a version.

entries.name: all
doc: Whether every member satisfies the predicate. True for an empty set.
Stops at the first member that fails. Counting the members that pass answers
the same question, but it runs the predicate on every one of them and builds
an array to hold the answer — work that cannot change the result.

entries.name: any
doc: Whether any member satisfies the predicate. False for an empty set.
Stops at the first member that passes, for the same reason.

entries.name: at
doc: The member at a position in order, or `None` when there is none.

entries.name: cartesian
doc: Every pairing of one set's members with the other's.

entries.name: contains
doc: Whether a value is a member.

entries.name: containsAll
doc: Whether every given member is in the set.
The question `isSubsetOf` asks, for a caller holding members rather than a
set: one merge of two ordered runs, not one lookup per member.

entries.name: count
doc: How many members the predicate accepts.

entries.name: difference
doc: Every member of the first set that is not in the second.

entries.name: empty
doc: A set with no members.

entries.name: equals
doc: Whether two sets hold the same members.
Sizes are compared first: two sets of different size cannot be equal, and
asking costs nothing next to walking them.

entries.name: filter
doc: Only the members the predicate accepts.

entries.name: find
doc: The first member the predicate accepts, or `None`.

entries.name: fold
doc: Every member combined into one value, in order.

entries.name: fromArray
doc: A set built from an array, with duplicates dropped.

entries.name: greatest
doc: The largest member, or `None` for an empty set.

entries.name: insert
doc: The set with a member added, or unchanged when it is already there.

entries.name: insertAll
doc: Every given member added.
One merge of two ordered runs rather than one insertion per member, which is
the difference between walking the set once and walking it for each item.

entries.name: intersectAll
doc: Every member of every set that is in all of them.
An empty array of sets answers with an empty set, since there is nothing for
a member to be in.

entries.name: intersection
doc: Every member of both sets.

entries.name: intersects
doc: Whether the two sets share any member. The complement of `isDisjointFrom`,
named because a reader asking "do these overlap" should not have to negate.

entries.name: isDisjointFrom
doc: Whether the two sets share no members.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the set has no members.

entries.name: isSubsetOf
doc: Whether every member of the first set is in the second.
One merge of two ordered runs. A size comparison would reject an oversized
candidate without walking either set, but `size` here counts the members it
walks, so asking costs what it saves; that guard belongs with a set that
carries its own count.

entries.name: isSupersetOf
doc: Whether every member of the second set is in the first.
Containment read from the other side, which is all a superset is. Stating it
that way keeps one definition of the rule rather than two that must agree.

entries.name: least
doc: The smallest member, or `None` for an empty set.

entries.name: map
doc: Every member transformed. The result may be smaller when the
transformation sends two members to the same value.

entries.name: partition
doc: The members the predicate accepts, and the members it rejects.

entries.name: remove
doc: The set with a member removed, or unchanged when it is not there.

entries.name: removeAll
doc: Every given member taken away, in one pass for the same reason.

entries.name: removeGreatest
doc: The set without its largest member.

entries.name: removeIf
doc: Only the members the predicate rejects.
The complement of `filter`, so a caller states the condition the way they
think of it rather than negating a predicate at the call site.

entries.name: removeLeast
doc: The set without its smallest member.

entries.name: singleton
doc: A set with one member.

entries.name: size
doc: The number of members.

entries.name: split
doc: The members a comparison places before a value, and those it places after.
The value itself is in neither, which is what makes this a split rather than
a partition. The comparison is supplied because a set is generic and the
language has no ordering bound to write yet.

entries.name: symmetricDifference
doc: Every member of exactly one of the two sets.

entries.name: toArray
doc: Every member, in order.

entries.name: union
doc: Every member of either set.

entries.name: unionAll
doc: Every set combined.

entries.name: array
doc: Every element rendered and joined, wrapped in brackets.

entries.name: bool
doc: A truth value as `true` or `false`.

entries.name: char
doc: A character as itself, without the quotes rendering would add.

entries.name: int
doc: A whole number as text, with a leading minus when it is negative.

entries.name: joined
doc: Every element rendered and joined with a separator, with no brackets.

entries.name: mapLines
doc: Every entry of a map rendered on its own line as `key: value`.

entries.name: option
doc: A value that may be absent, rendered as its content or as a placeholder.

entries.name: pair
doc: A pair rendered as its two sides, separated.

entries.name: render
doc: Any value rendered the way the prompt renders it.
Text renders with its quotes, so a rendered `"1"` is never mistaken for the
number. Use `text` when the quotes are not wanted.

entries.name: result
doc: A result rendered as its success or its failure, with a marker for which.

entries.name: table
doc: A table of rows rendered with each column padded to its widest cell.
The common reason a program renders anything at all, so it is here rather
than written again by every caller.

entries.name: text
doc: Text as itself, and anything else rendered.
This is what a program wants when it is building a message: the quotes on a
rendered string are for a reader inspecting a value, not for a reader of the
message it ends up in.

entries.name: listen
doc: A request from outside the program to stop.
A supervisor — a container runtime, an init system, a terminal — stops a
service by asking rather than by killing: it sends a signal, waits a
configured moment, and only then kills. That moment is the whole
opportunity to finish the requests already in flight, close what is open,
and leave nothing half-written.
A program that cannot hear the request spends the moment unaware and is
killed in the middle of whatever it was doing. Every deployment then drops
live traffic, and nothing in the program says why, because from inside it
looks like being switched off at the wall.
Two signals are heard, and they mean the same thing here: the one a
supervisor sends, and the one a terminal sends when a person presses
Ctrl-C. The signal that cannot be heard by anything, which a supervisor
sends when the waiting is over, is not among them — which is why the
waiting is worth using.
The request is recorded, not acted on. What to do about it belongs to the
program: a server drains its connections, a worker finishes the job in
hand, a batch writes what it has. Acting inside the handler would mean
acting at a moment nothing chose, in the middle of any statement at all.
Begin listening, and say whether listening is possible here.
`false` means this platform has no signals of this kind, so no request will
ever arrive and `requested` will answer `false` forever. A service should
report that rather than announce a graceful shutdown it cannot perform.
Calling this more than once is allowed and does nothing after the first
time, so a component may make sure it is listening without knowing whether
something else already did.

entries.name: requested
doc: Whether a stop has been asked for.
Asking costs a read, so this belongs at the top of a loop, between one unit
of work and the next — which is exactly where a program is able to stop
cleanly. It never becomes false again: a request once made stands, and a
program that resumed after being asked to stop would simply be killed a
moment later.

entries.name: running
doc: Whether the program may keep going.
The same question the other way round, for the loop that reads better as a
condition than as a test and a break.

entries.name: start
doc: Listen, and say whether the program is already being asked to stop.
The two things a service does at startup, in the order it must do them: a
request that arrives between listening and the first check is not missed,
because the flag it sets is the one this reads.

entries.name: key
doc: Constructs a 128-bit key from two 64-bit words.

entries.name: keyFromBytes
doc: Parses a 16-byte array into a 128-bit SipKey in little-endian order.

entries.name: sipHash24
doc: Computes the 64-bit SipHash-2-4 digest for `bytes` using key `k`.

entries.name: sipHash24Int
doc: Computes SipHash-2-4 directly over a 64-bit integer without allocating byte arrays.

entries.name: sipHash24Text
doc: Computes the 64-bit SipHash-2-4 digest directly over a UTF-8 text string.

entries.name: SipKey
doc: A 128-bit key consisting of two 64-bit unsigned words.

entries.name: all
doc: Whether every entry satisfies the predicate. True for an empty map.

entries.name: any
doc: Whether any entry satisfies the predicate. False for an empty map.

entries.name: ceiling
doc: The smallest entry whose key is not less than the given one.

entries.name: containsKey
doc: Whether a key has an entry.

entries.name: empty
doc: An empty map ordered by the given comparison.
The comparison answers whether its first key comes strictly before its
second. Strictly, because two keys that each come before the other are two
keys the order cannot tell apart, and this treats keys it cannot tell apart
as the same key.

entries.name: filter
entries.signature: &Std.SortedMap.SortedMap[K, V] -> fn(K, V) -> Bool -> Std.SortedMap.SortedMap[K, V]
doc: Only the entries the predicate accepts.

entries.name: first
doc: The smallest key and its value, or `None` for an empty map.

entries.name: floor
doc: The largest entry whose key is not greater than the given one.
The question a lookup table asks. A postage rate for a parcel of 900 grams
is the rate for the heaviest bracket at or below 900, and the table has no
entry for 900 itself.

entries.name: fold
entries.signature: &Std.SortedMap.SortedMap[K, V] -> fn(A, K, V) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every entry combined into one value, in key order.

entries.name: fromPairs
entries.signature: &Array[(K, V)] -> fn(K, K) -> Bool -> Std.SortedMap.SortedMap[K, V]
doc: A map built from pairs, ordered by the given comparison.
A later pair replaces an earlier one with the same key.

entries.name: get
doc: The value stored under a key, or `None`.

entries.name: getOr
doc: The value stored under a key, or a fallback.

entries.name: higher
doc: The smallest entry whose key comes strictly after the given one.

entries.name: insert
doc: The map with an entry added, replacing any entry under the same key.

entries.name: insertIfAbsent
doc: An entry added only when its key has none.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the map holds nothing.

entries.name: keys
doc: Every key, in order.

entries.name: last
doc: The largest key and its value, or `None` for an empty map.

entries.name: lower
doc: The largest entry whose key comes strictly before the given one.

entries.name: mapValues
doc: Every value transformed, keeping the keys and their order.

entries.name: merge
doc: Two maps combined, with the second map's entries winning.
The result is ordered by the first map's comparison, which is the one the
caller reached for when they wrote the merge.

entries.name: nth
doc: The entry at a position in key order, or `None` when there is none.
An ordered structure knows which entry is the tenth; a map that only answers
about keys does not, and a caller wanting a median, a percentile, or a page
of results has to read everything out to count.

entries.name: pairs
doc: Every entry as a pair, in key order.

entries.name: range
doc: Every entry whose key is at least `from` and strictly before `until`.
Half-open, so adjacent ranges tile without overlapping and without a gap:
the entries from one boundary to the next, then from that next one onward,
name every entry exactly once.

entries.name: remove
doc: The map with a key's entry removed, or unchanged when there is none.

entries.name: restrictRange
doc: The map with only the entries in the half-open range kept.

entries.name: reversed
doc: The map with its entries in the reverse of its order.
The entries are already sorted, so this reverses them rather than sorting
again, and carries a comparison that agrees with the new arrangement.

entries.name: size
doc: How many entries the map holds.

entries.name: SortedMap
doc: A map whose keys are kept in an order the caller chose, and which can be
asked about a key's neighbours rather than only about the key itself.
`Map` answers one question well: what is stored under this exact key. A rate
table, a version range, a timeline, and a histogram bucket all ask a
different one — what is stored under the largest key not greater than this
— and `Map` can only answer it by reading every entry out and scanning, which
walks the whole map to find something an ordered structure walks a fraction
of. `Map` also orders by the runtime's own order on values, so sorting by a
record's field, by a case-insensitive spelling, or downwards is not
something a caller can ask for at all.
The entries are held in one array, sorted, and reached by halving the range
each step, so a lookup passes a handful of entries rather than all of them.
Insertion and removal move an element into or out of the middle of that
array, which the runtime's arrays do about as cheaply as they are read, so
keeping the order costs no more than looking through it.
The comparison is carried with the entries rather than passed to each call.
A map compared one way on Monday and another way on Tuesday is not a map,
and the operations below would each need the caller to remember which — so
the order is fixed when the map is created and every later operation reads
it from there.

entries.name: upsert
entries.signature: &Std.SortedMap.SortedMap[K, V] -> K -> V -> fn(V) -> V -> Std.SortedMap.SortedMap[K, V]
doc: An entry's value transformed, inserting a starting value when it is absent.

entries.name: values
doc: Every value, in the order of its key.

entries.name: cell
doc: A cell holding a value.

entries.name: Cell
doc: A value more than one thread may read and replace.
The type parameter is carried by the cell rather than by what it holds, so
a cell of numbers and a cell of text are different types and putting the
wrong thing in one is a compile error.

entries.name: count
doc: What a counter holds.

entries.name: counter
doc: A counter starting at a value.

entries.name: Counter
doc: A number more than one thread may add to without losing an addition.

entries.name: Counter
doc: A number more than one thread may add to without losing an addition.

entries.name: get
doc: What a cell holds.

entries.name: increment
doc: Add to a counter and answer what it then holds.
The lock is what makes this safe: reading and writing a cell are two steps,
and two threads adding at once without one would each read the same number
and write the same number, losing an addition.

entries.name: lock
doc: Take a lock, waiting until it is free.

entries.name: mutex
doc: A new lock, not held.

entries.name: Mutex
doc: A lock, held by at most one thread at a time.

entries.name: set
doc: Replace what a cell holds, discarding what it held.

entries.name: swap
doc: Replace what a cell holds and answer what it held, in one step nothing can
come between.
This is the only write, because it is the only one that composes. A read
followed by a write is two steps, and another thread can act between them:
a counter built that way loses additions, and loses them only under the
load that makes the loss hardest to reproduce. A caller that needs to
decide what to write from what is there wants `Counter` or a lock.

entries.name: SyncError
doc: Why a shared value could not be reached.

entries.name: unlock
doc: Release a lock.
Only the thread that acquired a lock may release it. Releasing an unlocked
lock or one held by another thread returns an error.

entries.name: withLock
doc: Run an action with a lock held, and release it after the action returns.
There is no unlock a caller can forget, because there is no unlock. A lock
released only on the normal return path would usually be unsafe. Pudu does
not recover from a runtime abort inside the action; program teardown owns
that path and discards all runtime synchronization resources.

entries.name: absent
doc: A check that holds when an optional value is absent.

entries.name: all
doc: A check that holds when every value satisfies the test.
The first value that does not is what the failure names, because the reader
wants the one that broke rather than the count of those that did not.

entries.name: Check
doc: One check: what it was called, and what it found.

entries.name: closeTo
doc: A check that holds when two exact numbers differ by no more than a
tolerance.
A `Decimal`, because the reason to compare within a tolerance is almost
always a figure a float would already have got wrong.

entries.name: combine
doc: Two reports added together.

entries.name: combineAll
doc: Every report added together.

entries.name: contains
doc: A check that holds when a sequence contains a value.

entries.name: differs
doc: A check that holds when two values differ.

entries.name: each
doc: The same check over a table of cases.
Each case answers its own name and its own check, so a table of twenty
inputs is twenty named checks rather than one check that stops at the first
input it dislikes. A failure names the case, which is what makes a table
worth having: the reader is told which row broke.
The name comes from a function rather than a template with holes in it.
A template would be a small unchecked language inside a string — the same
thing [[Std Fmt]] refuses — and a function is checked, can say anything about
the case, and cannot disagree with the case's type.

entries.name: eachOf
doc: The same check over a table of cases, where each case builds its own check.
For a table whose rows compare two values rather than answering yes or no,
so the failure can say what it expected and found.

entries.name: equals
doc: A check that holds when two values are the same.
Both values are rendered when it fails, which is what makes a failure
readable: the reader is shown the difference rather than told there was one.

entries.name: errored
doc: A check that holds when a result failed.

entries.name: failedOf
doc: How many checks did not.

entries.name: fails
doc: A check that holds exactly when the one it is given does not.
For a failure that is known and expected — a bug being tracked, a limit
being documented. It reports when the inner check starts holding, which is
what turns a known failure into something that tells you when it is fixed
rather than something that stays red until someone looks.

entries.name: failuresOf
doc: What each failing check said.

entries.name: filtered
doc: Only the checks whose name the test accepts, through the whole tree.
Focusing is a function over a suite here rather than a mark on a check,
because a suite is a value: a caller filters the one they have and runs the
result. Nothing is hidden in the suite that a reader of it cannot see.

entries.name: group
doc: A group of groups under a name.

entries.name: held
doc: Whether a check held.

entries.name: lines
doc: A report as lines, the failures first and a summary last.
Failures first because they are what a reader opened the output for, and a
summary last because it is what they check when there are none.

entries.name: names
doc: The names of the checks in a suite and every group beneath it.
For a caller listing what a suite covers without running it.

entries.name: not
doc: A check that holds when the condition does not.

entries.name: Outcome
doc: What one check found.
A check that held carries nothing else; one that did not carries what it
expected and what it found, because that difference is the whole reason to
run a test rather than count one. A suite that answers "thirty-nine of forty"
has told the reader the least useful true thing about their program.

entries.name: passed
doc: Whether every check held.
A suite with nothing in it holds, because it asserted nothing and nothing it
asserted was wrong. A reader who expected checks to run is told by the count,
which is why the count is reported beside this rather than hidden behind it.

entries.name: passedOf
doc: How many checks held.

entries.name: pending
doc: Whether a check was left to be written.

entries.name: pendingOf
doc: How many checks were left to be written.

entries.name: present
doc: A check that holds when an optional value is present, whatever it holds.

entries.name: rendered
doc: The report rendered as one block of text.

entries.name: report
doc: What a suite run by `pudu test` should answer.
How many checks held, or the negative of how many did not. The runner reads
the count to total a run and the sign to decide a verdict, and it can do
neither from a status: a suite that answers zero for success is
indistinguishable from one that checked nothing, and a suite answering one
for failure is indistinguishable from one that checked a single thing.
A suite that both held everything and checked nothing answers zero, which
the runner refuses. That is the intent — a file that has stopped asserting
should be noticed, and it is invisible to every other signal.

entries.name: Report
doc: What running a suite found, counted and with the failures kept.
The failures themselves rather than only their number, so a caller decides
how to present them. Running answers this; nothing here writes anything.

entries.name: run
doc: The report a suite answers, counted through every group beneath it.

entries.name: runIf
doc: A check kept only when a condition holds, and left pending otherwise.
Pending rather than dropped, so a suite that skipped something says so. A
check that vanishes on a condition makes a suite quietly smaller on the
machine where the condition is false.

entries.name: sameElements
doc: A check that holds when two sequences hold the same values, in any order.
For a result whose order is not part of what was promised. Comparing sorted
copies rather than counting, so a repeated value has to be repeated on both
sides.

entries.name: skipIf
doc: A check left pending when a condition holds, and kept otherwise.

entries.name: status
doc: The status a program should leave with, which is zero only when every check
held.
A test runner that always leaves with zero is a test runner nothing can be
built on: the thing reading it cannot tell a pass from a failure.
This is what a program run by `pudu run` should answer, where zero means
nothing went wrong. A suite run by `pudu test` answers `report` instead,
where zero means nothing was checked — the two readers want opposite
things from the same number, so each has its own way to say it.

entries.name: succeeded
doc: A check that holds when a result succeeded.

entries.name: suite
doc: A group of checks under a name.

entries.name: Suite
doc: A named group of checks, and the groups beneath it.
Groups nest because a program's tests do. A report counts through the whole
tree and names a failure by the path that reaches it, so "ordering / sorts"
says where to look without the reader searching for the name.

entries.name: summary
doc: One line saying how many of how many held.

entries.name: that
doc: A check that holds when the condition does.
The plainest form, and the one that cannot say what went wrong: a condition
that is false has no other information in it. Prefer `equals` where there are
two values to compare, because it can say what they were.

entries.name: todo
doc: A check not yet written, carrying why.
Neither a pass nor a failure: it is counted apart so a suite cannot quietly
shrink by deleting what has not been done. A reader is told the number and
the reason rather than being left to notice an absence.

entries.name: total
doc: How many checks ran.
A pending check is not one of them: it was not run, and counting it here
would let a suite look larger for work that has not been done.

entries.name: withCheck
doc: The suite with another check in it.

entries.name: withGroup
doc: The suite with another group beneath it.

entries.name: forAll
entries.signature: Str -> UInt64 -> Int -> fn(Std.Random.Generator) -> (Std.Random.Generator, T) -> fn(T) -> Array[T] -> fn(T) -> Bool -> Std.Test.Check
doc: A check that a property holds for every generated value.
The seed is given rather than taken from a clock, so the check is a pure
function of it and a suite stays a value that can be run twice with the same
answer. A failure reports the seed alongside the counterexample, which is
what makes a random test something a reader can reproduce instead of
something they run again and hope about.
A counterexample is reduced before it is reported, and the report says how
many steps that took — a value shrunk from one that was found is worth more
than either alone, because it shows the property was tested at scale and
still fails at the smallest size.

entries.name: forAllInts
entries.signature: Str -> UInt64 -> Int -> Int -> fn(Int) -> Bool -> Std.Test.Check
doc: A property over whole numbers below a bound.

entries.name: Gen
doc: A source of values of one type.
The same shape `Std.Random` already uses — a generator in, a generator and a
value out — so anything in that module is one of these without adapting, and
a caller writes their own the same way.

entries.name: Shrink
doc: Smaller candidates to try in place of a value that failed.
Ordered nearest-to-simplest first. A shrink that answers the value it was
given, or anything not smaller, would not terminate; the runner bounds its
own work rather than trusting that, but a shrink that grows is still wrong.

entries.name: shrinkArray
doc: Shorter sequences to try: whole chunks removed first, then one element
simplified at a time.
Chunks first because a counterexample is usually short and reaching it by
removing one element at a time takes as many tries as the sequence is long.

entries.name: shrinkInt
doc: Simpler whole numbers to try: zero, then halfway back toward it, and the
positive twin of a negative.
Halving rather than stepping, so a counterexample of a million reduces in
about twenty tries rather than a million.

entries.name: shrinkNothing
doc: Nothing simpler to try, for a value with no smaller form.

entries.name: shrinkText
doc: Shorter text to try, by the same rule sequences use.

entries.name: allChars
doc: Whether every character satisfies the predicate. True for empty text.

entries.name: anyChar
doc: Whether any character satisfies the predicate. False for empty text.

entries.name: at
doc: The character at a position, or `None` when there is none.
The built-in `charAt` fails outside the text; this is the total form.

entries.name: before
doc: Whether one text sorts before another.

entries.name: breakOn
doc: The text before the first occurrence of a needle, and the rest including it.
A miss answers with the whole text and empty text, so a caller that
concatenates the two halves always gets back what it started with.

entries.name: breakOnEnd
doc: The text after the last occurrence of a needle, and everything before it.
Empty text and the whole text when the needle is absent, so a caller that
joins the two halves always gets back what it started with.

entries.name: capitalize
doc: Text with its first character in upper case and the rest unchanged.

entries.name: center
doc: Text padded on both sides to at least `width` characters.

entries.name: chunksOf
doc: The text in pieces of at most `size` characters.

entries.name: commonPrefix
doc: The longest text both begin with, and what remains of each after it.

entries.name: compare
doc: Two texts compared without materialising the comparison as a number.
Answers -1, 0, or 1, which is what a sort needs.

entries.name: cons
doc: A character placed before some text.

entries.name: countChars
doc: How many characters satisfy the predicate.

entries.name: countOccurrences
doc: How many times a needle occurs, without overlapping.

entries.name: countOf
doc: The count this text spells, or nothing.
A count is never below nothing, so a sign is not admitted rather than
admitted and then rejected somewhere later. This is the reading a length, a
port, a quantity, or an index wants: `-1` is not a short length, it is not a
length, and the difference is worth having in the type of the answer rather
than in a check every caller remembers.

entries.name: drop
doc: Every character after the first `skipped`.

entries.name: dropAround
doc: Leading and trailing characters the predicate accepts removed.

entries.name: dropEnd
doc: Every character but the last `skipped`.

entries.name: dropWhile
doc: Everything after the longest leading run the predicate accepts.

entries.name: dropWhileEnd
doc: Trailing characters the predicate accepts removed.

entries.name: equalsIgnoreCase
doc: Whether two texts are equal ignoring case.

entries.name: filterChars
doc: Only the characters the predicate accepts.

entries.name: find
doc: The position of the first occurrence, or `None` when there is none.
The built-in `indexOf` answers `-1`; this is the form a caller can match on
without remembering which sentinel means absent.

entries.name: findChar
doc: The first character the predicate accepts, or `None`.

entries.name: findIndex
doc: The position of the first character the predicate accepts, or `None`.

entries.name: flatMapChars
doc: Every character transformed into text, and that text joined.

entries.name: foldChars
entries.signature: Str -> fn(A, Char) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every character folded into one value, left to right.

entries.name: foldCharsRight
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Char, A) -> A -> A -> A
doc: Every character folded into one value, right to left.

entries.name: fromChars
doc: Text rebuilt from characters.

entries.name: fromLines
doc: Lines joined with newlines between them.

entries.name: fromWords
doc: Words joined with single spaces between them.

entries.name: groupChars
doc: Runs of adjacent equal characters, as text.

entries.name: head
doc: The first character, or `None` for empty text.

entries.name: initial
doc: Everything but the last character.

entries.name: isBlank
doc: Whether text contains only whitespace, or nothing at all.

entries.name: join
doc: Every piece joined with a separator between them.

entries.name: last
doc: The last character, or `None` for empty text.

entries.name: mapChars
doc: Every character transformed.

entries.name: padLeft
doc: Text padded on the left to at least `width` characters.

entries.name: padRight
doc: Text padded on the right to at least `width` characters.

entries.name: partition
doc: The characters the predicate accepts, and the characters it rejects.

entries.name: prefixes
doc: Every prefix, shortest first.

entries.name: rest
doc: Everything but the first character. Empty text answers empty text.

entries.name: scanChars
entries.signature: Str -> fn(A, Char) -> A -> A -> Array[A]
doc: Every running result of folding the characters.

entries.name: singleton
doc: Text of exactly one character.

entries.name: snoc
doc: A character placed after some text.

entries.name: span
doc: The longest leading run the predicate accepts, and the rest.

entries.name: splitAt
doc: The text split at a position.

entries.name: splitNonEmpty
doc: The pieces of text separated by a separator, with empty pieces removed.
The built-in `split` keeps them, because "a,,b" has three fields; this is
the form for splitting on whitespace runs and similar.

entries.name: stripPrefix
doc: Text with a prefix removed, or unchanged when it is not there.

entries.name: stripSuffix
doc: Text with a suffix removed, or unchanged when it is not there.

entries.name: suffixes
doc: Every suffix, longest first.

entries.name: take
doc: The first `wanted` characters, or the whole text when it is shorter.

entries.name: takeEnd
doc: The last `wanted` characters, or the whole text when it is shorter.

entries.name: takeWhile
doc: The longest leading run of characters the predicate accepts.

entries.name: toChars
doc: Every character, as an array.

entries.name: toLines
doc: Every line, with a trailing newline producing no final empty line.

entries.name: toTitle
doc: The title-case form: the first character of each word in upper case.

entries.name: trimEnd
doc: Whitespace removed from the end.

entries.name: trimStart
doc: Whitespace removed from the start.

entries.name: uncons
doc: The first character and the rest, or `None` for empty text.

entries.name: unfold
entries.signature: Int -> S -> fn(S) -> Option[(Char, S)] -> Str
doc: Text grown from a seed until the step answers `None`.
The step count is bounded because a strict language cannot recover from a
step that never stops.

entries.name: unsnoc
doc: Everything but the last character and that character, or `None` when empty.

entries.name: wholeOf
doc: The whole number this text spells, or nothing.
A leading sign is admitted, because a temperature, a balance, and an offset
are all legitimately below nothing. Surrounding space is ignored; anything
else in the text means the text does not spell a number, and answering
nothing is the honest reading — a reader that stopped at the first
character it did not recognise would read "12a" as twelve.

entries.name: words
doc: Every word, splitting on single spaces and discarding empty pieces.

entries.name: zipChars
doc: The characters of two texts paired, stopping at the shorter.

entries.name: append
doc: Append a fragment without copying the accumulated prefix.

entries.name: appendAll
doc: The builder with each of these pieces added, in order.

entries.name: appendLine
doc: Append a line and an explicit LF, including when the line is empty.

entries.name: Builder
doc: Persistent fragments, materialized as text only by `finish`.

entries.name: chunkCount
doc: The number of stored fragments, not a text or byte length.

entries.name: concat
doc: Join builder structures without materializing either text prefix.

entries.name: empty
doc: A builder holding nothing.

entries.name: finish
doc: Allocate the final text by joining every fragment once.

entries.name: isEmpty
doc: Whether the builder holds nothing.

entries.name: andThen
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(A, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(A) -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: One parser after another, the second chosen by the first's value.

entries.name: anyCharacter
doc: Any one character at all.
