entries.name: asText
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[Char], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Str, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The text a parser's characters spell.

entries.name: attempt
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: A parser that consumes nothing when it fails, so `orElse` may try another.

entries.name: between
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(A, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: A parser between two others, keeping only the middle value.

entries.name: bigInteger
doc: One or more digits as an arbitrary-precision whole number.
A leading minus is admitted, so a negative number reads as one value rather
than as an operator a caller has to reassemble. The magnitude is
accumulated in `BigInt` because the text may name a number larger than any
fixed width, and deciding that too early would turn a range question into a
parse failure at the wrong place.

entries.name: blanks
doc: Space and tab, but never a line ending.
A line-oriented format means its line endings, so the whitespace a field
separator may absorb has to stop before them.

entries.name: both
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(A, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[((A, B), Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Two parsers in order, keeping both values.

entries.name: character
doc: One particular character.

entries.name: choice
entries.signature: &Array[fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]] -> Str -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The first parser that succeeds.

entries.name: count
entries.signature: Int -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Exactly this many of a parser, and a problem if the input runs out first.
"Exactly n" is what separates a format from a shape that resembles it. An
ISO date is four digits, a dash, two digits, a dash, two digits; `2026-1-1`
is a different thing wearing the same punctuation, and without this there is
no way to say so.

entries.name: digit
doc: One ASCII decimal digit.

entries.name: endOfInput
doc: The end of the input, consuming nothing.

entries.name: explain
doc: A problem written for a person to read.

entries.name: explainIn
doc: A problem written for a person reading a file, with the line and column.

entries.name: fail
doc: A parser that consumes nothing and always fails.

entries.name: hexadecimal
doc: A whole hexadecimal number, at least one digit.

entries.name: hexDigit
doc: One hexadecimal digit's value.

entries.name: identifier
doc: A run of letters, digits, and underscores beginning with a letter.

entries.name: Input
doc: What a parser has not read yet, and how far it has come.
The text that remains is carried rather than an index into the whole input.
Character access walks from the start of a text, so an index into the whole
input costs what has already been passed, and a scan of a file costs the
square of its length. Reading the front of what remains costs nothing, and
advancing costs only what it moves over, so a scan is linear.
`position` is how many characters have been consumed. It is what a problem
points at, and what tells `orElse` whether a branch committed.

entries.name: integer
doc: One or more digits as an `Int`, the common case of `integerIn`.

entries.name: integerIn
entries.signature: N -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(N, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] where N: Integer
doc: A whole number counted in the caller's own integer type.
The witness carries the type: `integerIn(0u8)` parses a `UInt8`. A number
the text names but the type cannot hold is a **parse problem**, reported at
the position where it was read, rather than a silently wrapped value — which
is the same stance the language takes everywhere else about a number that
does not fit.

entries.name: keepFirst
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(A, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(A, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Two parsers in order, keeping the first's value.

entries.name: keepSecond
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(A, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Two parsers in order, keeping the second's value.

entries.name: label
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Say what a parser wanted, in the reader's words rather than the grammar's.
Replaced only where the parser failed without consuming. A parser that read
part of what it wanted has already told a more precise story, and covering
it with the outer name would lose where the trouble was.

entries.name: lazy
entries.signature: fn() -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: A parser built only when it is run.
A recursive grammar needs this and cannot be written without it: a rule that
mentions itself would build itself forever at the moment it was defined.
Wrapping the mention defers it to the moment it is used, which is when the
input decides whether the recursion happens at all.

entries.name: letter
doc: One ASCII letter.

entries.name: line
doc: One whole line, without its ending, and the ending consumed.

entries.name: lineAndColumn
doc: Where a position falls in the source, counted from one as a reader counts.
A problem carries only how many characters were consumed, because counting
lines on every step would charge every parse for an answer almost no parse
asks for. The count is made here instead, once, when a person is about to
read it.

entries.name: lineEnd
doc: A line ending, or the end of the input.
The last line of a file often has no ending, and refusing it there would
reject a file that every other reader accepts.

entries.name: literal
doc: A particular piece of text.

entries.name: lookAhead
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Succeed exactly where the parser would, consuming nothing.
Deciding which record follows without reading it is this.

entries.name: many
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Nought or more, until the parser stops.
A parser that succeeds without consuming would loop forever, so the loop
stops when the position does not move. That is a defect in the parser it was
given, and stopping is the only thing this can do about it that terminates.

entries.name: manyTill
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(E, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Repeat a parser until the end parser succeeds, keeping what came before.
The end is consumed. A record that runs "until the next header" is this.

entries.name: map
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(A, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(A) -> B -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(B, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: A parser's value transformed.

entries.name: newline
doc: One line ending, however the file writes it.
A file written on one system and read on another carries `\r\n`, and a
parser that only knows `\n` leaves a stray `\r` at the end of every field.
That is the commonest way a format parser is wrong about real data.

entries.name: noneOf
doc: One character not in a set.

entries.name: notFollowedBy
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[((), Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Succeed, consuming nothing, only where the parser would fail.

entries.name: oneOf
doc: One character from a set.

entries.name: option
entries.signature: T -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: A parser's value, or a fallback when it fails without consuming.

entries.name: optional
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Option[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: A parser's value if it succeeds, and nothing if it fails without consuming.

entries.name: orElse
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The first parser, or the second when the first consumed nothing.
A parser that failed *after* consuming input does not fall through: the
input it read told it which branch was meant, and trying another would
report a problem from the wrong one. A caller who wants the fallback anyway
wraps the first in `attempt`.

entries.name: Parser
doc: A parser: a function from input to a step.
A function rather than a type of its own, so every combinator below is an
ordinary function and a caller can write their own without asking this
module's permission.

entries.name: partial
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> Str -> Result[(T, Int), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Run a parser over text, allowing input to remain.

entries.name: Problem
doc: What a parser wanted where it stopped.
The position is kept so a caller can point at the input rather than repeat
it, and the description says what was wanted rather than what was found —
a reader can see what was found.

entries.name: pure
doc: A parser that consumes nothing and answers with a value.

entries.name: quoted
doc: Text between double quotes, with the usual escapes read.

entries.name: restOfLine
doc: Everything up to, but not including, the next line ending.

entries.name: run
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> Str -> Result[T, Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Run a parser over text, requiring it to consume all of it.
Text left over is a problem: a caller that wanted a prefix says so with
`partial`, and one that did not would otherwise accept a truncated parse.

entries.name: satisfy
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Char) -> Bool -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Char, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: One character the predicate accepts.

entries.name: separatedBy
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(S, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Nought or more, separated by another parser.

entries.name: separatedSome
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(S, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: One or more, separated by another parser.

entries.name: sepEndBy
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(S, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Items separated by, and optionally ended by, a separator.
A trailing separator is ordinary in a file: the last line of a list still
ends with a newline.

entries.name: sepEndSome
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(S, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The same, requiring at least one item.

entries.name: signed
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(N, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(N, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] where N: Integer
doc: An optional sign, applied to a number.

entries.name: skipMany
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[((), Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: Run a parser and keep nothing, as many times as it succeeds.

entries.name: skipSome
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[((), Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The same, requiring at least one.

entries.name: some
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Array[T], Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: One or more.

entries.name: space
doc: One space, tab, carriage return, or newline.

entries.name: spaces
doc: Nought or more whitespace, discarded.

entries.name: Step
doc: What one step of parsing produced: a value and what remains, or a problem.

entries.name: symbol
doc: A particular piece of text, with trailing whitespace discarded.

entries.name: takeNotOf
doc: The longest run made of none of these characters, possibly none.

entries.name: takeNotOf1
entries.signature: Str -> Str -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Str, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The same, requiring at least one character.

entries.name: takeOf
doc: The longest run made only of these characters, possibly none.
The set is the vocabulary `oneOf` and `noneOf` already use. A run scanned
against a set costs one step rather than one step for every character it
covers, and a predicate written as a function costs a call each time it is
asked — which is the whole difference between reading a line and reading a
file. `takeWhile` stays for a rule a set cannot state.

entries.name: takeOf1
entries.signature: Str -> Str -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Str, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The same, requiring at least one character.

entries.name: takeWhile
entries.signature: fn(Char) -> Bool -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Str, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The longest run of characters the predicate accepts, as text, possibly none.
Reading a run in one step rather than one character at a time is what keeps
a token from costing an array of characters and a rebuild. A field, a name,
or a line of sequence data is one of these.

entries.name: takeWhile1
entries.signature: Str -> fn(Char) -> Bool -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(Str, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: The same, requiring at least one character.

entries.name: token
entries.signature: fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem] -> fn(Std.Text.Parse.Input) -> Result[(T, Std.Text.Parse.Input), Std.Text.Parse.Problem]
doc: A parser with any whitespace after it discarded, which is what a token is.

entries.name: byteLength
doc: How many bytes the text occupies.

entries.name: fromBytes
doc: Index LF delimiters without decoding or copying the source bytes.

entries.name: fromText
doc: Encode UTF-8 explicitly before building the byte-coordinate index.

entries.name: line
doc: Return a line without its LF or CRLF delimiter, preserving standalone CR.

entries.name: lineCount
doc: How many lines the text has.

entries.name: position
doc: Locate an absolute byte offset. A byte inside UTF-8 still has a byte column.

entries.name: Position
doc: One-based line and byte column; offset is zero-based and may name EOF.

entries.name: slice
doc: Return an exact half-open byte range; invalid bounds never clamp silently.

entries.name: Source
doc: Byte storage and ascending line starts, built together by the constructors.

entries.name: absolute
doc: A duration with its sign removed.

entries.name: add
doc: A duration added to an instant.

entries.name: atUtc
doc: A date and a time of day read as an instant in UTC.

entries.name: between
doc: The time from the first instant to the second, negative when it is behind.

entries.name: currentInstant
doc: The instant this is called at, on the system clock.
The system clock can move backwards when it is adjusted, which is why
measuring a duration uses `elapsed` rather than two of these.

entries.name: Date
doc: A civil date with no instant until a zone is applied.
The distinction from an instant is the one date handling gets wrong most
often: a birthday is a date everywhere, while a meeting is an instant.

entries.name: days
doc: A duration of days, taken as exactly twenty-four hours.
Calendar days are not all that long; a day that crosses a clock change is a
question for `Date`, not for a duration.

entries.name: describe
doc: A duration written the way a person reads one, such as `1h 5m 3s`.
Milliseconds appear only when they are the whole of it, because a duration
long enough to have hours does not need them.

entries.name: Duration
doc: A length of time, as milliseconds.

entries.name: durationMillis
doc: The milliseconds a duration lasts.

entries.name: durationSeconds
doc: The whole seconds a duration lasts.

entries.name: earliest
doc: The earlier of two instants.

entries.name: elapsed
doc: Milliseconds on a clock that only moves forward, for measuring a duration.
Two readings may be subtracted; one alone means nothing.

entries.name: format
doc: An instant rendered in UTC with a pattern.
The pattern vocabulary is the platform's: `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S` and the rest.

entries.name: formatLocal
doc: An instant rendered in the machine's own zone with a pattern.

entries.name: fromRfc3339
doc: An instant read from RFC 3339.

entries.name: hours
doc: A duration of hours.

entries.name: Instant
doc: A point on the system clock, as milliseconds since the start of 1970.
A distinct type from a plain number so a duration and an instant cannot be
confused for one another, which is the mistake date handling is made of.

entries.name: instantOf
doc: An instant built from milliseconds since the start of 1970.

entries.name: isAfter
doc: Whether the first instant is after the second.

entries.name: isBefore
doc: Whether the first instant is before the second.

entries.name: latest
doc: The later of two instants.

entries.name: localOffsetMinutes
doc: The machine's own offset from UTC, in minutes east of it.

entries.name: millis
doc: A duration of milliseconds.

entries.name: minus
doc: One duration taken from another.

entries.name: minutes
doc: A duration of minutes.

entries.name: parse
doc: An instant read with a pattern.

entries.name: parseDate
doc: A date read from `YYYY-MM-DD`.

entries.name: plus
doc: Two durations added.

entries.name: renderDate
doc: A date written as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

entries.name: renderTime
doc: A time of day written as `HH:MM:SS`.

entries.name: scale
doc: A duration multiplied by a whole number.

entries.name: seconds
doc: A duration of seconds.

entries.name: subtract
doc: A duration taken from an instant.

entries.name: TimeOfDay
doc: A time of day with no date and no zone.

entries.name: toDate
doc: An instant rendered as a date in UTC.

entries.name: toMillis
doc: The milliseconds an instant stands at.

entries.name: toRfc3339
doc: An instant rendered as RFC 3339, in UTC.
The form to write when a machine will read it back, because it sorts as text
in the same order it sorts as time.

entries.name: toSeconds
doc: The whole seconds an instant stands at.

entries.name: toTimeOfDay
doc: An instant rendered as a time of day in UTC.

entries.name: civilFromDays
doc: The civil date a day number stands on.

entries.name: dayOfYear
doc: Which day of its year a moment falls on, counting the first as one.

entries.name: daysFromCivil
doc: The day number a civil date stands on, counting from the start of 1970.
The calendar repeats exactly every four hundred years, so a date is placed
by counting whole cycles and then the position within one. That is what
makes this arithmetic rather than a table, and what makes it as correct in
the year 3000 as in this one.

entries.name: daysInMonth
doc: How many days a month holds in a given year.

entries.name: FormatError
doc: Why text does not name a time.

entries.name: fromHttpDate
doc: The moment a message header names.

entries.name: fromRfc3339
doc: The moment interchange text names.
An offset other than zero is applied rather than rejected, so a value that
arrived from a machine keeping local time is read as the moment it names
rather than as the digits it was written with.

entries.name: isLeapYear
doc: Whether a year carries an extra day.

entries.name: millisOf
doc: The moment fields name, as the time at zero offset.
Fields outside their range are carried rather than refused: the thirteenth
month is January of the next year, which is what makes adding a month to
December work without the caller checking first.

entries.name: parse
doc: The moment a pattern reads out of text.
Only the numeric directives and `%b` can be read back, because they are the
ones whose width says where they end. A pattern holding one that cannot be
read is reported rather than guessed at, since a reader that guessed would
answer a moment nobody wrote.

entries.name: Parts
doc: A moment taken apart into the fields a person writes.
The year is the proleptic one, so a year before the calendar was adopted
still counts the same way; a library that changed rules partway through
would make arithmetic across the boundary silently wrong.

entries.name: partsOf
doc: A moment taken apart, as the time at zero offset.

entries.name: render
doc: A moment written by a pattern.
The directives are the ones a reader already knows: `%Y` the year, `%m` the
month, `%d` the day, `%H` `%M` `%S` the time, `%L` the milliseconds, `%j`
the day of the year, `%a` and `%A` the weekday, `%b` and `%B` the month by
name, `%p` the half of the day, `%I` the hour on a twelve-hour clock, `%s`
the seconds since the start of 1970, `%z` the offset, and `%%` a literal
percent. A directive this list does not name is written through unchanged,
so a pattern holding one is still readable rather than silently emptied.

entries.name: renderDuration
doc: A length of time written the way the interchange format writes one.
A duration of no length is written `PT0S` rather than as nothing, because
the format has no empty duration and a reader would refuse one.

entries.name: toHttpDate
doc: A moment written the way a message header carries one.
Always at zero offset and always in English, because the format says so:
this is a value two programs exchange, not one a person is shown.

entries.name: toRfc3339
doc: A moment written in the interchange form, at zero offset.
Written in Pudu rather than asked of the machine, so it can be folded into
a constant and gives the same answer wherever it runs. A rendering that
reached the runtime would make a program's output depend on which machine
compiled it.

entries.name: weekdayOf
doc: Which day of the week a moment falls on, counting Sunday as zero.
The first of January 1970 was a Thursday, which is why the count starts
four days along.

entries.name: civilFromDays
doc: The civil date represented by a Unix-epoch day number.

entries.name: daysFromCivil
doc: A civil date as a day number counted from the start of 1970.

entries.name: daysInMonth
doc: How many days a month holds, or zero for a month outside 1 through 12.

entries.name: floorDiv
doc: Division rounded toward negative infinity.

entries.name: floorMod
doc: The non-negative remainder paired with floor division for a positive divisor.

entries.name: isLeapYear
doc: Whether a proleptic Gregorian year carries an extra day.

entries.name: close
doc: Close a connection, telling the far end it ended.

entries.name: closeWithin
doc: Close a connection, bounding the protocol goodbye before the socket closes.

entries.name: connect
doc: Open a connection and prove the far end is the host that was named.
There is no argument that turns the proof off. A caller given one would
eventually use it to make something work, and what it produces is a
connection encrypted against a stranger rather than private with the
intended server — worse than an unsecured one, because it looks safe.
Trust comes from the machine's own store, so an organisation that has told
its machines about an internal authority is believed without this library
keeping a list that would go stale.

entries.name: connectWithin
doc: Open and verify a connection within the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: foldChunks
entries.signature: &Std.Tls.Secured -> T -> fn(T, Bytes) -> T -> Result[T, Std.Tls.TlsError]
doc: Combine everything the far end sends into one value, holding one chunk at a
time. What it costs does not depend on how much arrives.
The value is threaded rather than gathered by the step function, because a
function literal carries a copy of what it captured: a step assigning to a
variable outside itself would leave that variable as it found it.

entries.name: peerOf
doc: The host this connection was opened against, which is the name that was
proven rather than whatever the certificate happened to offer.

entries.name: receive
doc: The next bytes, or nothing when the far end has finished.
The count asked for is not a promise. The protocol hands over whole
records, so what arrives is what one record held, and a caller needing an
exact number reads until it has them — as over any other connection.

entries.name: receiveAll
doc: Everything the far end sends until it finishes, joined once rather than
once per chunk. Named so its cost is visible.

entries.name: receiveUntil
doc: Read until a marker arrives, answering what came before it and what came
after.
The marker can arrive split across two records, so the buffer is searched
whole each time rather than only the newest piece. The remainder is
answered because it is the start of the next message.

entries.name: receiveWithin
doc: Read the next bytes within the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: Secured
doc: A connection whose contents only the two ends can read.

entries.name: send
doc: Send bytes, and keep sending until every one has gone.

entries.name: sendText
doc: Send text, as its UTF-8 encoding.

entries.name: sendTextWithin
doc: Send text within the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: sendWithin
doc: Send bytes within the stated milliseconds.

entries.name: TlsError
doc: Why a secured connection did not do what it was asked.
A refusal to trust is kept apart from every other kind, because it is the
one a caller must not retry around: a certificate that did not verify is a
connection to somebody, and which somebody is exactly what could not be
established.

entries.name: upgradeWithin
doc: Consume a plain connection at an agreed TLS boundary, verifying the host.
The plain token is retired on both success and failure; do not use it again.

entries.name: withConnection
entries.signature: Str -> Int -> fn(Std.Tls.Secured) -> Result[T, Std.Tls.TlsError] -> Result[T, Std.Tls.TlsError]
doc: Open a connection, hand it to an action, and close it however the action
ended. There is no close a caller can forget, because there is no close.

entries.name: asBoolean
doc: The truth a value holds, or nothing when it is not one.

entries.name: asFractional
doc: The fractional number's text, or nothing when the value is not one.

entries.name: asList
doc: The items a list holds, or nothing when the value is not one.

entries.name: asMoment
doc: The date or time text a value holds, or nothing when it is not one.

entries.name: asTable
doc: The pairings a table holds, or nothing when the value is not one.

entries.name: asText
doc: The text a value holds, or nothing when it is not text.

entries.name: asWhole
doc: The whole number a value holds, or nothing when it is not one.

entries.name: at
doc: The value at a position of a list, or nothing when there is none.

entries.name: encode
doc: A document written as text.
Plain values are written first and tables afterwards, because a key written
after a section header belongs to that section: emitting them in the order
they happen to sit in would silently move a top-level setting inside the
section above it. That is the one mistake a writer of this format can make
that produces a valid file meaning something else.

entries.name: field
doc: The value under a key of a table, or nothing when there is none.

entries.name: keys
doc: The keys a table holds, in the order they were read.

entries.name: path
doc: The value a dotted path names, walking tables one key at a time.
This is how a program reads a setting it knows the shape of. A path through
something that is not a table answers nothing rather than reporting, so a
caller reading an optional section writes one lookup rather than one per
level.

entries.name: renderKey
doc: A key written the way the format writes one.

entries.name: renderValue
doc: A value written the way it appears to the right of a key.
Tables written here are the inline form, because that is the only form a
value in that position may take. `encode` writes a document's own tables as
sections instead, which is what a person reading a configuration expects.

entries.name: table
doc: A table holding nothing.

entries.name: Toml
doc: A configuration value.
Numbers are kept apart the way the format keeps them: a whole number is
`Whole`, and anything with a fractional part or an exponent stays as the
text it was written in. A reader that turned `1` into a floating value
would lose the distinction a caller cares about, and one that turned
`0.1` into a binary float would answer with a number nobody wrote.
A date or time is `Moment`, holding the text unchanged. The format has four
of them and they differ in what they leave unsaid — a local time names no
day, a local date names no instant — so deciding which is which belongs to
the caller, who can hand the text to `Std.Time.Format`.

entries.name: TomlError
doc: Why text does not name a configuration.

entries.name: withField
doc: A table with a pairing added, replacing any already under the key.

entries.name: read
doc: A configuration read from text.
The document is built as it is read rather than collected and assembled
afterwards, because a section header changes where every later key belongs:
a reader that gathered keys first would have to remember which header each
arrived under, which is the same bookkeeping done less directly.

entries.name: readValue
doc: A value, and where it ended.

entries.name: digitsIn
doc: The number a run of digits names in a base, or nothing when a character is
not a digit of it.

entries.name: looksLikeMoment
doc: Whether a word is written the way a date or time is.

entries.name: readEscape
doc: One escape, and where it ended.

entries.name: readKey
doc: One key, bare or quoted.

entries.name: readMultiline
entries.signature: Str -> Int -> Str -> Result[(Str, Int), Std.Toml.TomlError]
doc: Text written across lines, and where it ended.
A line ending straight after the opening marks is dropped, because a writer
who put the opening on its own line meant the text to start on the next.

entries.name: readQuoted
doc: Quoted text, and where it ended.
A literal string, written with an apostrophe, holds exactly its characters:
the format gives it no escapes at all, which is what makes it the right way
to write a path on a machine whose separator is a backslash.

entries.name: readScalar
entries.signature: Str -> Int -> Int -> Result[(Str, Int), Std.Toml.TomlError]
doc: A scalar written as hexadecimal digits.

entries.name: skipBlank
doc: Past whitespace, comments, and line endings.

entries.name: skipInline
doc: Past spaces and tabs only, so a line ending still ends the line.

entries.name: valueOf
doc: What an unquoted word means.
A moment is recognised by its shape rather than parsed, because the format
has four of them and which one a text names is a question `Std.Time.Format`
answers. Keeping the text means nothing is lost deciding here.

entries.name: wholeOf
doc: A whole number, or nothing when the word is not one.
Underscores separate digits for a reader and mean nothing to the value, so
they are dropped first. A leading marker names the base the digits are in.

entries.name: at
doc: The subtree at a path, or `None` when the path leads nowhere.
The inverse of `pathTo`: a path that search answered with always leads back
to the node it found.

entries.name: breadthFirst
doc: Every value, nearest the root first, level by level.

entries.name: childrenOf
doc: The children of a node, in order.

entries.name: contains
doc: Whether any node carries this value.

entries.name: count
doc: How many nodes the test accepts.

entries.name: degree
doc: How many children a node has directly.

entries.name: find
doc: The first value the test accepts, in preorder, or `None`.

entries.name: flatMap
doc: Each value replaced by a whole tree, grafted where the value stood.
The tree a node produces takes that node's place, and the node's own
children follow the produced tree's children beneath the same root. A
transform that answers `leaf` for every value is `map`; one that answers a
deeper tree expands the hierarchy in place, which is what an outline does
when a heading is replaced by the section it names.

entries.name: fold
doc: Every value combined into one, each node before its children.
The flat reading: the values arrive in preorder and the shape is gone. Use
`foldTree` where what a node answers depends on what its children answered.

entries.name: foldTree
doc: Each node combined with what its children answered.
The general fold over this shape, and the one the others are special cases
of: `size` is a fold that adds one to the sum below, `height` is a fold that
adds one to the largest, `preorder` is a fold that prepends. A node is given
its own value and the answers from beneath it, so anything that depends on a
subtree can be written without a second walk.

entries.name: Forest
doc: A sequence of trees standing side by side.
The shape a tree's children already have, named so a function that takes or
answers several trees says which it means. There is no distinguished root
among them, which is what separates a forest from a tree.

entries.name: height
doc: How many nodes lie on the longest path from the root, the root included.
A leaf is 1 rather than 0, so height counts nodes exactly as `size` does and
the two never disagree about whether the root is one of them.

entries.name: isLeaf
doc: Whether a node has nothing beneath it.

entries.name: leaf
doc: A node with nothing beneath it.

entries.name: leaves
doc: Every value that has nothing beneath it, in preorder.

entries.name: levels
doc: The values at each depth, nearest the root first.
Held a level at a time rather than a node at a time: the whole of one depth
is gathered, then its children become the next depth. That keeps the walk to
one pass and needs no queue, and the levels are what a caller usually wanted
anyway — a menu's rows, a chart's ranks.

entries.name: map
doc: Every value transformed, keeping the shape and the order.

entries.name: mapOption
doc: Every value transformed, keeping the shape, where transforming may answer
nothing.
The first absence is the answer, for the reason `mapResult` stops at the
first failure: a tree missing a node is not the tree that was asked for.

entries.name: mapResult
doc: Every value transformed, keeping the shape, where transforming may fail.
The first failure is the answer and the rest is not attempted, because a
tree half-transformed is not a tree anyone asked for. This is written for
`Result` rather than for whatever a caller's failure happens to be: naming
the carrier would need a type parameter that stands for a type constructor,
which the language does not have.

entries.name: mapWithPath
doc: Every value transformed, told where in the tree it sits.
The path is the child index taken at each step from the root, so the root is
given an empty path. A transform that needs to know its depth reads the
path's length; one that needs to know it is a first child reads its last
step.

entries.name: node
doc: A node with the given children, in the order given.

entries.name: outline
doc: The tree drawn as indented lines, each value shown as the session shows it.
Two spaces per level, deepest last within each branch, which is the shape an
outline already has when a person writes one.

entries.name: pathTo
doc: The path to the first node the test accepts, in preorder, or `None`.
The root answers an empty path, which is a found node rather than a missing
one — the difference `Option` is carrying here.

entries.name: postorder
doc: Every value, each node after its children, children in order.
The order a hierarchy has to be taken apart in: nothing is visited until
everything beneath it has been, which is what a total, a deletion, or a
dependency build needs.

entries.name: preorder
doc: Every value, each node before its children, children in order.
The order a reader gives a hierarchy when they read it aloud: the heading,
then everything under the heading, then the next heading.

entries.name: prune
doc: The tree with every node the test rejects removed, along with everything
beneath it, or `None` when the root itself is rejected.
A rejected node takes its subtree with it rather than promoting its
children, because a hierarchy whose middle disappeared would put a node
under a parent it never had.

entries.name: reversed
doc: The tree with its children in the reverse of their order, at every depth.

entries.name: sameShape
doc: Whether two trees hold the same values in the same shape and order.

entries.name: sequenceOption
doc: A tree of options turned into an option holding a tree.

entries.name: sequenceResult
doc: A tree of results turned into a result holding a tree.
Written for `Result` rather than for any carrier, because naming the carrier
once would need a type parameter standing for a type constructor, which the
language does not have.

entries.name: size
doc: How many nodes the tree holds, the root included.

entries.name: trailTo
doc: The values from the root down to the first node the test accepts.
What a breadcrumb trail is: the headings above the thing that was found,
the found one last.

entries.name: Tree
doc: A value with a sequence of trees beneath it.
A syntax tree, an outline, a menu, a reporting line, a dependency view: each
is one thing that holds a number of things of the same kind. Written out
each time, that is a record and a handful of walks, rewritten per program
and subtly different in each — one counts the root, another does not; one
keeps the order children were given, another sorts them.
The shape here settles those questions once. Every node carries a value and
a sequence of children, and a node with no children is not a separate case:
it is a node whose sequence is empty. That is what removes the `Option` a
hand-written hierarchy usually has at every branch.
Children keep the order they were given. A hierarchy where order did not
matter would be a node holding a `Set`, and that is a different structure
with a different type.

entries.name: unfold
doc: A tree grown from a starting value.
`grow` answers what a node holds and the seeds of its children, and the tree
ends where it answers no seeds. Nothing here bounds the growing: a `grow`
that never answers an empty sequence describes an infinite tree and will not
finish, exactly as a `while` whose condition never fails will not. Use
`unfoldTo` where the depth is not known to be finite.

entries.name: unfoldForest
doc: A forest grown from several starting values.
The same growing as `unfold`, for the case where there is no single root —
a set of top-level items, the entries of a directory, the roots of a
dependency graph.

entries.name: unfoldResult
entries.signature: S -> fn(S) -> Result[(T, Array[S]), E] -> Result[Std.Tree.Tree[T], E]
doc: A tree grown from a starting value, where growing may fail.
The first failure is the answer and no further seeds are grown. Growing runs
depth first, in the order `unfold` runs, so the failure reported is the one
a reader following the tree downward would meet first. A breadth-first order
would report a different failure for the same input; it is not offered
because there is no way to abstract over the carrier, so each order would be
a separate named function for each carrier.

entries.name: unfoldTo
doc: A tree grown from a starting value, stopping at a given depth.
The depth counts nodes, so a depth of 1 answers a leaf and a depth of 0 or
less answers a leaf as well: there is always a root, because a tree with no
nodes is not one.

entries.name: valueOf
doc: The value a node carries.

entries.name: withChild
doc: The tree with a child added after the ones already there.

entries.name: zipWith
doc: Two trees combined node by node, as far as both go.
Where one has more children than the other at some node, the extra ones are
dropped: there is nothing to combine them with, and inventing a value would
be answering a question that was not asked.

entries.name: curry
doc: A pair-taking function applied to two arguments, the inverse of `uncurry`.

entries.name: duplicate
doc: A value paired with itself.

entries.name: first
doc: The first member of a pair.

entries.name: mapBoth
doc: Both members transformed by the same function.

entries.name: mapFirst
doc: A pair with its first member transformed.

entries.name: mapSecond
doc: A pair with its second member transformed.

entries.name: of
doc: A pair built from two values.

entries.name: second
doc: The second member of a pair.

entries.name: swap
doc: A pair with its members exchanged.

entries.name: uncurry
doc: A two-argument function applied to a pair, so a function written for two
arguments can be used where a pair is what there is.

entries.name: Answered
doc: Where an event is answered.
A property of the event rather than of the framework. The server-rendered
model that sends every interaction across the network makes a control that
could have answered immediately wait for it; one that answers everything
locally cannot reach what only the server knows. Saying which per event is
the only arrangement that is right in both cases.

entries.name: applied
doc: A screen with the changes applied.
Present so that the two ends can be checked against each other: applying
the changes to the earlier screen must give the later one, and that is a
comparison of values.

entries.name: Change
doc: One difference between two screens.

entries.name: changes
doc: The changes that turn one screen into the other.
Both trees are walked together. A node whose element name changed is
replaced whole rather than reconciled, because an element that became a
different element shares nothing with what it was, and matching its children
anyway produces a tree that is wrong and renders plausibly.

entries.name: childOf
doc: The path to a child of a node.

entries.name: component
entries.signature: S -> fn(S) -> Std.Html.Html -> fn(S, E) -> S -> Std.Ui.Component[S, E]
doc: A component from its three parts.

entries.name: Component
doc: A screen: what is known, what that shows as, and how an event changes it.
The view is a function rather than a stored value, so rendering twice with
the same state gives the same view. That is what makes the difference
between two renders exactly the difference the state made, and it is why a
screen can be checked by comparing values rather than by driving one.

entries.name: depthOf
doc: How deep a path reaches.

entries.name: given
doc: The component after an event.

entries.name: givenAll
doc: The component after several events, in order.

entries.name: holding
doc: The component with its state replaced, for a caller that learned the state
from somewhere other than an event.

entries.name: nodeAt
doc: Where the node a path names is, as the node itself.

entries.name: Path
doc: The path to a node: the indices that reach it from the root.
A value both ends can hold without either keeping a copy of the tree, which
is what lets one end describe a change to a screen the other end is showing.

entries.name: render
doc: What the component currently shows.

entries.name: root
doc: The path to the root.

entries.name: showing
doc: A component that shows something and answers nothing, for a screen that is
only ever read.

entries.name: stateOf
doc: What the component currently knows.

entries.name: unchanged
doc: Whether two screens are the same, which is the question a sender asks
before sending anything at all.

entries.name: within
doc: A component whose view is wrapped in another, so a screen is made of
screens without either knowing about the other's state.

entries.name: Hydration
doc: Wraps a server-rendered component in an isolated progressive island element.

entries.name: island
doc: Wrap server-rendered content as an island, hydrated on arrival.

entries.name: islandWithHydration
doc: Wrap server-rendered content as an island, hydrated as the mode says.

entries.name: microRuntime
doc: The script that mounts islands, allowed by the given nonce.

entries.name: serverActionForm
doc: Builds an accessible HTML form with automatic CSRF token protection.

entries.name: accepts
doc: Whether this session acts on an event by that name.

entries.name: advanced
doc: The session after an event the caller already made sense of.

entries.name: decode
doc: What a viewer sent, read from the message that carried it.
A message that is not an event at all answers nothing rather than a
half-read one, because a half-read event dispatches something the viewer
did not do.

entries.name: discardedCount
doc: How many messages were discarded for naming an event this session does not
accept.
Kept rather than dropped silently, so a page being probed is visible rather
than merely unaffected.

entries.name: encode
doc: An update as the message that carries it.

entries.name: event
doc: An event, for a caller building one directly.

entries.name: Event
doc: What a viewer sent.

entries.name: firstAnswer
doc: The first thing a viewer receives: the whole page.

entries.name: given
doc: The session after a viewer's event, and what to send them.
An event the session does not accept changes nothing and is counted. The
component's update function is written against the events the program has;
handing it arbitrary text would make every component responsible for its
own filtering, differently.

entries.name: markupOf
doc: The page as markup, for the response that carries it.

entries.name: rejoined
doc: What a viewer receives when they rejoin after the connection dropped.
A whole page, never a difference. The state is known; what is unknown is
what the viewer's screen currently shows, and a difference against an
unknown screen produces a wrong screen that renders plausibly.

entries.name: session
doc: A session over a component, accepting the events it names.
The screen is rendered immediately, so what this end believes is on the
viewer's screen is true from the first moment rather than after the first
event.

entries.name: Session
doc: A viewer's screen, held here.
The component is the state and how it renders; `shown` is what this end
last sent, which is the only thing a difference can be computed against.
`accepted` names the events this session will act on — what arrives is text
from whoever is on the other end, and the other end is not necessarily the
page this server rendered.

entries.name: shownBy
doc: What the session currently believes is on the viewer's screen.

entries.name: stateOf
doc: What the component knows.

entries.name: Update
doc: What this end sends after an event.
A whole page or a difference, never both, because they answer different
questions: the first says what the screen is, the second says what it
became.

entries.name: worthSending
doc: Whether an update has anything to send.

entries.name: addQuery
doc: The URL with a query key added, keeping any values it already had.

entries.name: decodeComponent
doc: Text with its percent escapes read back.
An escape that is not two hex digits is left as written, because a caller
showing the result is better served by the original than by a guess.

entries.name: defaultPort
doc: The port a scheme uses when none is written.

entries.name: effectivePort
doc: The port a URL uses, falling back to the one its scheme implies.

entries.name: encodeComponent
doc: Text with the characters a URL cannot carry replaced by percent escapes.
Unreserved characters are left alone, which keeps a readable URL readable.

entries.name: parse
doc: A URL read from text, or what stopped the reader.

entries.name: parseQuery
doc: A query string read into pairs. A key with no `=` carries empty text.

entries.name: queryValue
doc: The first value given for a query key, or `None`.

entries.name: queryValues
doc: Every value given for a query key, in order.

entries.name: removeQuery
doc: The URL with every value for a key removed.

entries.name: render
doc: A URL written back as text, with every part encoded again.

entries.name: renderQuery
doc: Query pairs written back as text.

entries.name: segments
doc: The path in pieces, with empty pieces dropped.

entries.name: Url
doc: The parts of a URL, each already decoded.

entries.name: UrlError
doc: What stopped a URL from being read.

entries.name: withPath
doc: The URL with a different path.

entries.name: equal
doc: Whether two identifiers are the same, compared as the numbers they are.

entries.name: fromBytes
doc: An identifier from sixteen bytes, or the count that was not sixteen.
The version and variant are left as they arrived: bytes that came from
elsewhere describe whatever made them, and rewriting them here would make
this report a version the identifier does not have.

entries.name: fromText
doc: The identifier text names, hyphenated or not.
The hyphens are dropped before the digits are read rather than checked in
place, so the form a program stored without them parses too. Their
positions carry no information the digits do not.

entries.name: isNil
doc: Whether an identifier is the one that names nothing.

entries.name: nil
doc: The identifier whose every byte is zero, which names nothing.
Useful as a stated absence where a caller needs a value of the type and an
`Option` would be carried through code that has nothing to do with it.

entries.name: toBytes
doc: The sixteen bytes an identifier is.

entries.name: toText
doc: The hyphenated lower-case form an identifier is quoted in.

entries.name: Uuid
doc: A universally unique identifier: sixteen bytes, whatever produced them.
Held as bytes rather than as text because that is what it is. Only
rendering turns it into the hyphenated form a person reads, and two
identifiers compare as the numbers they are rather than as the spelling
somebody happened to write them in.

entries.name: UuidError
doc: Why text does not name an identifier.

entries.name: version4
doc: A random identifier.
The generator is passed and answered rather than kept, so a program that
seeded it reproduces the same identifiers. That is what makes a test that
failed on one identifier able to fail on it again.
`Std.Random` is reproducible on purpose and seeded from a readable clock,
which makes these fit for a key in a database and unfit for anything a
person must not be able to guess. A session token wants a random source
this project has not yet reviewed.

entries.name: version7
doc: An identifier that sorts by when it was made.
The first six bytes are the millisecond the clock read, most significant
first, so identifiers made in order compare in order. That is what a
database index wants: a random identifier scatters writes across the whole
index, while one that increases appends to the end of it.
The remaining bytes are random, so two identifiers made in the same
millisecond are still distinct.

entries.name: versionOf
doc: Which scheme produced an identifier, read from the byte that records it.
An identifier that came from elsewhere may say something this list does not
name, so the number is answered rather than a variant per known version.

entries.name: about
entries.signature: Str -> Str -> fn(Map[Str, Str]) -> Bool -> &Map[Str, Str] -> Std.Validate.Report
doc: A rule over the whole form rather than one field, for a check that needs
more than one value.
Written this way rather than by letting a field's rule name another field:
a reference makes the order fields are checked in significant, and then a
report depends on a declaration order nobody thought was load-bearing.

entries.name: also
doc: Two reports together, for a program that checked in more than one place.

entries.name: check
doc: What a whole form's rules found.
Fields are checked in the order they were declared and each field's rules
in the order they were given, so a message assembled from a report reads
the way the form does.

entries.name: checkField
doc: What one field's rules found.
Every rule is applied, not just up to the first that fails: a person
correcting a form wants the whole list, and giving it to them one at a time
turns one correction into as many round trips as there are mistakes.

entries.name: describe
doc: What a rule expects, as text.

entries.name: Failure
doc: One thing that is wrong.
The field and what was expected. Not what was submitted: the sender knows
what they sent, and echoing it is how a message becomes somewhere a script
gets rendered.

entries.name: failureCount
doc: How many things are wrong.

entries.name: failuresFor
doc: What is wrong with one field.

entries.name: faulty
doc: Whether one field is wrong.

entries.name: faultyFields
doc: The fields that are wrong, each once, in the order they first appeared.

entries.name: field
doc: A field and its value.

entries.name: Field
doc: One field and what was submitted for it.

entries.name: nothingWrong
doc: Nothing wrong.

entries.name: passed
doc: Whether a report found nothing.

entries.name: render
doc: What a report says, one line per failure.

entries.name: Report
doc: Everything that is wrong.

entries.name: Rule
doc: What a value must be, and what to say when it is not.
A value, so a form's rules can be listed, compared, and reused between the
place a value arrives and the place it is stored — which is the only way
those two stay in agreement. A rule written twice diverges.

entries.name: satisfied
doc: Whether a value satisfies a rule.

entries.name: valuesOf
doc: The submitted values, by field, for a rule that needs more than one.

entries.name: wholeOf
doc: A value read as a whole number, once the rules said it is one.

entries.name: decodeSleb128
doc: Decodes a signed 64-bit integer from ZigZag LEB128 bytes starting at `offset`.

entries.name: decodeUleb128
doc: Decodes an unsigned 64-bit integer from LEB128 bytes starting at `offset`.

entries.name: encodedLengthUleb128

Matched on the name as written and on the local name alike, so a caller

entries.name: decode
doc: What this reads.
Elements, attributes, text, CDATA, comments, the declaration, and the five
entities the format defines plus numeric character references. That is what
a SOAP envelope, a SAML assertion, an RSS feed, and a configuration file
are made of.
It reads rather than validates: no schema, no DTD, no entity declarations.
A DTD is refused rather than skipped, because a document that declares its
own entities means something this cannot work out, and the way that
normally goes wrong — a declaration that expands to gigabytes, or one that
reads a file off the machine — is not a failure worth having.
Read a document, answering its root element.

entries.name: descendants
doc: Every element anywhere inside this one with a given name.
What a reader of a feed or a report wants: the items, wherever the format
decided to put them.

entries.name: element
doc: An element with a name and nothing else.

entries.name: elements

entries.name: encode

entries.name: escape

entries.name: explain

entries.name: localName

entries.name: Node
doc: A node of a document.
Text and elements are the two kinds a reader acts on. Comments and
processing instructions are dropped while reading rather than carried,
because a document is read here to get at what it says, and a reader that
had to skip them at every level would skip them wrongly somewhere.

entries.name: path

entries.name: prefixOf

entries.name: render

entries.name: Tag
doc: One element: its name, its attributes, and what is inside it.
Namespaces are kept as they were written — `soap:Body` stays that name —
rather than resolved against their declarations. Resolving would mean every
document had to declare correctly before anything could be read from it,
and a service reading one endpoint's replies knows what prefix that
endpoint uses. `localName` is there for the cases where it does not.

entries.name: path
doc: A value reached by a dotted path, which is how a setting is usually named.

entries.name: Yaml
doc: A value a YAML document holds.
The same shape a JSON document has, because that is what YAML documents in
practice hold: the format's own extras — anchors, tags, multiple documents
in one file, the several ways of writing a string — are ways of writing
these, not additional kinds of value.
Numbers are kept apart as whole and fractional for the same reason `Std.Toml`
keeps them apart: a fractional value read into a binary float and written
back is no longer the text that was read, and configuration is compared as
text more often than it is calculated with. A fractional value is carried as
what was written, and a caller that wants a number converts it.
